On the Learning Dynamics of RLVR at the Edge of Competence

Yu Huang   Zixin Wen11footnotemark: 1   Yuejie Chi Yuting Wei22footnotemark: 2   Aarti Singh33footnotemark: 3   Yingbin Liang  Yuxin Chen22footnotemark: 2 ††thanks: Department of Statistics and Data Science, Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania.††thanks: Machine Learning Department, Carnegie Mellon University.††thanks: Department of Statistics and Data Science, Yale University.††thanks: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, The Ohio State University. Note: Equal contribution.
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has been a main driver of recent breakthroughs in large reasoning models. Yet it remains a mystery how rewards based solely on final outcomes can help overcome the long-horizon barrier to extended reasoning. To understand this, we develop a theory of the training dynamics of RL for transformers on compositional reasoning tasks. Our theory characterizes how the effectiveness of RLVR is governed by the smoothness of the difficulty spectrum. When data contains abrupt discontinuities in difficulty, learning undergoes grokking-type phase transitions, producing prolonged plateaus before progress recurs. In contrast, a smooth difficulty spectrum leads to a relay effect: persistent gradient signals on easier problems elevate the model’s capabilities to the point where harder ones become tractable, resulting in steady and continuous improvement. Our theory explains how RLVR can improve performance at the edge of competence, and suggests that appropriately designed data mixtures can yield scalable gains. As a technical contribution, our analysis develops and adapts tools from Fourier analysis on finite groups to our setting. We validate the predicted mechanisms empirically via synthetic experiments.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) such as OpenAI-o3 (OpenAI,, 2024) and DeepSeek (DeepSeek-AI,, 2025) have shown striking performance in complex reasoning tasks. A key enabler of this recent progress is reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) (Shao et al.,, 2024; Lambert et al.,, 2024; Gao et al.,, 2024), which fine-tunes pre-trained base models via reinforcement learning (RL) using automatically verifiable, outcome-based feedback, such as a binary signal indicating whether the final answer is correct.

This raises an immediate question: if RLVR relies on outcome-based feedback only at the end of a reasoning trajectory, how can such sparse reward mechanism drive effective learning on long-horizon problems? As the horizon grows, RL algorithms encounter an inherent search barrier, because useful signals are buried within an exponentially expanding space of trajectories. While recent studies have sought to understand the mechanism of RLVR (Yeo et al.,, 2025; Wu et al.,, 2025; Yue et al.,, 2025; Sun et al.,, 2025; Yuan et al.,, 2025; Wen et al.,, 2025), existing findings often provide mixed and inconclusive results across different tasks and setups. It remains unclear under what conditions the outcome rewards are sufficient to ensure effective RL.

A recent controlled study (Zhang et al.,, 2025) proposed an important insight: RLVR is only effective when training operates near the model’s edge of competence, where the model can solve the problems with non-random accuracy but has not yet mastered them. This suggests a principle for RL data design: one should select problems that are right at the edge of the model’s competence for effective training. Yet, this principle is mainly descriptive: it suggests where RL tends to work, but does not explain why its effectiveness is confined to this regime. This motivates us to ask the following intriguing question:

Why does RLVR primarily improve performance near the edge of the model’s competence?

To address this question, we study a multi-step compositional reasoning setting where solving a problem requires sequential steps, yet feedback is provided only through a terminal reward. Our model is a minimal transformer model (Vaswani et al.,, 2017), which is the backbone architecture of most LLMs. It consists of a softmax-based attention layer followed by a multilayer perceptron (MLP) layer. We fix the MLP to perfectly implement the atomic operation, modeling the regime where the model already possesses the requisite atomic skill and RLVR only needs to learn how to compose these skills (Yuan et al.,, 2025). We study RL training on this task under outcome-based rewards via the standard policy gradient algorithm REINFORCE (Williams,, 1992). Within this setting, we track the learning dynamics of the transformer model and identify the factors that govern progress across increasing horizons, thereby shedding insights on when RLVR can (or cannot) scale to long-horizon compositional reasoning. An overview of our main contributions is provided below.

  1. 1.

    A comparative study between short-horizon learning vs. long-horizon barrier. We first show that with outcome-based rewards, REINFORCE-style policy gradient algorithms provably learn short-horizon compositions. Meanwhile, even if the initial policy achieves non-zero reward, the gradient field at initialization is exponentially flat beyond a critical horizon, indicating an optimization barrier for near-random policies. Alternatively, we show that supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can provably learn beyond the critical horizon by providing intermediate feedback for sequential compositional reasoning.

  2. 2.

    A theory of phase transitions in RLVR on mixed-difficulty data distribution. On an easy-to-hard mixture over horizons, we establish polynomial-time convergence guarantees for outcome-based RL training. We further show that the shape of the difficulty spectrum in the mixture governs the dynamics: when the difficulty spectrum contains discontinuities, the learning process undergoes long plateaus followed by abrupt improvement, exhibiting grokking-like phase transitions (Sun et al.,, 2025); In comparison, a smoother spectrum yields a relay effect that maintains the momentum of reward growth, ensuring steady progress through increasingly harder problems.

  3. 3.

    Novel techniques from Fourier analysis on groups. We introduce a Fourier analysis (Terras,, 1999) framework that transforms the problem of trajectory-level success conditioning into tractable calculations based on Fourier analysis for convolutions of measures. Our new framework allows us to compute the magnitude of policy gradients in long-horizon group composition problems by resorting to the spectral properties of the group representations, which greatly simplifies the estimation of combinatorial event probabilities.

An optimization perspective for RL at the edge of competence.

Together, our results provide an optimization-based explanation for why RLVR is most effective near the edge of the model’s competence. The key mechanism is the relay effect: when the training distribution includes problems slightly above the model’s current capability, successful solutions generated by the policy provide sufficient gradient signal to bootstrap learning on harder ones, sustaining steady reward improvement. However, this relay breaks down when there is a large gap between the model’s current competence and the next level of difficulty. In this regime, the gradient signal is overwhelmed by noise from rare random successes, and training stalls in prolonged plateaus. Thus, RLVR’s effectiveness is governed not merely by whether the model achieves non-zero reward, but by whether the difficulty landscape provides a smooth curriculum for the relay effect to operate. Figure 1 illustrates the contrast between these two regimes.

2 Related Work

Empirical understanding of RLVR mechanisms.

With RLVR’s recent success and apparent scalability, there has been growing interest in understanding its mechanics, sparking an active debate: what does RLVR actually teach base LLMs beyond pre-training? The existing literature provides mixed evidence. Some works characterize RL primarily as a capability refiner or reranker (Yeo et al.,, 2025; Wu et al.,, 2025; Yue et al.,, 2025; Zhao et al.,, 2025), whereas others argue that RL can induce substantial reasoning gains beyond the base model (Sun et al.,, 2025; Yuan et al.,, 2025; Wen et al.,, 2025; Liu et al.,, 2025). Related findings suggest that RLVR can yield notable improvements even from spurious rewards (Shao et al.,, 2025) or extremely limited RL data (e.g., one-shot) (Wang et al., 2025b, ). Complementary evidence further highlights an entropy-based mechanism as a potential driver of such gains (Cui et al.,, 2025; Wang et al., 2025a, ). Recently, Zhang et al., (2025) helps reconcile these views by showing that genuine capability gains arise mainly when there is sufficient headroom beyond pre-training and the RL data are calibrated to the model’s edge of competence.

Theory of RL training for LLM.

The empirical success of RLVR has spurred theoretical studies from various perspectives (Chen et al., 2025a, ; Chen et al., 2025b, ; Zhu et al.,, 2025; Ran-milo et al.,, 2026; Rad et al.,, 2026; Lyu et al.,, 2025; Bu et al.,, 2025; Tsilivis et al.,, 2025; Davis and Recht,, 2025). Of particular relevance are gradient-based analyses with transformer policies (Lyu et al.,, 2025; Bu et al.,, 2025; Ran-milo et al.,, 2026). Bu et al., (2025) formalize the benefits of curriculum-style RL post-training, while Lyu et al., (2025) studies learnability in settings with intermediate supervision. In contrast, we focus on outcome-based RL where no dense feedback is available. A closely related work (Ran-milo et al.,, 2026) shows that outcome-based RL can induce step-by-step reasoning under gradient flow, with asymptotic guarantees under static data conditions. We go beyond this by analyzing realistic gradient dynamics along the full learning trajectory and characterizing phase transitions in both reward and gradient.

Grokking in supervised learning and RL.

Grokking characterizes delayed generalization in supervised learning, where performance stays flat for long periods before improving abruptly (Power et al.,, 2022). Similar plateau-to-jump dynamics also appear in RLVR training (Sun et al.,, 2025), and have been described as “aha moments” in RL systems such as DeepSeek-R1-Zero (DeepSeek-AI,, 2025). Prior work investigates mechanisms behind such phase changes (Nanda et al.,, 2023; Kumar et al.,, 2024; Liu et al., 2022b, ; Tian,, 2025), while our theory on the learning dynamics provides a mechanistic explanation for both the plateau and the subsequent transition in RLVR.

3 Problem Setup

In this section, we formalize our theoretical setting. We first define the compositional reasoning problem, then describe the minimalist transformer architecture and the policy gradient objective used to study RL training dynamics.

3.1 Compositional Reasoning

To study the mechanistic challenges of multi-step reasoning, we consider the state-tracking task (Liu et al., 2022a, ; Merrill et al.,, 2024; Huang et al., 2025b, ). This setting serves as a simple example of compositional reasoning: while each individual step is computationally simple, the task requires the precise sequential composition of LL transitions in order to compute the final result.

Definition 3.1 (LL-step compositional reasoning).

Let 𝒴\mathcal{Y} be a finite set (the state space) and 𝒢\mathcal{G} a finite group, acting on 𝒴\mathcal{Y} via (g,y)↦g⁡(y)(g,y)\mapsto g(y). For any initial state y0∈𝒴y_{0}\in\mathcal{Y} and sequence of transitions g1,…,gL∈𝒢g_{1},\dots,g_{L}\in\mathcal{G}, we can obtain a trajectory yℓ=gℓ​(yℓ−1)y_{\ell}=g_{\ell}(y_{\ell-1}) where ℓ=1,…,L\ell=1,\dots,L. The goal is to predict the final state yLy_{L} given the sequence (y0,g1,…,gL)(y_{0},g_{1},\dots,g_{L}). We define LL as the length or horizon of the problem.

Our analysis requires some structural assumptions on the group action of 𝒢\mathcal{G} on 𝒴\mathcal{Y}, which we present below.

Assumption 3.1 (Group structure and action).

We assume 𝒢\mathcal{G} is a finite non-abelian simple group that acts simply transitively on the set 𝒴\mathcal{Y}, which implies that there is a bijective correspondence between group elements and states, such that |𝒢|=|𝒴|=d|\mathcal{G}|=|\mathcal{Y}|=d. We focus on the asymptotic regime where the state space scales (d→∞d\rightarrow\infty).

Remark 3.1.

Due to the inherent mixing properties of non-abelian groups (Larsen and Shalev,, 2007), different sequences of operations rarely lead to the same state unless the sequences are identical. However, in abelian groups, composing the same operations in different orders yields the same result. Requiring the group to be non-abelian reduces this type of shortcut solutions and leads to cleaner analysis.

Next, we specify the format of reasoning data and the distribution over such instances.

Definition 3.2 (Reasoning problems).

Fix a set of positional identifiers 𝒳⊂ℝd\mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} consisting of mutually orthogonal vectors. We encode each token as a position–symbol pair (x,s)(x,s) where x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} and s∈𝒢∪𝒴s\in\mathcal{G}\cup\mathcal{Y}. A length-LL reasoning instance is ZL=(ZpL,ZaL)Z^{L}=(Z_{p}^{L},Z_{a}^{L}) consisting of:

  • •

    problem description (prompt): a sequence of LL transition tokens:

    ZpL=((xp,1,g1),(xp,2,g2),…,(xp,L,gL)),Z_{p}^{L}=\big((x_{p,1},g_{1}),(x_{p,2},g_{2}),\dots,(x_{p,L},g_{L})\big),

    where xp,ℓ∈𝒳x_{p,\ell}\in\mathcal{X} are distinct and gℓ∈𝒢g_{\ell}\in\mathcal{G}.

  • •

    compositional solution: a sequence of (L+1)(L+1) state tokens:

    ZaL=((xa,0,y0),(xa,1,y1),…,(xa,L,yL)),Z_{a}^{L}=\big((x_{a,0},y_{0}),(x_{a,1},y_{1}),\dots,(x_{a,L},y_{L})\big),

    where yℓ=gℓ​(yℓ−1)y_{\ell}=g_{\ell}(y_{\ell-1}) for all ℓ∈[L]\ell\in[L].

  • •

    position alignment: the prompt and solution positions are related by a fixed unknown permutation 𝔰:𝒳→𝒳\mathfrak{s}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{X} such that xa,ℓ−1=𝔰⁡(xp,ℓ)x_{a,\ell-1}=\mathfrak{s}(x_{p,\ell}), ∀ℓ∈[L]\forall\ell\in[L].

Now we are ready to define the data distribution for the reasoning problems.

Definition 3.3 (Data distribution 𝒟L\mathcal{D}^{L}).

Given a problem length LL, we sample a reasoning instance ZL=(ZpL,ZaL)Z^{L}=(Z_{p}^{L},Z_{a}^{L}) as in Definition 3.2 by the following process:

  1. 1.

    g1,…,gLg_{1},\dots,g_{L} is sampled from 𝒢\mathcal{G} uniformly without replacement;

  2. 2.

    the initial state y0y_{0} is sampled uniformly at random from the set 𝒴\mathcal{Y};

  3. 3.

    we sample distinct prompt identifiers {xp,1,…,xp,L}\{x_{p,1},\dots,x_{p,L}\} uniformly from 𝒳\mathcal{X};

  4. 4.

    Set xa,ℓ−1=𝔰⁡(xp,ℓ),∀ℓ∈{1,…,L}.x_{a,\ell-1}=\mathfrak{s}(x_{p,\ell}),\ \forall\ell\in\{1,\dots,L\}. Additionally, xa,Lx_{a,L} is sampled from 𝒳∖{xa,k}k=0L−1\mathcal{X}\setminus\{x_{a,k}\}_{k=0}^{L-1}.

  5. 5.

    the intermediate states are computed via the group action: yℓ=gℓ​(yℓ−1)y_{\ell}=g_{\ell}(y_{\ell-1}).

We say ZL≜(ZpL,ZaL)Z^{L}\triangleq(Z_{p}^{L},Z_{a}^{L}) is sampled from 𝒟L\mathcal{D}^{L}. Since both {gℓ}ℓ=1L\{g_{\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{L} and {xp,ℓ}ℓ=1L\{x_{p,\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{L} are sampled without replacement, the length is bounded by L≤min⁡{|𝒳|−1,d}L\leq\min\{|\mathcal{X}|-1,d\}.

Assumption 3.2.

We assume |𝒳|=Θ⁡(dcx)|\mathcal{X}|=\Theta(d^{c_{x}}) for some constant cx∈(0.1,1)c_{x}\in(0.1,1). We denote Lmax=|𝒳|−1L_{\max}=|\mathcal{X}|-1 as the unique symbols in 𝒳\mathcal{X} defines the maximum problem length.

Embeddings and tokenizer.

We embed each symbol s∈𝒢∪𝒴s\in\mathcal{G}\cup\mathcal{Y} into ℝ2​d\mathbb{R}^{2d} via an orthonormal map 𝖾𝗆𝖻:𝒢∪𝒴→ℝ2​d\mathsf{emb}:\mathcal{G}\cup\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}^{2d}. With a slight abuse of notation, whenever a symbol ss is used as a model input (or appears inside network computations), we write ss to mean its embedding 𝖾𝗆𝖻⁡(s)∈ℝ2​d\mathsf{emb}(s)\in\mathbb{R}^{2d}. We also fix a bijective tokenizer τ:𝒴→[d]\tau:\mathcal{Y}\to[d] to index states for the next-state prediction objective, so that predicting y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y} is equivalent to predicting the class label τ⁡(y)∈[d]\tau(y)\in[d].

3.2 Transformer Architecture

Building on the reasoning format in Definition 3.2 and 3.3, we now define a simple transformer that predicts the next state in the solution trace given the prompt and the current state token.

Definition 3.4 (One-layer transformer (Vaswani et al.,, 2017)).

We consider a simplified transformer consisting of a single attention module followed by a one-hidden-layer MLP. For a prompt ZpL=((xp,ℓ,gℓ))ℓ=1LZ_{p}^{L}=((x_{p,\ell},g_{\ell}))_{\ell=1}^{L} and the current solution token Za,k=(xa,k,yk)Z_{a,k}=(x_{a,k},y_{k}), the transformer with parameter θ=(W,Q)\theta=(W,Q) outputs an (unnormalized) score vector over the next-state index in [d][d]:

𝖳𝖥θ​(Za,k,ZpL)=𝖬𝖫𝖯W​(𝖠𝗍𝗍𝗇Q​(Za,k,ZpL))∈ℝd.\displaystyle\mathsf{TF}_{\theta}(Z_{a,k},Z_{p}^{L})=\mathsf{MLP}_{W}\left(\mathsf{Attn}_{Q}(Z_{a,k},Z_{p}^{L})\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.
Attention Layer.

The attention module uses the current solution position xa,kx_{a,k} to form weights over the prompt positions {xp,ℓ}ℓ=1L\{x_{p,\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{L}, and returns a vector that aggregates the transition embeddings. Specifically, given a query weight Q∈ℝd×dQ\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}, we define:

𝖠𝗍𝗍𝗇Q​(Za,k,ZpL)≜12​(yk+∑ℓ=1L𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧a,k→p,ℓ​(Za,k,ZpL)⋅gℓ)∈ℝ2​d,\displaystyle\textstyle\mathsf{Attn}_{Q}(Z_{a,k},Z_{p}^{L})\triangleq\frac{1}{2}\Big(y_{k}+\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathbf{Attn}_{a,k\to p,\ell}(Z_{a,k},Z_{p}^{L})\cdot g_{\ell}\Big)\in\mathbb{R}^{2d}, (1)

where the attention weight 𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧a,k→p,ℓ​(Za,k,ZpL)\mathbf{Attn}_{a,k\to p,\ell}(Z_{a,k},Z_{p}^{L}) is obtained by softmax-normalizing the inner products ⟨Q​xa,k,xp,ℓ⟩\langle Qx_{a,k},x_{p,\ell}\rangle:

𝗌𝗈𝖿𝗍𝗆𝖺𝗑​((,,,,,))ℓ.\displaystyle\mathsf{softmax}\Big((\langle Qx_{a,k},x_{p,1}\rangle,\dots,\langle Qx_{a,k},x_{p,L}\rangle)\Big)_{\ell}. (2)

Here for any u∈ℝnu\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, 𝗌𝗈𝖿𝗍𝗆𝖺𝗑​(u)i≜exp⁡(ui)∑j=1nexp⁡(uj)\mathsf{softmax}(u)_{i}\triangleq\frac{\exp(u_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}\exp(u_j)}. In standard transformer architectures, the score typically takes the form ⟨WQ​xa,k,WK​xp,ℓ⟩\langle W_{Q}x_{a,k},W_{K}x_{p,\ell}\rangle rather than using a single matrix QQ. We adopt the equivalent reparameterization commonly used in theoretical works to simplify analysis without changing expressivity (Huang et al.,, 2023; Yang et al.,, 2024; Zhang et al.,, 2024). The factor 12\frac{1}{2} normalizes the combined contribution of the residual term yky_{k} and the attention output.

Remark 3.2.

We compute attention scores using only positional identifiers xa,k,xp,ℓx_{a,k},x_{p,\ell}, a standard simplification in theoretical analyses of transformers (Jelassi et al.,, 2022; Huang et al., 2025a, ; Wen et al.,, 2024; Kim and Suzuki,, 2024; Cheng et al.,, 2026). This decoupling separates token association from reasoning with vector embeddings (states and transitions), which will be carried out by the subsequent MLP computation. Since the attention scores depend only on (xa,k,xp,1:L)(x_{a,k},x_{p,1:L}), we suppress the arguments and write 𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧a,k→p,ℓ\mathbf{Attn}_{a,k\to p,\ell} instead of 𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧a,k→p,ℓ​(Za,k,ZpL)\mathbf{Attn}_{a,k\to p,\ell}(Z_{a,k},Z_{p}^{L}) when clear from context.

MLP layer.

Given the attention output in ℝ2​d\mathbb{R}^{2d}, the MLP maps it to logits in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} for next-state prediction (indexed by τ:𝒴→[d]\tau:\mathcal{Y}\to[d]). With mm hidden units and ReLU activation σ⁡(z)=max⁡{0,z}\sigma(z)=\max\{0,z\}, for each j∈[d]j\in[d],

[𝖬𝖫𝖯W​(Z)]j=∑r=1mσ⁡(⟨Wj,r,Z⟩),Wj,r∈ℝ2​d.\textstyle\bigl[\mathsf{MLP}_{W}(Z)\bigr]_{j}=\sum_{r=1}^{m}\sigma\left(\langle W_{j,r},Z\rangle\right),\quad W_{j,r}\in\mathbb{R}^{2d}.

In our study, we will keep WW fixed and assume the MLP has already acquired pre-trained atomic skills for one-step transitions: given a state yy and a transition gg, it implements the map y↦g⁡(y)y\mapsto g(y). Our focus is therefore on how the attention module supports long-horizon composition once the model already possesses the one-step atomic skill, which has been actively studied in recent RLVR exploration (Yuan et al.,, 2025; Park et al.,, 2025).

Induced next-state distribution.

Given the transformer’s output 𝖳𝖥θ​(Za,k,ZpL)\mathsf{TF}_{\theta}(Z_{a,k},Z_{p}^{L}), we define the induced next-state distribution (policy) by softmax normalization:

πθ​(j∣Za,k,ZpL)≜𝗌𝗈𝖿𝗍𝗆𝖺𝗑​(𝖳𝖥θ​(Za,k,ZpL))j,\displaystyle\pi_{\theta}\big(j\mid Z_{a,k},Z_{p}^{L}\big)\triangleq\mathsf{softmax}\Big(\mathsf{TF}_{\theta}(Z_{a,k},Z_{p}^{L})\Big)_{j}, (3)

where j∈[d]j\in[d]. We equivalently write for y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y}, πθ​(y∣Za,k,ZpL)≜πθ​(τ⁡(y)∣Za,k,ZpL)\pi_{\theta}(y\mid Z_{a,k},Z_{p}^{L})\triangleq\pi_{\theta}(\tau(y)\mid Z_{a,k},Z_{p}^{L}). In our reasoning format, the answer positions (xa,1,…,xa,L)(x_{a,1},\dots,x_{a,L}) are part of the instance and are not predicted; the model only predicts the next state symbol at each step. Starting from the prefix ZL,0=[Za,0,ZpL]Z^{L,0}=[Z_{a,0},Z_{p}^{L}], the induced distribution over the generated state sequence y^L=(y^1,…,y^L)\widehat{y}^{L}=(\widehat{y}_{1},\dots,\widehat{y}_{L}) factorizes autoregressively as

πθ​(y^L∣ZL,0)\displaystyle\pi_{\theta}(\widehat{y}^{L}\mid Z^{L,0}) =∏k=0L−1πθ​(y^k+1∣Z^a,k,ZpL),\displaystyle=\prod_{k=0}^{L-1}\pi_{\theta}(\widehat{y}_{k+1}\mid\widehat{Z}_{a,k},Z_{p}^{L}), (4)
where Z^a,k=(xa,k,y^k),y^0=y0.\displaystyle\widehat{Z}_{a,k}=(x_{a,k},\widehat{y}_{k}),\ \widehat{y}_{0}=y_{0}.

When no confusion arises, we abbreviate the conditioning as (y0,GL)(y_{0},G^{L}), where GL=(g1,…,gL)G^{L}=(g_{1},\dots,g_{L}). Formally, πθL(⋅∣y0,GL)\pi_{\theta}^{L}(\cdot\mid y_{0},G^{L}) still conditions on the full instance ZLZ^{L} (including (xp,1:L,xa,0:L)(x_{p,1:L},x_{a,0:L}) and the fixed permutation π\pi); we simply suppress these positional variables in the notation.

3.3 Pretrained Atomic Skills

We assume that the MLP module provides a pre-trained atomic skill for single-step transitions, and we keep its parameter WW fixed throughout RL training. This allows us to focus on long-horizon composition in the attention dynamics.

For each output index j∈[d]j\in[d] and hidden neuron r∈[m]r\in[m], let us define the feature magnitude

Vj,r​(s)≜⟨Wj,r,s⟩,s∈𝒢∪𝒴.V_{j,r}(s)\triangleq\langle W_{j,r},s\rangle,\qquad s\in\mathcal{G}\cup\mathcal{Y}.

For each pair (g,y)(g,y), let j=τ⁡(g⁡(y))j=\tau(g(y)) be the correct next-state index. Within the neuron group {Wj,r}r∈[m]\{W_{j,r}\}_{r\in[m]}, we designate a unique neuron rg⋅y∈[m]r_{g\cdot y}\in[m] associated with this pair11 1 Our theory can also accommodate the setting where, for each feature, there is a non-overlapping group of neurons r1,r2,…,rk∈[m]r_{1},r_{2},\dots,r_{k}\in[m] that jointly satisfies the same activation pattern (e.g., ∑i=1kσ⁡(Vj,ri​(g)+Vj,ri​(y))=2​B\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sigma\!\big(V_{j,r_{i}}(g)+V_{j,r_{i}}(y)\big)=2B). We do not adopt this setting to simplify the proof.. We define B=CB​log⁡dB=C_{B}\log d with sufficiently large integer CB=O⁡(1)C_{B}=O(1) and σ0=d−1/2\sigma_{0}=d^{-1/2}, and assume the features satisfy:

Vj,rg⋅y​(g)=B,Vj,rg⋅y​(y)=B+2​σ0;\displaystyle V_{j,r_{g\cdot y}}(g)=B,\qquad V_{j,r_{g\cdot y}}(y)=B+2\sigma_{0}; (5a)
Vj,rg⋅y​(s)=−B,∀s∈(𝒢∪𝒴)∖{g,y};\displaystyle V_{j,r_{g\cdot y}}(s)=-B,\quad\forall s\in(\mathcal{G}\cup\mathcal{Y})\setminus\{g,y\}; (5b)
Vj,r​(s)=0,∀r∉{rg⋅y}τ⁡(g⁡(y))=j,∀s∈𝒢∪𝒴.\displaystyle V_{j,r}(s)=0,\quad\forall r\notin\{r_{g\cdot y}\}_{\tau(g(y))=j},\ \forall s\in\mathcal{G}\cup\mathcal{Y}. (5c)
Proposition 3.1.

Under Assumption 3.1-3.2, if the MLP weight WW satisfies (5a)–(5c), given any QQ, for any y0∈𝒴y_{0}\in\mathcal{Y} and G1=(g1)G^{1}=(g_{1}) with g1∈𝒢g_{1}\in\mathcal{G}, we have

πθ​(g1​(y0)|y0,G1)=1−1𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒​d.\displaystyle\pi_{\theta}\big(g_{1}(y_{0})\big|y_{0},G^{1}\big)=1-\frac{1}{\mathsf{poly}d}.

Note that for L=1L=1, the model necessarily attends to the only prompt Zp,1Z_{p,1}. Combined with the residual connection, the MLP receives an aggregate input 12​(g1+y0)\frac{1}{2}(g_{1}+y_{0}). Proposition 3.1 thus guarantees that an MLP equipped with the above structural properties can perfectly implement the atomic group action.

Remark 3.3.

At a high level, when the MLP input contains the correct pair (g,y)(g,y), a unique activated neuron creates a large positive margin for the correct logit, while mismatched symbols produce canceling (negative) contributions. Consequently, the MLP predicts g⁡(y)g(y) with near-perfect accuracy. Prior analysis (Huang et al., 2025b, ) shows that an MLP can learn such a feature-separated structure under supervised training with suitable initialization.

Therefore, we abstract this one-step capability as the following structural assumption on WW.

Assumption 3.3 (Pretrained MLP).

The MLP weight WW is fixed and satisfies (5a)–(5c).

How does the transformer reason sequentially?

Solving the LL-step state-tracking task reduces to carrying out the single-step operation LL times: retrieve the required transition gℓg_{\ell} from the prompt and apply it to the current predicted state y^ℓ−1\widehat{y}_{\ell-1}. Under the above assumption, the pre-trained MLP contains all the atomic skills for one-step transitions, and the remaining challenge is association: the attention layer must find the correct gℓg_{\ell} for the current reasoning step, which shall be learned in RL or SFT.

3.4 Outcome-based RL Objective

We train the induced policy πθ\pi_{\theta} using an outcome-based RL objective with a terminal reward. Given an instance ZL∼𝒟LZ^{L}\sim\mathcal{D}^{L} (equivalently, (y0,GL)(y_{0},G^{L})), we generate a state sequence y^L=(y^1,…,y^L)\widehat{y}^{L}=(\widehat{y}_{1},\dots,\widehat{y}_{L}) with the policy πθ\pi_{\theta} via (4). We assign reward 11 if the final prediction y^L\hat{y}_{L} matches the true final state yLy_{L}, and 00 otherwise:

r(y^L∣y0,GL)≜𝟙{y^L=yL},r(\widehat{y}^{L}\mid y_{0},G^{L})\triangleq\mathds{1}\big\{\widehat{y}_{L}=y_{L}\big\},

where yL=gL(⋯g1(y0))y_{L}=g_{L}(\cdots g_{1}(y_{0})). The RL objective is defined as the expected terminal reward:

𝒥L(θ)=𝔼ZL[𝔼y^L∼πθL(⋅∣y0,GL)[r(y^L∣y0,GL)]].\mathcal{J}_{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{Z^{L}}\Big[\mathbb{E}_{\widehat{y}^{L}\sim\pi_{\theta}^{L}(\cdot\mid y_{0},G^{L})}\big[r(\widehat{y}^{L}\mid y_{0},G^{L})\big]\Big]. (6)

For comparison, we also consider an SFT-type objective (Chu et al.,, 2025). Unlike the outcome-based RL objective, which provides a terminal reward only after the full rollout, this supervised objective uses teacher forcing (Huang et al., 2025b, ; Kim and Suzuki,, 2024; Wen et al.,, 2024; Yang et al.,, 2025): at each step kk we condition on the ground-truth current state yk−1y_{k-1} and apply immediate supervision to the next state yky_{k}. Formally, the SFT objective is written as

𝖫𝗈𝗌𝗌L(θ)≜𝔼ZL[1L∑k=1L−logπθ(yk∣yk−1,GL)].\mathsf{Loss}_{L}(\theta)\triangleq\mathbb{E}_{Z^{L}}\Big[\frac{1}{L}\sum_{k=1}^{L}-\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{k}\mid y_{k-1},G^{L})\Big]. (7)
Learning algorithm.

We consider the REINFORCE algorithm of policy gradient (Williams,, 1992):

∇𝒥L(θ)=𝔼ZL,y^L[r(y^L∣y0,GL)∇logπθL(y^L∣y0,GL)].\displaystyle\nabla\mathcal{J}_{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{Z^{L},\widehat{y}^{L}}\Big[r(\widehat{y}^{L}\mid y_{0},G^{L})\nabla\log\pi_{\theta}^{L}(\widehat{y}^{L}\mid y_{0},G^{L})\Big].

Since we keep WW fixed, we study the gradient ascent on QQ with length-normalized (He et al.,, 2025; Gao et al.,, 2024) policy gradient:

Q(t+1)=Q(t)+η​∇Q𝒥~L​(θ(t)),Q^{(t+1)}=Q^{(t)}+\eta\nabla_{Q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L}\big(\theta^{(t)}\big), (8)

where 𝒥~L​(θ(t))=1L​𝒥L​(θ(t))\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L}\big(\theta^{(t)}\big)=\frac{1}{L}\mathcal{J}_{L}\big(\theta^{(t)}\big) and η>0\eta>0 is the step size. Similarly, we consider the gradient descent for optimizing the SFT loss:

Q(t+1)=Q(t)−η​∇Q𝖫𝗈𝗌𝗌L​(θ(t)).Q^{(t+1)}=Q^{(t)}-\eta\nabla_{Q}\mathsf{Loss}_{L}\big(\theta^{(t)}\big). (9)
Assumption 3.4 (Initialization).

At t=0t=0, Q(0)Q^{(0)} is initialized to be zero matrix 𝟎d×d\mathbf{0}_{d\times d}.

For simplicity, in the following dicsussions, we let A(t)A^{(t)} represent the value of AA at iteration tt, dropping the explicit dependence on the θ(t)\theta^{(t)} or Q(t)Q^{(t)} where the context allows.

4 Learning Short-horizon Compositional Reasoning

In this section, we examine the RL dynamics of transformers on short-horizon compositional tasks. We prove that RL successfully learns compositional reasoning up to a critical horizon, beyond which a flat-gradient barrier emerges due to the nature of sparse, outcome-based rewards. In contrast, we demonstrate that SFT can overcome this limitation by leveraging immediate supervision.

4.1 RL for Short-horizon Compositions

Following the setup in Section 3.3, the transformer 𝖳𝖥θ(0)\mathsf{TF}_{\theta^{(0)}} at initialization executes the atomic one-step skill, yet its attention is approximately uniform at t=0t=0, and thus the induced policy does not reliably implement multi-step compositions. Our first result shows that, for any short horizon L≤CB=O⁡(1)L\leq C_{B}=O(1) (determined by the pretrained MLP parameters), policy-gradient RL learns the LL-step composition and yields the intended attention concentration pattern.

Theorem 4.1 (RL for short-horizon problems).

Suppose Assumption 3.1-3.3 hold and assume that 𝖳𝖥θ(0)\mathsf{TF}_{\theta^{(0)}} is initialized according to Assumption 3.4. Then for any L∈[2,CB]L\in[2,C_{B}], η=1𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(d)\eta=\frac{1}{\mathsf{poly}(d)} and ϵ∈(1logΩ⁡(1)⁡(d),14)\epsilon\in\big(\frac{1}{\log^{\Omega(1)}(d)},\frac{1}{4}\big), the transformer 𝖳𝖥θ(t)\mathsf{TF}_{\theta^{(t)}} trained via (8) on the objective 𝒥L\mathcal{J}_{L} after TL,ϵ=O⁡(Lmax​log⁡(L/ϵ)η​log⁡d⋅d(1−ϵ)​CB−1)T_{L,\epsilon}=O\big(\frac{L_{\max}\log({L}/{\epsilon})}{\eta\log d}\cdot d^{(1-\epsilon)C_{B}-1}\big) iterations attains:

  1. 1.

    Reward optimality: At t=TL,ϵt=T_{L,\epsilon}, the reward is optimal:

    𝒥L(t)≥1−O​(1dCB​(1−ϵ)−1).\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{L}^{(t)}\geq 1-O\quantity(\frac{1}{d^{C_B(1-\epsilon) - 1}}).
  2. 2.

    Optimal short-horizon attention: At t=TL,ϵt=T_{L,\epsilon}, for any ℓ≤L\ell\leq L, we have

    𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧a,ℓ−1→p,ℓ(t)≥1−ϵ.\displaystyle\mathbf{Attn}_{a,\ell-1\to p,\ell}^{(t)}\geq 1-\epsilon.
Significance of the result.

Theorem 4.1 provides the first provable guarantee that a transformer can learn multi-step compositional reasoning via outcome-only policy gradients, when the initialization reliably implements only the atomic one-step skill. The guarantee exhibits an explicit short-horizon regime (L≤CBL\leq C_{B}) in which learning is efficient. Beyond reward optimality, the theorem also identifies the emergent attention concentration pattern, giving a mechanistic characterization of how the learned transformer implements the LL-step composition.

4.2 Critical Horizon and Exponentially Flat Region

When LL exceeds the critical threshold CBC_{B}, the near-uniform attention at initialization yields little useful signal to the MLP. As a consequence, the model behaves almost randomly on long compositional instances. With only outcome-based rewards, the resulting policy-gradient signal becomes exponentially small, even when the model receives a nonzero reward, as shown in the result below.

Proposition 4.1 (Exponentially flat region).

Suppose Assumption 3.1-3.3 hold and assume that the 𝖳𝖥θ(0)\mathsf{TF}_{\theta^{(0)}} is initialized according to Assumption 3.4. Then for any horizon L>2​CBL>2C_{B}, whenever the feature magnitude maxx,x′∈𝒳⁡⟨Q​x,x′⟩≤0.01\max_{x,x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}}\langle Qx,x^{\prime}\rangle\leq 0.01, we have 𝒥L(t)=1d​(1±o⁡(1))\mathcal{J}_{L}^{(t)}=\frac{1}{d}(1\pm o(1)), and

maxx,x′∈𝒳⁡|⟨[∇Q𝒥~L(t)]​x,x′⟩|≤O~​(1Lmax)⋅d−Ω⁡(L).\displaystyle\max_{x,x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}}\bigg|\Big\langle\big[\nabla_{Q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L}^{(t)}\big]x,x^{\prime}\Big\rangle\bigg|\leq\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{1}{L_{\max}}\right)\cdot d^{-\Omega(L)}.
Why is the landscape flat for RL initially?

Conceptually, the initial training horizon controls the concentration of signals the model could learn from each sample, which dilutes due to the O⁡(dL)O(d^{L}) possible trajectories if the model uniformly traverses the actions specified by the problem instance. In this case, outcome-based reward, due to the lack of process feedback, makes it extremely difficult to pick up sufficient signals from policy gradients.

4.3 SFT Succeeds Beyond the Critical Horizon

As a complementary comparison, we consider an SFT objective as in (7). Since SFT provides intermediate supervision rather than only an outcome-based reward, it remains effective even for long-horizon problems.

Theorem 4.2 (SFT provably escapes initial flat region).

Suppose Assumption 3.1-3.3 hold and assume that 𝖳𝖥θ(0)\mathsf{TF}_{\theta^{(0)}} is initialized according to Assumption 3.4. Then for any length 2≤L≤𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀​d2\leq L\leq\mathsf{polylog}d, η=1𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(d)\eta=\frac{1}{\mathsf{poly}(d)} and ϵ∈(1logΩ⁡(1)⁡(d),14)\epsilon\in(\frac{1}{\log^{\Omega(1)}(d)},\frac{1}{4}), the transformer 𝖳𝖥θ(t)\mathsf{TF}_{\theta^{(t)}} trained via (9) on the objective 𝖫𝗈𝗌𝗌L\mathsf{Loss}_{L} for

TL,ϵ=O⁡(Lmax​log⁡(L/ϵ)​d(1−ϵ)​CB−1η​ϵ​log⁡d+Lmax​Lη​log⁡d)\displaystyle T_{L,\epsilon}=O\Big(\frac{L_{\max}\log({L}/{\epsilon})d^{(1-\epsilon)C_{B}-1}}{\eta\epsilon\log d}+\frac{L_{\max}L}{\eta\log d}\Big)

iterations, satisfies:

  1. 1.

    Loss convergence: At t=TL,ϵt=T_{L,\epsilon}, the loss converges:

    𝖫𝗈𝗌𝗌L(t)≤O​(1dCB​(1−ϵ)−1).\displaystyle\mathsf{Loss}_{L}^{(t)}\leq O\quantity(\frac{1}{d^{C_B(1-\epsilon) - 1}}).
  2. 2.

    Optimal attention: For any ℓ≤L\ell\leq L, we shall have

    𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧a,ℓ−1→p,ℓ(t)≥1−ϵ.\displaystyle\mathbf{Attn}_{a,\ell-1\to p,\ell}^{(t)}\geq 1-\epsilon.

Thus Theorem 4.2 has shown that SFT can successfully train the transformer to solve the composition reasoning beyond the critical horizon.

5 Learning Dynamics of Mixed-difficulty RL

In practice, RL datasets typically contain instances of mixed complexity, either due to data collection or explicit curriculum strategies (Zeng et al.,, 2025; Parashar et al.,, 2025; Chen et al., 2025c, ), which can fundamentally alter optimization dynamics. Motivated by this potential, we study policy-gradient training under mixed-difficulty distributions and show that large difficulty gaps lead to grokking-like phase transitions, whereas smoother mixtures yield a relay effect that carries progress from easier to harder horizons.

5.1 Easy-to-Hard Mixture

To model mixed difficulty, we consider a mixture over multiple reasoning horizons. Let us choose difficulty ratio R>1R>1 and fix a starting horizon L1≥2L_{1}\geq 2. Define a set of horizons ℒR={L1,L2,…,LK}\mathcal{L}_{R}=\{L_{1},L_{2},\ldots,L_{K}\} by the recursion:

Lk=min⁡{⌈R​Lk−1⌉,Lmax},2≤k≤K,L_{k}=\min\{\lceil RL_{k-1}\rceil,L_{\max}\},\qquad 2\leq k\leq K,

where K=⌈logR⁡(Lmax/L1)⌉K=\lceil\log_{R}(L_{\max}/L_{1})\rceil so that LK=LmaxL_{K}=L_{\max}. We then define the mixed-difficulty objective as the uniform mixture

𝒥mix,R​(θ)=𝔼L∼Unif⁡(ℒR)​[𝒥L​(θ)].\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{mix},R}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{L\sim\mathrm{Unif}(\mathcal{L}_{R})}\big[\mathcal{J}_{L}(\theta)\big]. (10)

To optimize 𝒥mix,R\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{mix},R}, we consider a length-normalized update:

Q(t+1)=Q(t)+η​∇Q𝒥~mix,R​(θ(t)),\displaystyle Q^{(t+1)}=Q^{(t)}+\eta\nabla_{Q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathrm{mix},R}(\theta^{(t)}), (11)

where ∇Q𝒥~mix,R​(θ)=𝔼L∼Unif⁡(ℒR)​[∇Q𝒥~L​(θ)]\nabla_{Q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathrm{mix},R}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{L\sim\mathrm{Unif}(\mathcal{L}_{R})}[\nabla_{Q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L}(\theta)], and recall 𝒥~L​(θ)=1L​𝒥L​(θ)\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L}\big(\theta\big)=\frac{1}{L}\mathcal{J}_{L}\big(\theta\big).

5.2 Grokking Dynamics Under Large Difficulty Ratios

Intuitively, under mixed-difficulty training, the shorter-horizon tasks are simpler and thus are expected to be solved first, and the learning progress then gradually extends to longer horizons. When the difficulty spectrum is coarse, i.e., when the mixture ratio RR is large, this inter-horizon progression need not be smooth: the policy can spend an extended period with near-zero reward on the next horizon before making visible gains. This plateau-and-jump pattern resembles grokking, an empirical phase-transition phenomenon (Power et al.,, 2022; Sun et al.,, 2025): after an extended period of receiving near-zero reward, the policy abruptly climbs to near-perfect accuracy. Our next theorem formalizes this behavior in the mixed-horizon setting by quantitatively characterizing the length of the plateau and the subsequent transition.

To state the result, we introduce two observable states for each horizon that capture (i) when progress first becomes visible and (ii) when the horizon is essentially solved.

Stopping times for mastery and visible states.

For any horizon Lk∈ℒRL_{k}\in\mathcal{L}_{R}, we say that the task at horizon LkL_{k} has visible return at iteration tt if 𝒥Lk(t)≥0.01\mathcal{J}_{L_{k}}^{(t)}\geq 0.01:

T𝗏𝗂𝗌,k≜min⁡{t:𝒥Lk(t)≥0.01}.T_{\mathsf{vis},k}\triangleq\min\{t:\mathcal{J}_{L_{k}}^{(t)}\geq 0.01\}. (12)

We say the horizon LkL_{k} is mastered at iteration tt if 𝒥Lk(t)≥0.99\mathcal{J}_{L_{k}}^{(t)}\geq 0.99:

T𝗆𝖺𝗌,k≜min⁡{t:𝒥Lk(t)≥0.99}.T_{\mathsf{mas},k}\triangleq\min\{t:\mathcal{J}_{L_{k}}^{(t)}\geq 0.99\}. (13)
Theorem 5.1 (Grokking dynamics).

Let 𝒥mix,R\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{mix},R} be the mixed-difficulty objective with ratio ω⁡(1)≤R≤Lmax2​CB\omega(1)\leq R\leq\frac{L_{\max}}{2C_{B}} and starting horizon L1=CBL_{1}=C_{B}. Under Assumptions 3.1–3.4, consider the RL training process under the length-normalized update (11) with step size η=1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(d)\eta=1/\mathsf{poly}(d). Then for each 1≤k≤K−21\leq k\leq K-2, the following hold:

  1. 1.

    Long inter-difficulty plateaus. Before the next horizon Lk+1L_{k+1} makes noticeable progress (i.e., before it enters the visible-return state), the inter-horizon plateau length satisfies

    T𝗏𝗂𝗌,k+1−T𝗆𝖺𝗌,k=Θ~​(Lmaxη)⋅dCB−1.\displaystyle T_{\mathsf{vis},k+1}-T_{\mathsf{mas},k}=\widetilde{\Theta}\Big(\frac{L_{\max}}{\eta}\Big)\cdot d^{C_{B}-1}. (14)
  2. 2.

    Grokking-like phase transitions. Once Lk+1L_{k+1} enters the visible reward state, it reaches mastery quickly: T𝗆𝖺𝗌,k+1−T𝗏𝗂𝗌,k+1≤O~​(Lmaxη)⋅Lk+1T_{\mathsf{mas},k+1}-T_{\mathsf{vis},k+1}\leq\widetilde{O}\big(\frac{L_{\max}}{\eta}\big)\cdot L_{k+1}.

Theorem 5.1 shows that each transition Lk→Lk+1L_{k}\!\to\!L_{k+1} consists of a long near-zero-return plateau followed by a rapid rise to mastery once return becomes visible. Aggregating these transitions yields a time-to-mastery bound for the longest horizon, in which the total runtime is dominated by the plateaus.

Corollary 5.1.

Under the assumptions of Theorem 5.1, suppose cx<CB−2CB+2c_{x}<\frac{C_{B}-2}{C_{B}+2}, the first time the longest horizon LmaxL_{\max} reaches mastery satisfies

T𝗆𝖺𝗌,K=Θ~​(Lmaxη)⋅dCB−1≜𝒯𝗉𝗅𝖺𝗍.\displaystyle T_{\mathsf{mas},K}=\widetilde{\Theta}\Big(\frac{L_{\max}}{\eta}\Big)\cdot d^{C_{B}-1}\triangleq{\mathcal{T}}_{\mathsf{plat}}. (15)
Why does grokking happen in RL?

For long-horizon tasks, reward can either come from fully correct traces or from rare lucky guesses that reach the correct final answer despite intermediate mistakes. Before the policy can reliably generate correct traces at long horizons, the reward stays near-zero, and the gradient signal mainly consists of those from the lucky guesses, which are random and uninformative. Meanwhile, gradient updates from shorter horizons keep sharpening the internal features long after their rewards have saturated. This hidden progress would eventually lead to a non-trivial success rate at long horizons, resulting in a rapid improvement of rewards within a few iterations. Our analysis in Lemma 6.2 makes this mechanism explicit by tracking how the hidden feature sharpening translates into the long-horizon policy improvement.

5.3 Relay Dynamics under Moderate Difficulty Ratios

The grokking dynamics above highlight that when the mixture is highly discontinuous, training can stall at each new horizon: even after LkL_{k} is mastered, the next horizon Lk+1L_{k+1} may remain in the near-zero-reward regime for a long plateau before its reward becomes visible. We now show that, when the difficulty spectrum is sufficiently smooth (RR is a moderate constant), training exhibits a relay effect: progress on easier horizons continuously supports the next harder horizon, preventing prolonged plateaus.

Our next theorem formalizes the relay regime by providing an upper bound on T𝗏𝗂𝗌,k+1−T𝗆𝖺𝗌,kT_{\mathsf{vis},k+1}-T_{\mathsf{mas},k}, which will be significantly smaller than the long plateaus in the large difficulty regime.

Theorem 5.2 (Relay dynamics).

Let 𝒥mix,R\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{mix},R} be the mixed-difficulty objective with ratio 2≤R≤O⁡(1)2\leq R\leq O(1) and starting horizon L1=CBL_{1}=C_{B}. Under Assumptions 3.1–3.4, consider the RL training process under the length-normalized update (11) with step size η=1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒⁡(d)\eta=1/\mathsf{poly}(d). Then for each k≤K−2k\leq K-2, before Lk+1L_{k+1} enters the visible-return state, the inter-horizon plateau length satisfies

T𝗏𝗂𝗌,k+1−T𝗆𝖺𝗌,k≤O~​(Lmaxη)⋅d(1−CBCB+R)​CB−1.T_{\mathsf{vis},k+1}-T_{\mathsf{mas},k}\leq\widetilde{O}\Big(\frac{L_{\max}}{\eta}\Big)\cdot d^{(1-\frac{C_{B}}{C_{B}+R})C_{B}-1}.

Moreover, once Lk+1L_{k+1} enters the visible-return state, it reaches mastery rapidly: T𝗆𝖺𝗌,k+1−T𝗏𝗂𝗌,k+1≤O~​(Lmaxη)⋅Lk+1.T_{\mathsf{mas},k+1}-T_{\mathsf{vis},k+1}\leq\widetilde{O}\Big(\frac{L_{\max}}{\eta}\Big)\cdot L_{k+1}.

Compared with the grokking regime, Theorem 5.2 shortens each inter-horizon plateau by a factor dΘ⁡(1)d^{\Theta(1)}. Although a smoother spectrum induces more horizons, we have K=O⁡(logR⁡(Lmax/CB))≤O⁡(log⁡d)K=O(\log_{R}(L_{\max}/C_{B}))\leq O(\log d). Therefore, the total time to reach mastery at the longest horizon is still governed by the (much shorter) relay plateaus, leading to a strictly faster overall convergence bound than in the large-ratio regime.

Corollary 5.2.

Under the assumptions of Theorem 5.2, suppose cx<CB−2CB+2c_{x}<\frac{C_{B}-2}{C_{B}+2}, the first time the longest horizon LmaxL_{\max} reaches mastery satisfies T𝗆𝖺𝗌,K≤𝒯𝗋𝖾𝗅𝖺𝗒T_{\mathsf{mas},K}\leq{\mathcal{T}}_{\mathsf{relay}}, where

𝒯𝗋𝖾𝗅𝖺𝗒≤O~​(Lmaxη)⋅d(1−CBCB+R)​CB−1≤O~​(d−CB2CB+R)​𝒯𝗉𝗅𝖺𝗍.{\mathcal{T}}_{\mathsf{relay}}\leq\widetilde{O}\Big(\frac{L_{\max}}{\eta}\Big)\cdot d^{(1-\frac{C_{B}}{C_{B}+R})C_{B}-1}\leq\widetilde{O}\Big(d^{-\frac{C_{B}^{2}}{C_{B}+R}}\Big)\,{\mathcal{T}}_{\mathsf{plat}}.
Relay learning near the edge of competence.

Theorem 5.1 and Theorem 5.2 show that the mixed-horizon dynamics are governed by how quickly training can move from mastering LkL_{k} to making visible progress on Lk+1L_{k+1}. When RR is large, this handoff is delayed: after LkL_{k} is mastered, the policy can remain stuck for a long period with near-zero return on Lk+1L_{k+1}, until a sharp, grokking-like jump makes the next horizon suddenly solvable. When R=O⁡(1)R=O(1), the handoff becomes smooth: progress on LkL_{k} starts benefiting Lk+1L_{k+1} before LkL_{k} fully saturates, so the next horizon gains a visible return much sooner and training relays steadily across horizons. This behavior can be interpreted as learning at the edge of competence (Zhang et al.,, 2025). In the moderate-RR regime, the policy becomes “just competent enough” on LkL_{k} that success on Lk+1L_{k+1} is no longer purely random, yet LkL_{k} still provides a strong learning signal; the two horizons therefore improve in tandem. In the large-RR regime, the policy must become overwhelmingly competent on LkL_{k} before Lk+1L_{k+1} ceases to be random, creating the long plateau and the subsequent phase transition. See Section 6.2 for a more detailed, gradient-level mechanism explanation.

6 Proof Overview

This section explains the main proof idea behind our learning-dynamic results. The central technical ingredient is a characterization of the policy-gradient signal as a function of a step-wise probability, which reveals an explicit long-horizon thresholding mechanism.

6.1 Technical Preliminaries

We first map our reasoning mechanism to some step-invariant quantities. At step ℓ\ell, attention weights over prompt tokens are given by a softmax of scores ⟨Q​xa,ℓ−1,xp,ℓ′⟩\langle Qx_{a,\ell-1},x_{p,\ell^{\prime}}\rangle. Since xa,ℓ−1=𝔰⁡(xp,ℓ)x_{a,\ell-1}=\mathfrak{s}(x_{p,\ell}), correct retrieval means that the aligned prompt token xp,ℓx_{p,\ell} receives a strictly larger score than all misaligned tokens xp,ℓ′x_{p,\ell^{\prime}} with ℓ′≠ℓ\ell^{\prime}\neq\ell. With initialization Q(0)=𝟎Q^{(0)}=\mathbf{0} and the symmetry of 𝒟L\mathcal{D}^{L}, the expected policy-gradient update preserves a two-level score structure: for all x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} and x′≠xx^{\prime}\neq x,

⟨Q(t)​𝔰​(x),x⟩=q(t),⟨Q(t)​𝔰​(x),x′⟩=r(t).\displaystyle\big\langle Q^{(t)}\mathfrak{s}(x),x\big\rangle=q^{(t)},\quad\big\langle Q^{(t)}\mathfrak{s}(x),x^{\prime}\big\rangle=r^{(t)}.

Consequently, the attention weight is step-invariant: 𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧a,ℓ−1→p,ℓ(t)≡𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L(t)\mathbf{Attn}^{(t)}_{a,\ell-1\to p,\ell}\equiv\mathbf{Attn}_{L}^{(t)}. The following lemma translates 𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L(t)\mathbf{Attn}_{L}^{(t)} into the corresponding three classes of step-invariant next-state probabilities.

Lemma 6.1 (Step-invariant probability).

Given 𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L(t)\mathbf{Attn}_{L}^{(t)}, with a fixed MLP in Assumption 3.3, the next-state distribution assigns step-invariant probability masses to:

  • •

    Target: pL,1(t)≜πθ(t)​(gℓ​(y^ℓ−1)∣y^ℓ−1,GL)p_{L,1}^{(t)}\triangleq\pi_{\theta^{(t)}}\big(g_{\ell}(\widehat{y}_{\ell-1})\mid\widehat{y}_{\ell-1},G^{L}\big);

  • •

    Context distractor: pL,2(t)≜πθ(t)​(gℓ′​(y^ℓ−1)|y^ℓ−1,GL)p_{L,2}^{(t)}\triangleq\pi_{\theta^{(t)}}\big(g_{\ell^{\prime}}(\widehat{y}_{\ell-1})\big|\ \widehat{y}_{\ell-1},G^{L}\big) for any ℓ′≠ℓ\ell^{\prime}\neq\ell;

  • •

    Other distractor: pL,3(t)≜πθ(t)​(y|y^ℓ−1,GL)p_{L,3}^{(t)}\triangleq\pi_{\theta^{(t)}}\big(y\ \big|\ \widehat{y}_{\ell-1},G^{L}\big) for any y∉{gℓ′​(y^ℓ−1)∣ℓ′∈[L]}y\notin\{g_{\ell^{\prime}}(\widehat{y}_{\ell-1})\mid\ell^{\prime}\in[L]\}.

Moreover, pL,1(t)∝dCB​𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L(t)p_{L,1}^{(t)}\propto d^{C_{B}\mathbf{Attn}_{L}^{(t)}}. For later use, define the effective probability margin: ΔL(t):=pL,1(t)−pL,3(t)\Delta^{(t)}_{L}:=p^{(t)}_{L,1}-p^{(t)}_{L,3} and δL(t):=pL,2(t)−pL,3(t)\delta^{(t)}_{L}:=p^{(t)}_{L,2}-p^{(t)}_{L,3}.

6.2 Key Lemma for Gradient Estimation

The preceding discussion reduces the model’s one-step behavior to two scalars (q(t),r(t))(q^{(t)},r^{(t)}). We now state the main technical result: for length-LL tasks, the policy-gradient signal in the (q(t),r(t))(q^{(t)},r^{(t)}) coordinates admits an explicit characterization in terms of the step-level margin ΔL(t)\Delta_{L}^{(t)}. This turns the learning dynamics into an effective one-dimensional evolution of attention concentration.

Lemma 6.2 (Gradient characterization).

Throughout the mixed-training process, given L∈ℒRL\in\mathcal{L}_{R}, if the step-wise probability satisfies δL(t)ΔL(t)≪1L2​(1−ΔL(t))\frac{\delta^{(t)}_{L}}{\Delta^{(t)}_{L}}\ll\frac{1}{L^{2}}(1-\Delta^{(t)}_{L}) and pL,2(t)pL,1(t)≪1−pL,1(t)\frac{p^{(t)}_{L,2}}{p^{(t)}_{L,1}}\ll 1-p_{L,1}^{(t)}, then we have

∇q𝒥~L(t)\displaystyle\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}^{(t)}_{L} ∝(ΔL(t))L​(1−ΔL(t)),\displaystyle\propto(\Delta^{(t)}_{L})^{L}(1-\Delta^{(t)}_{L}), (16)
𝒥L(t)\displaystyle\mathcal{J}^{(t)}_{L} =1d+(1−1d)​(1±o⁡(1))⋅(ΔL(t))L.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d}+\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{d}\Bigr)(1\pm o(1))\cdot(\Delta^{(t)}_{L})^{L}. (17)

Moreover, |∇r𝒥~L(t)|≤O⁡(1Lmax)​∇q𝒥~L(t)|\nabla_{r}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}^{(t)}_{L}|\leq O(\frac{1}{L_{\max}})\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}^{(t)}_{L}.

Remark 6.1.

Lemma 6.2 shows that the policy gradient is essentially driven by the qq-direction, with |∇r𝒥~L||\nabla_{r}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L}| being lower-order. Its magnitude exhibits two regimes: when ΔL\Delta_{L} is small, the long-horizon factor (ΔL)L(\Delta_{L})^{L} exponentially suppresses the gradient; when ΔL≈1\Delta_{L}\approx 1, the update is in a convergence regime and is controlled by the shrinking term 1−ΔL1-\Delta_{L}. Since larger qq increases the target attention weight 𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L\mathbf{Attn}_{L} and hence the margin ΔL\Delta_{L} via Lemma 6.1, the takeaway is that length-LL learning is negligible until qq is large enough to make ΔL\Delta_{L} moderate, after which progress slows again as ΔL→1\Delta_{L}\to 1.

Two alternating phases in mixed-horizon training.

Under mixed-horizon training, learning typically proceeds from shorter to longer horizons: shorter tasks suffer weaker attention dilution, so they contribute usable gradient earlier and drive up qq; as qq grows, longer horizons gradually become gradient-effective and then start to show visible return. Consequently, learning alternates between (i) a gradient transfer phase, where ∇q𝒥~Lk\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{k}} dominates while ∇q𝒥~Lk+1\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{k+1}} remains negligible, and (ii) a reward-emergence phase, where ∇q𝒥~Lk+1\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{k+1}} becomes substantial and Lk+1L_{k+1} quickly reaches mastery.

Regime comparison: grokking vs. edge-of-competence relay.

The key difference is whether ∇q𝒥~Lk+1\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{k+1}} becomes non-negligible before ∇q𝒥~Lk\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{k}} has decayed to a saturated signal. Guided by Lemmas 6.2 and 6.1 , activating Lk+1L_{k+1} in the first place requires its target attention 𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧Lk+1\mathbf{Attn}_{L_{k+1}} to reach a constant-level regime so that the gate (ΔLk+1)Lk+1(\Delta_{L_{k+1}})^{L_{k+1}} is not exponentially suppressed; the handoff is then controlled by when

(ΔLk+1)Lk+1≈1−ΔLk.(\Delta_{L_{k+1}})^{L_{k+1}}\approx 1-\Delta_{L_{k}}.

For large R=ω⁡(1)R=\omega(1), reaching this regime for Lk+1L_{k+1} forces qq so large that LkL_{k} is already driven to 𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧Lk=1−o⁡(1)\mathbf{Attn}_{L_{k}}=1-o(1), making 1−ΔLk1-\Delta_{L_{k}} small (on the order of d−(CB−1)d^{-(C_{B}-1)}). Thus ∇q𝒥~Lk+1\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{k+1}} stays negligible over a long plateau, and reward emerges via a grokking-style jump. For moderate R=O⁡(1)R=O(1), the same catch-up happens while LkL_{k} is still away from full saturation (edge of competence), so ∇q𝒥~Lk\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{k}} and ∇q𝒥~Lk+1\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{k+1}} overlap and jointly drive progress, yielding a smooth relay.

6.3 Proof of Lemma 6.2: Fourier Analysis on Groups

We begin by discussing the central technical challenge in analyzing long-horizon policy gradients, and then introduce our Fourier-based techniques for tackling the challenges.

Key technical challenges.

The starting point is to express the policy gradient in terms of the one-step action distribution on the group. By simple transitivity, each transition y^ℓ−1→y^ℓ\widehat{y}_{\ell-1}\to\widehat{y}_{\ell} corresponds to a unique group element uℓ∈𝒢u_{\ell}\in\mathcal{G} such that y^ℓ=uℓ​(y^ℓ−1)\widehat{y}_{\ell}=u_{\ell}(\widehat{y}_{\ell-1}). Let μℓ\mu_{\ell} denote the one-step action law of uℓu_{\ell} on 𝒢\mathcal{G} (under the current policy), and write μℓ​(g)=ℙ⁡(uℓ=g)\mu_{\ell}(g)\;=\;\mathbb{P}(u_{\ell}=g). With this notation, the step-ℓ\ell gradient reduces to a posterior-vs-prior gap for the target action:

∇q𝒥L∝∑ℓ∈[L](ℙ⁡(uℓ=gℓ∣y^L=yL)−μℓ​(gℓ)).\textstyle\nabla_{q}\mathcal{J}_{L}\propto\sum_{\ell\in[L]}\Big(\mathbb{P}(u_{\ell}=g_{\ell}\mid\widehat{y}_{L}=y_{L})-\mu_{\ell}(g_{\ell})\Big).

Let G∗=gL∘⋯∘g1G_{\ast}=g_{L}\circ\cdots\circ g_{1}. Simple transitivity also implies that terminal success is exactly the group-product constraint

y^L=yL⟺uL∘⋯∘u1=G∗.\textstyle\widehat{y}_{L}=y_{L}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u_{L}\circ\cdots\circ u_{1}=G_{\ast}.

Hence the success probability and the numerator in the posterior can be written as point-evaluations of convolution products, for instance:22 2 see Section B.2 for formal definitions of convolution ∗\ast and Fourier transforms.

ℙ(y^L=yL)=(μL∗⋯∗μ1)(G∗).\textstyle\mathbb{P}(\widehat{y}_{L}=y_{L})\;=\;(\mu_{L}\ast\cdots\ast\mu_{1})(G_{\ast}).

The challenge is that these are high-order convolutions evaluated at a specific group element. When LL is large, a direct expansion in the group domain involves exponentially many mixed terms and offers no clean control: conditioning on uL∘⋯∘u1=G∗u_{L}\circ\cdots\circ u_{1}=G_{\ast} couples all steps, so the posterior ℙ(uℓ=⋅∣y^L=yL)\mathbb{P}(u_{\ell}=\cdot\mid\widehat{y}_{L}=y_{L}) is inherently trajectory-level and does not factorize into per-step statistics.

Fourier analysis to estimate the dominant signal.

To make these convolution powers tractable, we pass to the Fourier domain on 𝒢\mathcal{G} (Kondor,, 2008; Terras,, 1999), where convolution becomes multiplication, turning the LL-fold convolution into a structured product of Fourier operators: ∏ℓ∈[L]μ^ℓ​(λ)\prod_{\ell\in[L]}\widehat{\mu}_{\ell}(\lambda). Here μ^ℓ​(λ)\widehat{\mu}_{\ell}(\lambda) is the Fourier transform of μℓ\mu_{\ell} at an irreducible unitary representation λ\lambda††footnotemark: . Notice that the step-invariant three-way partition of next-token outcomes in Lemma 6.1 is equivalently a three-way partition of uℓu_{\ell}, and thus

μℓ(g)=pL,1𝟙{g=gℓ}+pL,2𝟙{g∈GL∖{gℓ}}+pL,3𝟙{g∈𝒢∖GL}.\mu_{\ell}(g)=p_{L,1}\mathds{1}\{g=g_{\ell}\}+p_{L,2}\mathds{1}\{g\in G^{L}\setminus\{g_{\ell}\}\}+p_{L,3}\mathds{1}\{g\in\mathcal{G}\setminus G^{L}\}.

Exploiting this structure, we obtain

μ^ℓ​(λ)=ΔL​λ​(gℓ)+δL​∑g∈GL∖{gℓ}λ⁡(g),\widehat{\mu}_{\ell}(\lambda)=\Delta_{L}\lambda(g_{\ell})+\delta_{L}\sum_{g\in G^{L}\setminus\{g_{\ell}\}}\lambda(g),

which splits into a target-aligned contribution and a residual contribution from context distractors. Taking products across LL steps, the leading contribution arises from selecting the aligned component at each step (under mild separation conditions on ΔL\Delta_{L} and δL\delta_{L}), which yields the characteristic (ΔL)L​(1−ΔL)(\Delta_{L})^{L}(1-\Delta_{L}) structure in the resulting posterior deviation.

Prior use of group representations in machine learning.

Group representation theory has been widely explored in machine learning to model and exploit symmetry (Esteves,, 2020; Marchetti et al.,, 2024) and to analyze structured distributions (Chen et al.,, 2020; Kondor,, 2008). Our use is different in both setting and goal: we bring Fourier analysis into the study of long-horizon, compositional RL objectives, where the terminal success event couples all steps and makes policy-gradient estimation inherently trajectory-dependent. The group structure turns this global conditioning into an LL-fold convolution object that can be controlled spectrally.

7 Experiments

In this section, we provide empirical support for our theoretical analysis through synthetic experiments.

7.1 General Setup

The experiment setting is designed to mirror our theoretical framework and assumptions in Section 3. We consider a cyclic group action over ℤ96\mathbb{Z}_{96}. We study two training paradigms:

  • •

    fixed-length training with reasoning lengths L∈{5,15,45}L\in\{5,15,45\};

  • •

    mixed-length training: ℒ3={5,15,45}\mathcal{L}_{3}=\{5,15,45\} and ℒ7={5,35}\mathcal{L}_{7}=\{5,35\}. The reasoning depth LL is stochastically assigned within each training batch (N=512N=512), where the problem length of each individual sample is uniformly drawn from ℒR\mathcal{L}_{R}.

We use an abelian cyclic action for experimental convenience; for the lengths we consider (L≥5L\geq 5), the commutativity-induced shortcut effects discussed in Remark 3.1 are mild.

Model and training settings.

We employ a one-layer detached attention layer paired with a fixed MLP transition head. First, the transition MLP is pretrained via supervised learning to master the one-step group operation (y,g)↦y⋅g(y,g)\mapsto y\cdot g, after which its parameters are frozen. The attention parameters QQ are subsequently trained using the REINFORCE algorithm to maximize the terminal reward. We utilize an exponential moving-average baseline (momentum 0.95) and an entropy penalty (10−310^{-3}) to facilitate stable policy gradients.

Evaluation.

We periodically compute the per-length average success rate by running greedy rollouts and calculating the fraction of episodes where the model correctly predicts the entire trajectory {y^L=yL}\{\widehat{y}_{L}=y_{L}\} over 30 batches of size 512. We additionally report an attention-alignment metric, peak attention-hit rate, defined as the fraction of steps where the argmax attention weight selects the unique prompt position corresponding to the current action token, i.e., the prompt index 𝔰−1​(xa,k)\mathfrak{s}^{-1}(x_{a,k}) within the sampled set {xp,ℓ}ℓ=1L\{x_{p,\ell}\}_{\ell=1}^{L}. A higher hit rate indicates that the attention layer recovers the underlying permutation 𝔰\mathfrak{s} by locating the correct prompt position at each step, consistent with attention concentration (𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L→1\mathbf{Attn}_{L}\to 1).

Results for fixed-length training.

The average reward and peak attention hit rate under fixed-length training are reported in Figure 2. We overlay three curves corresponding to training runs at different lengths in the same plot. We observe that the short-horizon setting (L1=5L_{1}=5) achieves nearly optimal reward together with strong attention concentration, whereas longer horizons exhibit near-flat plateaus in both reward and attention. This behavior is consistent with the predictions of Theorem 4.1 and Proposition 4.1.

Results for mixed-length training.

For mixed-length training, we consider two difficulty-ratio regimes: moderate (R=3R=3) and large (R=7R=7). As shown in Figure 3, successful learning curves exhibit a grokking-style plateau-then-jump behavior. Moreover, Figure 3(a) indicates that a suitable difficulty ratio shortens the plateau between consecutive horizons, leading to efficient relay dynamics. In contrast, Figure 3(b) shows that when the difficulty ratio is too large, the longer horizon (L=35L=35) remains at near-zero reward throughout training, whereas under a suitable RR (as in Figure 3(a)), L=45L=45 can already reach near-optimal reward. Together, these observations validate the predictions from Theorem 5.1 and Theorem 5.2 in the mixed-difficulty regime.

8 Conclusions

In this work, we analyze the training dynamics of RLVR on a multi-step compositional reasoning task. To the best of our knowledge, we provide the first end-to-end learning process analysis for outcome-based RL with transformer-based policies, together with explicit convergence guarantees. Our theory captures both grokking-like phase transitions and the relay effect under mixed difficulty, explaining how RLVR learns at the edge of competence and identifying data mixing as a scalable lever for accelerating progress to harder tasks. Technically, we introduce a novel Fourier analysis on groups that makes long-horizon conditioning and compositional structure tractable. We also provide evidence from synthetic experiments that corroborates our theoretical results.

Limitations and future directions.

One major limitation of our study is that we focus on a single dimension of distribution diversity: we control for all other factors and only scale the length of compositions in the data distribution. This simplification allows us to study the optimization dynamics of RL in a clean, abstracted setting. However, this design choice also limits the generality of our conclusions. In real world reasoning problems, hard reasoning problems may be different from easy problems in many aspects. For example, they may require more long-tailed distributed atomic skills than easy problems, and they may sit in very different semantic contexts than easy problems, both of which we cannot study theoretically yet. There are also other reasoning patterns, such as planning and search, which we cannot analyze in the current setting. We hope our work can inspire future research into these topics.

Appendix: Complete Proofs

Appendix A Preliminaries

In this section, we will introduce some useful notations and derive several preliminary policy gradient lemmas, which will be repeatedly used in the subsequent training-dynamics analysis. Throughout the proof, we use d𝗉d_{\mathsf{p}} to denote |𝒳||\mathcal{X}|.

A.1 Gradient Computations

Notations for gradient expressions.

Consider a problem instance of length LL, we denote a full answer trajectory with initial prefix Za,0Z_{a,0} by

Z^aL≜(Za,0,Z^a,1,…,Z^a,L).\widehat{Z}_{a}^{L}\triangleq\bigl(Z_{a,0},\widehat{Z}_{a,1},\ldots,\widehat{Z}_{a,L}\bigr).

For each 1≤ℓ≤L1\leq\ell\leq L, we denote the partial trajectory up to step ℓ\ell (including the initial prefix) by

Z^aL,ℓ≜(Za,0,Z^a,1,…,Z^a,ℓ).\widehat{Z}_{a}^{L,\ell}\triangleq\bigl(Z_{a,0},\widehat{Z}_{a,1},\ldots,\widehat{Z}_{a,\ell}\bigr).

We introduce the following shorthand notations (for j∈τ⁡(𝒴)j\in\tau(\mathcal{Y}), r∈[m]r\in[m], and ℓ,k∈[L]\ell,k\in[L]):

ℰj​(Z^aL,ℓ,ZpL)\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{j}(\widehat{Z}^{L,\ell}_{a},Z_{p}^{L}) ≜𝟙τ⁡(y^ℓ)=j−πθ​(j∣y^ℓ−1,GL),\displaystyle\triangleq\mathds{1}_{\tau(\widehat{y}_{\ell})=j}-\pi_{\theta}(j\mid\widehat{y}_{\ell-1},G^{L}), (18a)
Λj,r​(Z^aL,ℓ−1,ZpL)\displaystyle\Lambda_{j,r}(\widehat{Z}^{L,\ell-1}_{a},Z_{p}^{L}) ≜12​(⟨Wj,r,Z^a,k−1⟩+∑k∈[L]𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧a,ℓ−1→p,k⋅⟨Wj,r,Zp,k⟩).\displaystyle\triangleq\frac{1}{2}\Big(\big\langle W_{j,r},\widehat{Z}_{a,k-1}\big\rangle+\sum_{k\in[L]}\mathbf{Attn}_{{a,\ell-1}\rightarrow p,k}\cdot\big\langle W_{j,r},Z_{p,k}\big\rangle\Big). (18b)
Ξℓ,k​(Z^aL,ℓ,ZpL)\displaystyle\Xi_{\ell,k}(\widehat{Z}^{L,\ell}_{a},Z_{p}^{L}) ≜12​∑j∈τ⁡(𝒴)ℰj​(Z^aL,ℓ,ZpL)​∑r∈[m]σ′​(Λj,r​(Z^aL,ℓ−1,ZpL))​⟨Wj,r,Zp,k⟩.\displaystyle\triangleq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j\in\tau(\mathcal{Y})}\mathcal{E}_{j}(\widehat{Z}^{L,\ell}_{a},Z_{p}^{L})\sum_{r\in[m]}\sigma^{\prime}\big(\Lambda_{j,r}(\widehat{Z}^{L,\ell-1}_{a},Z_{p}^{L})\big)\langle W_{j,r},Z_{p,k}\rangle. (18c)

Here, πθ​(j∣y^ℓ−1,GL)=𝗌𝗈𝖿𝗍𝗆𝖺𝗑​(𝖳𝖥θ​(Z^a,ℓ−1,ZpL))j\pi_{\theta}(j\mid\widehat{y}_{\ell-1},G^{L})=\mathsf{softmax}\left(\mathsf{TF}_{\theta}\left(\widehat{Z}_{a,\ell-1},Z_{p}^{L}\right)\right)_{j}.

Fact A.1 (Gradients of Q).

Given a problem length LL, we have the following expression for the policy gradient w.r.t. the attention matrix QQ:

∇Q𝒥~L=1L𝔼ZL,y^L[𝟙y^L=yL∑ℓ=1L∇Qlogπθ(y^ℓ∣y^ℓ−1,GL)],\displaystyle\nabla_{Q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L}=\frac{1}{L}\mathbb{E}_{Z^{L},\widehat{y}^{L}}\left[\mathds{1}_{\widehat{y}_{L}=y_{L}}\,\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\nabla_{Q}\log\pi_{\theta}(\widehat{y}_{\ell}\mid\widehat{y}_{\ell-1},G^{L})\right],

where

∇Qlogπθ(y^ℓ∣y^ℓ−1,GL)\displaystyle\nabla_{Q}\log\pi_{\theta}(\widehat{y}_{\ell}\mid\widehat{y}_{\ell-1},G^{L})
=∑k∈[L]𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧a,ℓ−1→p,k⋅(Ξℓ,k​(Z^aL,ℓ,ZpL)−∑k′∈[L]𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧a,ℓ−1→p,k​Ξℓ,k′​(Z^aL,ℓ,ZpL))​xa,ℓ−1​xp,k⊤.\displaystyle=\sum_{{k}\in[L]}\mathbf{Attn}_{{a,\ell-1}\rightarrow p,k}\cdot\left(\Xi_{\ell,k}(\widehat{Z}^{L,\ell}_{a},Z_{p}^{L})-\sum_{{k}^{\prime}\in[L]}\mathbf{Attn}_{{a,\ell-1}\rightarrow p,k}\Xi_{\ell,k^{\prime}}(\widehat{Z}^{L,\ell}_{a},Z_{p}^{L})\right)x_{a,\ell-1}x_{p,k}^{\top}.

Moreover, the gradient of QQ for the supervised loss 𝖫𝗈𝗌𝗌L\mathsf{Loss}_{L} can be written as:

−∇Q𝖫𝗈𝗌𝗌L\displaystyle-\nabla_{Q}\mathsf{Loss}_{L}
=1L​𝔼ZL​[∑ℓ=1L∑k=1L𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧a,ℓ−1→p,k⋅(Ξℓ,k​(ZaL,ℓ,ZpL)−∑k′∈[L]𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧a,ℓ−1→p,k​Ξℓ,k′​(ZaL,ℓ,ZpL))​xa,ℓ−1​xp,k⊤].\displaystyle=\frac{1}{L}\mathbb{E}_{Z^{L}}\Big[\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\sum_{k=1}^{L}\mathbf{Attn}_{{a,\ell-1}\rightarrow p,k}\cdot\left(\Xi_{\ell,k}({Z}^{L,\ell}_{a},Z_{p}^{L})-\sum_{{k}^{\prime}\in[L]}\mathbf{Attn}_{{a,\ell-1}\rightarrow p,k}\Xi_{\ell,k^{\prime}}({Z}^{L,\ell}_{a},Z_{p}^{L})\right)x_{a,\ell-1}x_{p,k}^{\top}\Big].

Then we consider the gradient of x⊤​∇Q​log⁡πθ​(y^ℓ∣y^ℓ−1,GL)​x′{x}^{\top}\nabla_{Q}\log\pi_{\theta}(\widehat{y}_{\ell}\mid\widehat{y}_{\ell-1},G^{L})x^{\prime} for x,x′∈𝒳x,x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}.

Lemma A.1.

Given x,x′∈𝒳x,x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}, if x=𝔰⁡(x′)x=\mathfrak{s}(x^{\prime}), when xa,ℓ−1=xx_{a,\ell-1}=x for ℓ∈[L]\ell\in[L], then we have

x⊤​∇Q​log⁡πθ​(y^ℓ∣y^ℓ−1,GL)​x′\displaystyle{x}^{\top}\nabla_{Q}\log\pi_{\theta}(\widehat{y}_{\ell}\mid\widehat{y}_{\ell-1},G^{L})x^{\prime}
=𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧a,ℓ−1→p,ℓ⋅(Ξℓ,ℓ​(Z^aL,ℓ,ZpL)−∑k′∈[L]𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧a,ℓ−1→p,k′​Ξℓ,k′​(Z^aL,ℓ,ZpL))\displaystyle=\mathbf{Attn}_{{a,\ell-1}\rightarrow p,\ell}\cdot\left(\Xi_{\ell,\ell}(\widehat{Z}^{L,\ell}_{a},Z_{p}^{L})-\sum_{{k}^{\prime}\in[L]}\mathbf{Attn}_{{a,\ell-1}\rightarrow p,k^{\prime}}\Xi_{\ell,k^{\prime}}(\widehat{Z}^{L,\ell}_{a},Z_{p}^{L})\right)
=𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧a,ℓ−1→p,ℓ⋅(∑j∈τ⁡(𝒴)ℰj​(Z^aL,ℓ,ZpL)​∑r∈[m]σ′​(Λj,r​(Z^aL,ℓ−1,ZpL))⋅(⟨Wj,r,Zp,ℓ⟩−Λj,r​(Z^aL,ℓ−1,ZpL))).\displaystyle=\mathbf{Attn}_{{a,\ell-1}\rightarrow p,\ell}\cdot\bigg(\sum_{j\in\tau(\mathcal{Y})}\mathcal{E}_{j}(\widehat{Z}^{L,\ell}_{a},Z_{p}^{L})\sum_{r\in[m]}\sigma^{\prime}\big(\Lambda_{j,r}(\widehat{Z}^{L,\ell-1}_{a},Z_{p}^{L})\big)\cdot\Big(\langle W_{j,r},Z_{p,\ell}\rangle-\Lambda_{j,r}(\widehat{Z}^{L,\ell-1}_{a},Z_{p}^{L})\Big)\bigg).
Lemma A.2.

Given x,x′∈𝒳x,x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}, if x≠𝔰⁡(x′)x\neq\mathfrak{s}(x^{\prime}), when xp,ℓ′=x′x_{p,\ell^{\prime}}=x^{\prime} and xa,ℓ−1=xx_{a,\ell-1}=x for ℓ,ℓ′∈[L]\ell,\ell^{\prime}\in[L], noticing that ℓ′≠ℓ\ell^{\prime}\neq\ell, then we have

x⊤​∇Q​log⁡πθ​(y^ℓ∣y^ℓ−1,GL)​x′\displaystyle{x}^{\top}\nabla_{Q}\log\pi_{\theta}(\widehat{y}_{\ell}\mid\widehat{y}_{\ell-1},G^{L})x^{\prime}
=𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧a,ℓ−1→p,ℓ′⋅(Ξℓ,ℓ′​(Z^aL,ℓ,ZpL)−∑k′∈[L]𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧a,ℓ−1→p,k′​Ξℓ,k′​(Z^aL,ℓ,ZpL))\displaystyle=\mathbf{Attn}_{{a,\ell-1}\rightarrow p,\ell^{\prime}}\cdot\left(\Xi_{\ell,\ell^{\prime}}(\widehat{Z}^{L,\ell}_{a},Z_{p}^{L})-\sum_{{k}^{\prime}\in[L]}\mathbf{Attn}_{{a,\ell-1}\rightarrow p,k^{\prime}}\Xi_{\ell,k^{\prime}}(\widehat{Z}^{L,\ell}_{a},Z_{p}^{L})\right)
=𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧a,ℓ−1→p,ℓ′⋅(∑j∈τ⁡(𝒴)ℰj​(Z^aL,ℓ,ZpL)​∑r∈[m]σ′​(Λj,r​(Z^aL,ℓ−1,ZpL))⋅(⟨Wj,r,Zp,ℓ′⟩−Λj,r​(Z^aL,ℓ−1,ZpL))).\displaystyle=\mathbf{Attn}_{{a,\ell-1}\rightarrow p,\ell^{\prime}}\cdot\bigg(\sum_{j\in\tau(\mathcal{Y})}\mathcal{E}_{j}(\widehat{Z}^{L,\ell}_{a},Z_{p}^{L})\sum_{r\in[m]}\sigma^{\prime}\big(\Lambda_{j,r}(\widehat{Z}^{L,\ell-1}_{a},Z_{p}^{L})\big)\cdot\Big(\langle W_{j,r},Z_{p,\ell^{\prime}}\rangle-\Lambda_{j,r}(\widehat{Z}^{L,\ell-1}_{a},Z_{p}^{L})\Big)\bigg).

Observe that there are dL−1d^{L-1} intermediate-state sequences (y^1,…,y^L−1)∈𝒴L−1(\widehat{y}_{1},\dots,\widehat{y}_{L-1})\in\mathcal{Y}^{L-1} that lead to y^L=yL\widehat{y}_{L}=y_{L}. Only these trajectories yield a nonzero terminal reward. Hence, it suffices to restrict our attention to their contributions. Combining this with the preceding lemmas, a direct calculation gives

Lemma A.3.

Given x,x′∈𝒳x,x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}, we have

  • •

    if x=𝔰⁡(x′)x=\mathfrak{s}(x^{\prime}), then

    x⊤∇Q𝒥~Lx′=12​L​d𝗉𝔼ZL[∑v1:L∈𝒴L−1×{yL}(∏ℓ′=1Lπθ(vℓ′∣vℓ′−1,GL))⋅(∑ℓ=1L𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧a,ℓ−1→p,ℓ\displaystyle x^{\top}\nabla_{Q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L}x^{\prime}=\frac{1}{2Ld_{\mathsf{p}}}\mathbb{E}_{Z^{L}}\Bigg[\sum_{v_{1:L}\in\mathcal{Y}^{L-1}\times\{y_{L}\}}\Bigg(\prod_{\ell^{\prime}=1}^{L}\pi_{\theta}(v_{\ell^{\prime}}\mid v_{\ell^{\prime}-1},G^{L})\Bigg)\cdot\Big(\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathbf{Attn}_{{a,\ell-1}\rightarrow p,\ell}
    (∑j∈τ⁡(𝒴)ℰj(Z^aL,ℓ,ZpL)∑r∈[m]σ′(Λj,r(Z^aL,ℓ−1,ZpL))⋅(⟨Wj,r,Zp,ℓ⟩−Λj,r(Z^aL,ℓ−1,ZpL)))|y^1:ℓ=v1:ℓ)].\displaystyle~~~\bigg(\sum_{j\in\tau(\mathcal{Y})}\mathcal{E}_{j}(\widehat{Z}^{L,\ell}_{a},Z_{p}^{L})\sum_{r\in[m]}\sigma^{\prime}\big(\Lambda_{j,r}(\widehat{Z}^{L,\ell-1}_{a},Z_{p}^{L})\big)\cdot\Big(\langle W_{j,r},Z_{p,\ell}\rangle-\Lambda_{j,r}(\widehat{Z}^{L,\ell-1}_{a},Z_{p}^{L})\Big)\bigg)\Big|_{\widehat{y}_{1:\ell}=v_{1:\ell}}\Big)\Bigg].
  • •

    else,

    x⊤∇Q𝒥~Lx′=12​L​d𝗉​(d𝗉−1)𝔼ZL[∑v1:L∈𝒴L−1×{yL}(∏ℓ′=1Lπθ(vℓ′∣vℓ′−1,GL))⋅(∑ℓ=1L∑ℓ′≠ℓ𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧a,ℓ−1→p,ℓ′\displaystyle x^{\top}\nabla_{Q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L}x^{\prime}=\frac{1}{2Ld_{\mathsf{p}}(d_{\mathsf{p}}-1)}\mathbb{E}_{Z^{L}}\Bigg[\sum_{v_{1:L}\in\mathcal{Y}^{L-1}\times\{y_{L}\}}\Bigg(\prod_{\ell^{\prime}=1}^{L}\pi_{\theta}(v_{\ell^{\prime}}\mid v_{\ell^{\prime}-1},G^{L})\Bigg)\cdot\Big(\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\sum_{\ell^{\prime}\neq\ell}\mathbf{Attn}_{{a,\ell-1}\rightarrow p,\ell^{\prime}}
    (∑j∈τ⁡(𝒴)ℰj(Z^aL,ℓ,ZpL)∑r∈[m]σ′(Λj,r(Z^aL,ℓ−1,ZpL))⋅(⟨Wj,r,Zp,ℓ′⟩−Λj,r(Z^aL,ℓ−1,ZpL)))|y^1:ℓ=v1:ℓ)].\displaystyle~~~\bigg(\sum_{j\in\tau(\mathcal{Y})}\mathcal{E}_{j}(\widehat{Z}^{L,\ell}_{a},Z_{p}^{L})\sum_{r\in[m]}\sigma^{\prime}\big(\Lambda_{j,r}(\widehat{Z}^{L,\ell-1}_{a},Z_{p}^{L})\big)\cdot\Big(\langle W_{j,r},Z_{p,\ell^{\prime}}\rangle-\Lambda_{j,r}(\widehat{Z}^{L,\ell-1}_{a},Z_{p}^{L})\Big)\bigg)\Big|_{\widehat{y}_{1:\ell}=v_{1:\ell}}\Big)\Bigg].
Proof.

The two results are obtained by invoking Lemma A.1 and Lemma A.2, respectively. Specifically, for a given ℓ\ell, the event {xa,ℓ−1=x}\{x_{a,\ell-1}=x\} occurs with probability 1/d𝗉1/d_{\mathsf{p}}, while for k≠ℓk\neq\ell, the event {xp,ℓ−1=𝔰−1​(x),xp,k=x′,x′≠𝔰−1​(x)}\{x_{p,\ell-1}=\mathfrak{s}^{-1}(x),x_{p,k}=x^{\prime},x^{\prime}\neq\mathfrak{s}^{-1}(x)\} occurs with probability 1d𝗉​(d𝗉−1)\frac{1}{d_{\mathsf{p}}(d_{\mathsf{p}}-1)}. The remaining calculation details are omitted here for brevity. ∎

Similarly, for the gradient of SFT loss 𝖫𝗈𝗌𝗌L\mathsf{Loss}_{L}, we have

Lemma A.4.

Given x,x′∈𝒳x,x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}, we have

Notations for scalarized attention dynamics.

Based on the gradient update, the quantity ⟨x,Q​x′⟩\langle x,Qx^{\prime}\rangle takes only two possible values, depending on whether x=𝔰⁡(x′)x=\mathfrak{s}(x^{\prime}) (the matched position) or x≠𝔰⁡(x′)x\neq\mathfrak{s}(x^{\prime}) (a mismatched position). Accordingly, we define the (unnormalized) target and non-target attention scores as

q\displaystyle q ≜⟨Q​𝔰​(x),x⟩,x∈𝒳,\displaystyle\triangleq\left\langle Q\,\mathfrak{s}(x),\,x\right\rangle,\qquad x\in\mathcal{X}, (21a)
r\displaystyle r ≜⟨Q​𝔰​(x),x′⟩,x′∈𝒳∖{x}.\displaystyle\triangleq\left\langle Q\,\mathfrak{s}(x),\,x^{\prime}\right\rangle,\qquad x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}\setminus\{x\}. (21b)

With this notation, Lemma A.3 can be viewed as a policy-gradient update on (q,r)(q,r). Hence, it suffices to track the dynamics of these two scalars in the sequel. Thus, following (19), we have

∇q𝒥~L=12​L​d𝗉​𝔼ZL​[𝔍⁡(y0,GL)].\displaystyle\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L}=\frac{1}{2Ld_{\mathsf{p}}}\mathbb{E}_{Z^{L}}\left[\mathfrak{J}(y_{0},G^{L})\right]. (22)

Furthermore, under this reduction, for a fixed problem length LL, the attention weights 𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧a,ℓ−1→p,ℓ′\mathbf{Attn}_{a,\ell-1\to p,\ell^{\prime}} (for ℓ,ℓ′∈[L]\ell,\ell^{\prime}\in[L]) take only two distinct values depending on whether the prompt position matches:

𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧a,ℓ−1→p,ℓ\displaystyle\mathbf{Attn}_{a,\ell-1\to p,\ell} =eqeq+(L−1)​er,\displaystyle=\frac{e^{q}}{e^{q}+(L-1)e^{r}}, (23a)
𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧a,ℓ−1→p,ℓ′\displaystyle\mathbf{Attn}_{a,\ell-1\to p,\ell^{\prime}} =ereq+(L−1)​er,ℓ′≠ℓ.\displaystyle=\frac{e^{r}}{e^{q}+(L-1)e^{r}},\qquad\ell^{\prime}\neq\ell. (23b)

When the context is clear, we denote the target attention weight 𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧a,ℓ−1→p,ℓ\mathbf{Attn}_{a,\ell-1\to p,\ell} by 𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L\mathbf{Attn}_{L} for brevity.

Throughout the following analysis, we suppress the dependence on the underlying instance. When the context is clear, we abbreviate Λj,r​(Z^aL,ℓ−1,ZpL)\Lambda_{j,r}(\widehat{Z}^{L,\ell-1}_{a},Z_{p}^{L}) as Λj,r\Lambda_{j,r} and ℰj​(Z^aL,ℓ,ZpL)\mathcal{E}_{j}(\widehat{Z}^{L,\ell}_{a},Z_{p}^{L}) as ℰj\mathcal{E}_{j}.

Hence, combining the reduced attention pattern in (23), namely, one target receiving weight 𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L(t)\mathbf{Attn}_{L}^{(t)} and L−1L-1 symmetric non-targets, the above characterization of the activations Λj,r\Lambda_{j,r} implies a step-invariant, context-level structure for the next-state distribution πθ(⋅∣y^ℓ−1,GL)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\widehat{y}_{\ell-1},G^{L}). In particular, the candidates decompose into three groups: (i) the target gℓ⋅y^ℓ−1g_{\ell}\cdot\widehat{y}_{\ell-1}; (ii) the L−1L-1 symmetric non-targets {gℓ′⋅y^ℓ−1:ℓ′≠ℓ}\{g_{\ell^{\prime}}\cdot\widehat{y}_{\ell-1}:\ \ell^{\prime}\neq\ell\}; and (iii) the remaining d−Ld-L states outside the context induced set (i.e., vocabulary distractors). We formalize this decomposition in the following lemma.

Lemma A.7.

At step ℓ\ell, conditioning on y^ℓ−1\widehat{y}_{\ell-1} and GLG^{L}, the policy πθ(t)(⋅∣y^ℓ−1,GL)\pi^{(t)}_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\widehat{y}_{\ell-1},G^{L}) satisfies:

(24)

    πθ(t)​(j∣y^ℓ−1,GL)=d1−𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L(t)L−1​CBd𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L(t)​CB+(L−1)​d1−𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L(t)L−1​CB+(d−L)≜pL,2(t).\displaystyle\pi^{(t)}_{\theta}(j\mid\widehat{y}_{\ell-1},G^{L})=\frac{d^{\frac{1-\mathbf{Attn}_{L}^{(t)}}{L-1}C_{B}}}{d^{\mathbf{Attn}_{L}^{(t)}C_{B}}+(L-1)d^{\frac{1-\mathbf{Attn}_{L}^{(t)}}{L-1}C_{B}}+(d-L)}\triangleq p^{(t)}_{L,2}. (25)
