Moreover, πθ(t)​(j∣y^ℓ−1,GL)\pi^{(t)}_{\theta}(j\mid\widehat{y}_{\ell-1},G^{L}) does not depend on ℓ\ell. Hence, we suppress the index ℓ\ell and write pL,1(t)p^{(t)}_{L,1}, pL,2(t)p^{(t)}_{L,2}, and pL,3(t)p^{(t)}_{L,3} for brevity.

Probabilistic Event.

We conclude this subsection by introducing a probabilistic event that characterizes the potential for path collisions, where an incorrect sequence of operations inadvertently leads to the same outcome as the intended compositional path. Such an event serves as a key tool for bounding the interference from distracting trajectories in our subsequent analysis:

𝔈L≜{∃(g^1,…,g^L),g^ℓ∈{g1,…,gL} for all ℓ∈[L],s.t. g^L∘⋯g^1(y0)=yL}.\displaystyle\mathfrak{E}_{L}\triangleq\Big\{\exists(\widehat{g}_{1},\dots,\widehat{g}_{L}),\ \widehat{g}_{\ell}\in\{g_{1},\dots,g_{L}\}\text{ for all }\ell\in[L],\ \text{s.t. }\widehat{g}_{L}\circ\cdots\widehat{g}_{1}(y_{0})=y_{L}\Big\}.
Lemma A.8 (Probability of Trajectory Collision).

Under Assumption 3.1, let 𝒢\mathcal{G} be a finite non-abelian simple group of order dd. For a target state yL∈𝒴y_{L}\in\mathcal{Y} reached by a specific sequence of LL actions, the probability that any alternative sequence of LL actions (formed by the same set of available operators) hits yLy_{L} is bounded by:

ℙ⁡(𝔈L)=O⁡(LLd).\displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\mathfrak{E}_{L})=O\Big(\frac{L^{L}}{d}\Big). (27)
Proof.

To establish the bound, we consider the total number of possible compositional paths and the collision probability associated with each. In our setting, there are LL choices for each of the LL steps in a trajectory, resulting in at most LLL^{L} possible sequences within the set {g1,…,gL}L\{g_{1},\dots,g_{L}\}^{L}. According to the mixing properties of non-abelian simple groups (Larsen and Shalev,, 2007), any sequence that is not algebraically identical to the correct path (g^L∘⋯∘g^1)(\widehat{g}_{L}\circ\dots\circ\widehat{g}_{1}) induces a near-uniform distribution over 𝒴\mathcal{Y}. Consequently, for any single incorrect trajectory, the probability of it hitting the specific target state yLy_{L} is 1/d+o⁡(1/d)1/d+o(1/d). This asymptotic uniformity holds generally across the group, including the case where the target yLy_{L} is the initial state y0y_{0}. By applying the union bound over the collection of all LLL^{L} possible paths, we find that the total probability of an accidental collision is at most LL⋅(1/d+o⁡(1/d))L^{L}\cdot(1/d+o(1/d)). As the state space size d→∞d\to\infty, the probability of an accidental activation via an incorrect compositional path becomes negligible, yielding ℙ⁡(𝔈L)=O⁡(LL/d)\mathbb{P}(\mathfrak{E}_{L})=O(L^{L}/d). ∎

Appendix B Gradient Characterization for General Length

In this section, we use spectral analysis to derive explicit gradient formulas for q(t)q^{(t)} and r(t)r^{(t)} under the step-invariant constraints in Lemma A.7. For each fixed problem length LL, these characterizations provide the analytical foundation for our subsequent study of training dynamics across different training settings in later sections.

Action distribution induced by πθ\pi_{\theta}.

We introduce an action variable uℓ∈𝒢u_{\ell}\in\mathcal{G} as the unique group element applied at step ℓ\ell. By the simply-transitive action of 𝒢\mathcal{G} on 𝒴\mathcal{Y}, each transition y^ℓ−1→y^ℓ\widehat{y}_{\ell-1}\to\widehat{y}_{\ell} corresponds to a unique uℓu_{\ell} such that y^ℓ=uℓ​(y^ℓ−1)\widehat{y}_{\ell}=u_{\ell}(\widehat{y}_{\ell-1}). With this notation, Lemma A.7 can be equivalently stated as a step-invariant action distribution.

Lemma B.1.

Fix a step ℓ\ell and condition on (y^ℓ−1,GL)(\widehat{y}_{\ell-1},G^{L}). Then the policy πθ(⋅∣y^ℓ−1,GL)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\widehat{y}_{\ell-1},G^{L}) can be partitioned into the following three classes:

  • •

    target action (pL,1p_{L,1}): applying the correct in-context rule gℓg_{\ell},

    pL,1\displaystyle p_{L,1} :=πθ​(j∣y^ℓ−1,GL),j=τ⁡(gℓ​(y^ℓ−1)).\displaystyle:=\pi_{\theta}\left(j\mid\widehat{y}_{\ell-1},G^{L}\right),\qquad j=\tau\big(g_{\ell}(\widehat{y}_{\ell-1})\big). (28a)
  • •

    in-context distractor actions (pL,2p_{L,2}): applying an incorrect rule from the context,

    pL,2\displaystyle p_{L,2} :=πθ(j∣y^ℓ−1,GL),j∈τ({g(y^ℓ−1):g∈GL,g≠gℓ}).\displaystyle:=\pi_{\theta}\left(j\mid\widehat{y}_{\ell-1},G^{L}\right),\qquad j\in\tau\Big(\big\{g(\widehat{y}_{\ell-1}):g\in G^{L},g\neq g_{\ell}\big\}\Big). (28b)
  • •

    vocabulary distractor actions (pL,3p_{L,3}): any other token not corresponding to an in-context transition,

    pL,3\displaystyle p_{L,3} :=πθ​(j∣y^ℓ−1,GL),j∈τ⁡({g⁡(y^ℓ−1):g∉GL}).\displaystyle:=\pi_{\theta}\left(j\mid\widehat{y}_{\ell-1},G^{L}\right),\qquad j\in\tau\Big(\big\{g(\widehat{y}_{\ell-1}):g\notin G^{L}\big\}\Big). (28c)

B.1 Trajectory measure induced by 𝖳𝖥θ\mathsf{TF}_{\theta}

In this part, we formally define the trajectory measure induced by the model 𝖳𝖥θ\mathsf{TF}_{\theta} and derive an explicit gradient representation under this probabilistic framework. This formulation allows us to express the optimization objective in terms of conditional (posterior) probabilities over trajectories.

Given a problem instance (y0,GL)(y_{0},G^{L}), for any trajectory 𝒗=(v1,…,vL)\bm{v}=(v_{1},\ldots,v_{L}), we define the trajectory measure ℙ~θ,(y0,GL)\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}_{\theta,(y_{0},G^{L})} induced by 𝖳𝖥θ\mathsf{TF}_{\theta} as

ℙ~θ,(y0,GL)​(𝒗):=∏ℓ′=1Lπθ​(vℓ′∣vℓ′−1,GL).\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}_{\theta,(y_{0},G^{L})}(\bm{v}):=\prod_{\ell^{\prime}=1}^{L}\pi_{\theta}\left(v_{\ell^{\prime}}\mid v_{\ell^{\prime}-1},G^{L}\right). (29)

Under the induced measure (29), we can rewrite the gradient expression in (22) as

𝔍⁡(y0,GL)\displaystyle\mathfrak{J}(y_{0},G^{L}) =𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L⋅ℙ~θ,(y0,GL)​(vL=yL)⋅𝔼~θ,(y0,GL)​[∑ℓ=1L𝔊ℓ​(𝒗)|vL=yL],\displaystyle=\mathbf{Attn}_{L}\cdot\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}_{\theta,(y_{0},G^{L})}\left(v_{L}=y_{L}\right)\cdot\widetilde{\mathbb{E}}_{\theta,(y_{0},G^{L})}\left[\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathfrak{G}_{\ell}(\bm{v})\middle|v_{L}=y_{L}\right], (30)

where

ℙ~θ,(y0,GL)​(vL=yL)\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}_{\theta,(y_{0},G^{L})}\left(v_{L}=y_{L}\right) =∑𝒗∈𝒴L−1×{yL}ℙ~θ,(y0,GL)​(𝒗),\displaystyle=\sum_{\bm{v}\in\mathcal{Y}^{L-1}\times\{y_{L}\}}\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}_{\theta,(y_{0},G^{L})}(\bm{v}), (31)
𝔼~θ,(y0,GL)​[∑ℓ=1L𝔊ℓ​(𝒗)|vL=yL]\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathbb{E}}_{\theta,(y_{0},G^{L})}\left[\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathfrak{G}_{\ell}(\bm{v})\middle|v_{L}=y_{L}\right] =∑𝒗∈𝒴L−1×{yL}ℙ~θ,(y0,GL)​(𝒗)​∑ℓ=1L𝔊ℓ​(𝒗)ℙ~θ,(y0,GL)​(vL=yL).\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{\bm{v}\in\mathcal{Y}^{L-1}\times\{y_{L}\}}\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}_{\theta,(y_{0},G^{L})}(\bm{v})\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathfrak{G}_{\ell}(\bm{v})}{\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}_{\theta,(y_{0},G^{L})}\left(v_{L}=y_{L}\right)}. (32)

We now turn to the term 𝔊ℓ\mathfrak{G}_{\ell}. By Lemma A.6, we can rewrite 𝔊ℓ​(𝒗)\mathfrak{G}_{\ell}(\bm{v}) as

𝔊ℓ​(𝒗)\displaystyle\mathfrak{G}_{\ell}(\bm{v}) =∑j∈τ⁡(𝒴)ℰj​∑r∈[m]σ′​(Λj,r)​(Vj,r​(gℓ)−Λj,r)\displaystyle=\sum_{j\in\tau(\mathcal{Y})}\mathcal{E}_{j}\sum_{r\in[m]}\sigma^{\prime}\big({\Lambda}_{j,r}\big)\Big(V_{j,r}(g_{\ell})-{\Lambda}_{j,r}\Big)
=∑g∈𝒢ℰτ⁡(g⁡(y^ℓ−1))​(Vτ⁡(g⁡(y^ℓ−1)),rg⁡(y^ℓ−1)​(gℓ)−Λτ⁡(g⁡(y^ℓ−1)),rg⁡(y^ℓ−1))\displaystyle=\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}}\mathcal{E}_{\tau(g(\widehat{y}_{\ell-1}))}\Big(V_{\tau(g(\widehat{y}_{\ell-1})),r_{g(\widehat{y}_{\ell-1})}}(g_{\ell})-{\Lambda}_{\tau(g(\widehat{y}_{\ell-1})),r_{g(\widehat{y}_{\ell-1})}}\Big)
=𝟙{g(vℓ−1)=vℓ}(Vτ⁡(g⁡(y^ℓ−1)),rg⁡(y^ℓ−1)(gℓ)−Λτ⁡(g⁡(y^ℓ−1)),rg⁡(y^ℓ−1))\displaystyle=\mathds{1}\{g(v_{\ell-1})=v_{\ell}\}\Big(V_{\tau(g(\widehat{y}_{\ell-1})),r_{g(\widehat{y}_{\ell-1})}}(g_{\ell})-{\Lambda}_{\tau(g(\widehat{y}_{\ell-1})),r_{g(\widehat{y}_{\ell-1})}}\Big)
−∑g∈𝒢πθ(τ(g(vℓ−1))∣vℓ−1,GL)(Vτ⁡(g⁡(y^ℓ−1)),rg⁡(y^ℓ−1)(gℓ)−Λτ⁡(g⁡(y^ℓ−1)),rg⁡(y^ℓ−1)).\displaystyle\quad-\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}}\pi_{\theta}\left(\tau(g(v_{\ell-1}))\mid v_{\ell-1},G^{L}\right)\Big(V_{\tau(g(\widehat{y}_{\ell-1})),r_{g(\widehat{y}_{\ell-1})}}(g_{\ell})-{\Lambda}_{\tau(g(\widehat{y}_{\ell-1})),r_{g(\widehat{y}_{\ell-1})}}\Big).

Using the step-invariant three-way partition in Lemma A.7, the last term further simplifies to

𝔊ℓ​(𝒗)\displaystyle\mathfrak{G}_{\ell}(\bm{v}) =𝟙{g(vℓ−1)=vℓ}(Vτ⁡(g⁡(y^ℓ−1)),rg⁡(y^ℓ−1)(gℓ)−Λτ⁡(g⁡(y^ℓ−1)),rg⁡(y^ℓ−1))\displaystyle=\mathds{1}\{g(v_{\ell-1})=v_{\ell}\}\Big(V_{\tau(g(\widehat{y}_{\ell-1})),r_{g(\widehat{y}_{\ell-1})}}(g_{\ell})-{\Lambda}_{\tau(g(\widehat{y}_{\ell-1})),r_{g(\widehat{y}_{\ell-1})}}\Big)
−pL,1​((1−𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L)​B−σ0)\displaystyle\quad-p_{L,1}\Big((1-\mathbf{Attn}_{L})B-\sigma_{0}\Big)
+(L−1)​pL,2​((1+1−𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧LL−1)​B+σ0)\displaystyle\quad+(L-1)p_{L,2}\Big(\big(1+\tfrac{1-\mathbf{Attn}_{L}}{L-1}\big)B+\sigma_{0}\Big)
+(d−L)​pL,3​(B+σ0),\displaystyle\quad+(d-L)p_{L,3}\Big(B+\sigma_{0}\Big),

where we used that the in-context distractor set has size L−1L-1 and the remaining vocabulary set has size d−Ld-L.

Next, define the posterior probabilities (under the trajectory measure conditioned on success)

ρℓ,1\displaystyle\rho_{\ell,1} ≜ℙ~θ,(y0,GL)​(uℓ=gℓ|vL=yL),\displaystyle\triangleq\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}_{\theta,(y_{0},G^{L})}\left(u_{\ell}=g_{\ell}\middle|v_{L}=y_{L}\right), (33)
ρℓ,2\displaystyle\rho_{\ell,2} ≜ℙ~θ,(y0,GL)​(uℓ∈GL∖{gℓ}|vL=yL).\displaystyle\triangleq\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}_{\theta,(y_{0},G^{L})}\left(u_{\ell}\in G^{L}\setminus\{g_{\ell}\}\middle|v_{L}=y_{L}\right). (34)

Taking the conditional expectation of 𝔊ℓ​(𝒗)\mathfrak{G}_{\ell}(\bm{v}) given vL=yLv_{L}=y_{L} yields

𝔼~θ,(y0,GL)​[𝔊ℓ​(𝒗)|vL=yL]\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathbb{E}}_{\theta,(y_{0},G^{L})}\left[\mathfrak{G}_{\ell}(\bm{v})\middle|v_{L}=y_{L}\right] =ρℓ,1​((1−𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L)​B−σ0)−ρℓ,2​((1+1−𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧LL−1)​B+σ0)\displaystyle=\rho_{\ell,1}\Big((1-\mathbf{Attn}_{L})B-\sigma_{0}\Big)-\rho_{\ell,2}\Big(\big(1+\tfrac{1-\mathbf{Attn}_{L}}{L-1}\big)B+\sigma_{0}\Big)
−(1−ρℓ,1−ρℓ,2)​(B+σ0)\displaystyle\quad-(1-\rho_{\ell,1}-\rho_{\ell,2})\Big(B+\sigma_{0}\Big)
−pL,1​((1−𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L)​B−σ0)+(L−1)​pL,2​((1+1−𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧LL−1)​B+σ0)\displaystyle\quad-p_{L,1}\Big((1-\mathbf{Attn}_{L})B-\sigma_{0}\Big)+(L-1)p_{L,2}\Big(\big(1+\tfrac{1-\mathbf{Attn}_{L}}{L-1}\big)B+\sigma_{0}\Big)
+(1−pL,1−(L−1)​pL,2)​(B+σ0)\displaystyle\quad+\big(1-p_{L,1}-(L-1)p_{L,2}\big)\Big(B+\sigma_{0}\Big)
=[(ρℓ,1−pL,1)​(2−𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L)+(pL,2−ρℓ,2L−1)​(1−𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L)]​B.\displaystyle=\Bigg[(\rho_{\ell,1}-p_{L,1})(2-\mathbf{Attn}_{L})+\Big(p_{L,2}-\frac{\rho_{\ell,2}}{L-1}\Big){(1-\mathbf{Attn}_{L})}\Bigg]B.

Putting it back to (30), we have

∇q𝒥~L=12​L​d𝗉​𝔼ZL​[𝔍⁡(y0,GL)]\displaystyle\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L}=\frac{1}{2Ld_{\mathsf{p}}}\mathbb{E}_{Z^{L}}\left[\mathfrak{J}(y_{0},G^{L})\right]
=12​L​d𝗉​𝔼ZL​[𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L⋅ℙ~θ,(y0,GL)​(vL=yL)​B⋅∑ℓ((ρℓ,1−pL,1)​(2−𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L)+(pL,2−ρℓ,2L−1)​(1−𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L))].\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2Ld_{\mathsf{p}}}\mathbb{E}_{Z^{L}}\Big[\mathbf{Attn}_{L}\cdot\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}_{\theta,(y_{0},G^{L})}\left(v_{L}=y_{L}\right)B\cdot\sum_{\ell}\Big((\rho_{\ell,1}-p_{L,1})(2-\mathbf{Attn}_{L})+\Big(p_{L,2}-\frac{\rho_{\ell,2}}{L-1}\Big){(1-\mathbf{Attn}_{L})}\Big)\Big]. (35)

Intuitively, the gradient is driven by the gap between the posterior action probabilities conditioned on success and their unconditional counterparts. Therefore, controlling the gradient reduces to estimating the posterior probabilities ρℓ,1\rho_{\ell,1} and ρℓ,2\rho_{\ell,2} as functions of the probability tuple (pL,1,pL,2,pL,3)(p_{L,1},p_{L,2},p_{L,3}). In what follows, we suppress the dependence on (θ,(y0,GL))(\theta,(y_{0},G^{L})) whenever the context is clear.

B.2 Preliminaries: Harmonic Analysis on 𝒢\mathcal{G}

The trajectory measure introduced in the previous part involves cumulative products of group actions, which correspond to repeated convolutions of measures on the underlying group. A direct combinatorial analysis of these convolutions is often intractable. To address this, we work in the Fourier domain via the irreducible representations of the group.

In this section, we briefly review the basic facts of harmonic analysis on finite groups and collect the spectral tools we will use to decouple these convolution operations. For background and more detailed treatments, see Serre, (1977); Kondor, (2008).

Definition B.1 (Irreducible Representations).

Let 𝒢\mathcal{G} be a finite group of order |𝒢|=N|\mathcal{G}|=N. Let Λ\Lambda denote the set of equivalence classes of irreducible unitary representations of 𝒢\mathcal{G}. For each λ∈Λ\lambda\in\Lambda, λ:𝒢→U⁡(dλ)\lambda:\mathcal{G}\to U(d_{\lambda}) is homomorphism, where U⁡(dλ)U(d_{\lambda}) is the group of dλ×dλd_{\lambda}\times d_{\lambda} unitary matrices.

  • •

    The trivial representation is denoted by 𝟏\mathbf{1}, with d𝟏=1d_{\mathbf{1}}=1 and 𝟏​(g)=1,∀g\mathbf{1}(g)=1,\forall g.

  • •

    Orthogonality Relations: For λ,η∈Λ\lambda,\eta\in\Lambda:

    ⟨λi​j,ηk​l⟩=∑g∈𝒢λi​j​(g)​ηk​l​(g)¯=Ndλ​δλ​η​δi​k​δj​l\langle\lambda_{ij},\eta_{kl}\rangle=\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}}\lambda_{ij}(g)\overline{\eta_{kl}(g)}=\frac{N}{d_{\lambda}}\delta_{\lambda\eta}\delta_{ik}\delta_{jl}

    Specifically, for λ≠𝟏\lambda\neq\mathbf{1}, ∑g∈𝒢λ⁡(g)=𝟎dλ×dλ\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}}\lambda(g)=\mathbf{0}_{d_{\lambda}\times d_{\lambda}}.

Definition B.2 (Fourier Transform).

Let Λ\Lambda be the set of irreducible unitary representations of 𝒢\mathcal{G}. For any λ∈Λ\lambda\in\Lambda, let dλd_{\lambda} be its dimension. For a function f:𝒢→ℂf:\mathcal{G}\to\mathbb{C}, the Fourier transform is:

f^​(λ)≜∑h∈𝒢f⁡(h)​λ​(h).\widehat{f}(\lambda)\triangleq\sum_{h\in\mathcal{G}}f(h)\lambda(h).
Definition B.3 (Convolution).

The convolution of two functions f,ν:𝒢→ℂf,\nu:\mathcal{G}\to\mathbb{C} is defined as:

(f∗ν)​(g):=∑h∈𝒢f⁡(g​h−1)​ν​(h).(f*\nu)(g):=\sum_{h\in\mathcal{G}}f(gh^{-1})\nu(h).

The Fourier transform maps convolution to matrix multiplication:

f∗ν^​(g)=f^​(g)​ν^​(g).\widehat{f*\nu}(g)=\widehat{f}(g)\widehat{\nu}(g).
Lemma B.2 (Fourier Inversion Formula & Plancherel Identity).

Function f:𝒢→ℂf:\mathcal{G}\to\mathbb{C} can be reconstructed from its Fourier coefficients:

f⁡(g)=1N​∑λ∈Λdλ​Tr​(f^​(λ)​λ​(g)−1).f(g)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}d_{\lambda}\text{Tr}\left(\widehat{f}(\lambda)\lambda(g)^{-1}\right).

Using the inversion formula at g=eg=e (identity), we have the identity:

∑λ∈Λdλ2=N.\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}d_{\lambda}^{2}=N.

We distinguish the trivial representation 𝟏\mathbf{1} (where λ⁡(h)=1\lambda(h)=1) from non-trivial representations λ≠𝟏\lambda\neq\mathbf{1}. Note that ∑λ≠𝟏dλ2=N−1\sum_{\lambda\neq\mathbf{1}}d_{\lambda}^{2}=N-1.

Definition B.4 (Character Value & Spectral Decay Factor).

Let 𝒢\mathcal{G} be a finite group and let Λ\Lambda denote the set of its irreducible unitary representations. The character of a representation λ∈Λ\lambda\in\Lambda, denoted by χλ:𝒢→ℂ\chi_{\lambda}:\mathcal{G}\to\mathbb{C}, is defined as the trace of the linear operator λ⁡(g)\lambda(g) for each g∈𝒢g\in\mathcal{G}:

χλ​(g):=Tr⁡(λ⁡(g)).\chi_{\lambda}(g):=\mathrm{Tr}(\lambda(g)).

The scalar χλ​(g)\chi_{\lambda}(g) is referred to as the character value of the element gg corresponding to λ\lambda. Furthermore, we define the spectral decay factor, denoted by γ⁡(𝒢)\gamma(\mathcal{G}), as the maximum normalized character value over all non-trivial representations and non-identity elements:

γ⁡(𝒢):=maxλ∈Λ,λ≠𝟏g∈𝒢,g≠e⁡|χλ​(g)|dλ,\gamma(\mathcal{G}):=\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}\lambda\in\Lambda,\lambda\neq\mathbf{1}\\ g\in\mathcal{G},g\neq e\end{subarray}}\frac{|\chi_{\lambda}(g)|}{d_{\lambda}},

where dλd_{\lambda} denotes the dimension of the representation λ\lambda.

Remark B.1 (Magnitude of γ⁡(𝒢)\gamma(\mathcal{G})).

For any finite group 𝒢\mathcal{G}, it holds that 0≤γ⁡(𝒢)≤10\leq\gamma(\mathcal{G})\leq 1. Specifically, if 𝒢\mathcal{G} is abelian or has a non-trivial center Z⁡(𝒢)≠{e}Z(\mathcal{G})\neq\{e\}, then γ⁡(𝒢)=1\gamma(\mathcal{G})=1. If 𝒢\mathcal{G} is a non-abelian simple group, then γ⁡(𝒢)<1\gamma(\mathcal{G})<1. Furthermore, for many sequences of simple groups (e.g., P​S​L2​(q)PSL_{2}(q)), γ⁡(𝒢)→0\gamma(\mathcal{G})\to 0 as |𝒢|→∞|\mathcal{G}|\to\infty, indicating rapid spectral decay.

B.3 Spectral Decomposition of the Step Measure

With the harmonic analysis framework in place, we translate conditional expectations under the trajectory measure induced by 𝖳𝖥θ\mathsf{TF}_{\theta} into convolution equations on the group.

Reduction to Group Actions.

Since 𝒢\mathcal{G} acts simply transitively on 𝒴\mathcal{Y}, for any trajectory 𝒗\bm{v} with fixed v0=y0v_{0}=y_{0} there exists a unique sequence of group actions (u1,…,uL)∈𝒢L(u_{1},\ldots,u_{L})\in\mathcal{G}^{L} such that vℓ=uℓ​(vℓ−1)v_{\ell}=u_{\ell}(v_{\ell-1}) for ℓ∈[L]\ell\in[L]. Consequently,

vL=(uL⋯u1)(y0).v_{L}=(u_{L}\cdots u_{1})(y_{0}).

Let the target path be given by (g1,…,gL)(g_{1},\ldots,g_{L}) so that yL=(gL⋯g1)(y0)y_{L}=(g_{L}\cdots g_{1})(y_{0}), and define the target composition G∗≜gL⋯g1G_{\ast}\triangleq g_{L}\cdots g_{1}. Then the endpoint constraint is equivalent to the group equation

vL=yL⟺uL⋯u1=G∗.v_{L}=y_{L}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u_{L}\cdots u_{1}=G_{\ast}.

Under this representation, the posteriors of interest can be written as

ρℓ,1=ℙ~(uℓ=gℓ|uL⋯u1=G∗),ρℓ,2=ℙ~(uℓ∈GL∖{gℓ}|uL⋯u1=G∗).\rho_{\ell,1}=\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}\left(u_{\ell}=g_{\ell}\middle|u_{L}\cdots u_{1}=G_{\ast}\right),\qquad\rho_{\ell,2}=\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}\left(u_{\ell}\in G^{L}\setminus\{g_{\ell}\}\middle|u_{L}\cdots u_{1}=G_{\ast}\right).
Definition B.5 (One-step measure).

For each step ℓ∈[L]\ell\in[L], define a probability measure μℓ\mu_{\ell} on 𝒢\mathcal{G} by

μℓ​(h)≜ℙ~​(uℓ=h)={pL,1,h=gℓ,pL,2,h∈GL∖{gℓ},pL,3,h∈𝒢∖GL.\mu_{\ell}(h)\triangleq\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(u_{\ell}=h)=\begin{cases}p_{L,1},&h=g_{\ell},\\ p_{L,2},&h\in G^{L}\setminus\{g_{\ell}\},\\ p_{L,3},&h\in\mathcal{G}\setminus G^{L}.\end{cases}

Equivalently,

μℓ=pL,1​δgℓ+pL,2​δGL∖{gℓ}+pL,3​δ𝒢∖GL,\mu_{\ell}=p_{L,1}\delta_{g_{\ell}}+p_{L,2}\delta_{G^{L}\setminus\{g_{\ell}\}}+p_{L,3}\delta_{\mathcal{G}\setminus G^{L}},

where δS\delta_{S} denotes the (unnormalized) uniform measure on a set S⊆𝒢S\subseteq\mathcal{G}. Moreover, the marginal probability of the endpoint is given by

ℙ~(vL=yL)=(μL∗⋯∗μ1)(G∗).\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(v_{L}=y_{L})=(\mu_{L}*\cdots*\mu_{1})(G_{\ast}).

We now compute the Fourier transform μ^ℓ​(λ)\widehat{\mu}_{\ell}(\lambda) for a nontrivial irreducible representation λ≠𝟏\lambda\neq\mathbf{1}.

Definition B.6 (Spectral objects and effective parameters).

Given ℓ∈[L]\ell\in[L], for an irreducible representation λ\lambda of 𝒢\mathcal{G}, define the sample operator

Wℓ​(λ)≜∑h∈GL∖{gℓ}λ⁡(h).W_{\ell}(\lambda)\triangleq\sum_{h\in G^{L}\setminus\{g_{\ell}\}}\lambda(h).

We also define the effective parameters

ΔL≜pL,1−pL,3,δL≜pL,2−pL,3,σGL≜maxλ≠𝟏⁡maxℓ∈[L]​‖Wℓ​(λ)‖op,\Delta_{L}\triangleq p_{L,1}-p_{L,3},\qquad\delta_{L}\triangleq p_{L,2}-p_{L,3},\qquad\sigma_{G^{L}}\triangleq\max_{\lambda\neq\mathbf{1}}\max_{\ell\in[L]}\|W_{\ell}(\lambda)\|_{\mathrm{op}},

where ∥⋅∥op\|\cdot\|_{\text{op}} denotes the operator norm induced by ∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|_{2}, i.e., ‖A‖op≔sup‖x‖2=1‖A​x‖2\|A\|_{\text{op}}\coloneqq\sup_{\|x\|_{2}=1}\|Ax\|_{2}.

Lemma B.3 (Fourier transform of the one-step measure).

Let μℓ\mu_{\ell} be the one-step measure in Definition B.5. For any nontrivial irreducible representation λ≠𝟏\lambda\neq\mathbf{1},

μ^ℓ​(λ)=ΔL​λ​(gℓ)+δL​Wℓ​(λ).\widehat{\mu}_{\ell}(\lambda)=\Delta_{L}\lambda(g_{\ell})+\delta_{L}W_{\ell}(\lambda).
Proof.

By definition of μℓ\mu_{\ell},

μ^ℓ​(λ)=pL,1​λ​(gℓ)+pL,2​∑h∈GL∖{gℓ}λ⁡(h)+pL,3​∑h∈𝒢∖GLλ⁡(h).\widehat{\mu}_{\ell}(\lambda)=p_{L,1}\lambda(g_{\ell})+p_{L,2}\sum_{h\in G^{L}\setminus\{g_{\ell}\}}\lambda(h)+p_{L,3}\sum_{h\in\mathcal{G}\setminus G^{L}}\lambda(h).

For λ≠𝟏\lambda\neq\mathbf{1}, by Lemma B.2, we have ∑h∈𝒢λ⁡(h)=0\sum_{h\in\mathcal{G}}\lambda(h)=0, hence ∑h∈𝒢∖GLλ⁡(h)=−(λ⁡(gℓ)+Wℓ​(λ))\sum_{h\in\mathcal{G}\setminus G^{L}}\lambda(h)=-(\lambda(g_{\ell})+W_{\ell}(\lambda)). Substituting and collecting terms yields the claim. ∎

B.4 Posterior Estimation

Building on the operator decomposition, we compute the posterior probabilities by evaluating traces of the resulting spectral products. For notational convenience, we define the events

E≜{vL=yL},Aℓ≜{uℓ=gℓ},Bℓ≜{uℓ∈GL∖{gℓ}}.E\triangleq\{v_{L}=y_{L}\},\qquad A_{\ell}\triangleq\{u_{\ell}=g_{\ell}\},\qquad B_{\ell}\triangleq\{u_{\ell}\in G^{L}\setminus\{g_{\ell}\}\}.

Thus, the main task is to control ℙ~​(E)\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(E) as well as the joint probabilities ℙ~​(Aℓ∩E)\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(A_{\ell}\cap E) and ℙ~​(Bℓ∩E)\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(B_{\ell}\cap E).

Lemma B.4.

With E,Aℓ,BℓE,A_{\ell},B_{\ell} defined above, we have the expansions

ℙ~​(E)\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(E) =1d+(1−1d)​ΔLL+ℛE,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d}+\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)\Delta_{L}^{L}+\mathcal{R}_{E}, (36a)
ℙ~​(Aℓ∩E)\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(A_{\ell}\cap E) =pL,1d+(1−1d)​pL,1​ΔLL−1+ℛA,\displaystyle=\frac{p_{L,1}}{d}+\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)p_{L,1}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}+\mathcal{R}_{A}, (36b)
ℙ~​(Bℓ∩E)\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(B_{\ell}\cap E) =(L−1)​pL,2d+ℛB.\displaystyle=\frac{(L-1)p_{L,2}}{d}+\mathcal{R}_{B}. (36c)

Moreover, the remainders satisfy

|ℛE|\displaystyle|\mathcal{R}_{E}| ≤(1−1d)​[(ΔL+σGL​δL)L−ΔLL−L​σGL​δL​ΔLL−1+(L−1)​L​γ​(𝒢)​δL​ΔLL−1],\displaystyle\leq\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)\Big[(\Delta_{L}+\sigma_{G^{L}}\delta_{L})^{L}-\Delta_{L}^{L}-L\sigma_{G^{L}}\delta_{L}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}+(L-1)L\gamma(\mathcal{G})\delta_{L}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}\Big], (37a)
|ℛA|\displaystyle|\mathcal{R}_{A}| ≤pL,1​(1−1d)​[(ΔL+σGL​δL)L−1−ΔLL−1−(L−1)​σGL​δL​ΔLL−2+(L−1)2​γ​(𝒢)​δL​ΔLL−2],\displaystyle\leq p_{L,1}\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)\Big[(\Delta_{L}+\sigma_{G^{L}}\delta_{L})^{L-1}-\Delta_{L}^{L-1}-(L-1)\sigma_{G^{L}}\delta_{L}\Delta_{L}^{L-2}+(L-1)^{2}\gamma(\mathcal{G})\delta_{L}\Delta_{L}^{L-2}\Big], (37b)
|ℛB|\displaystyle|\mathcal{R}_{B}| ≤pL,2​(1−1d)​[σGL​((ΔL+σGL​δL)L−1−ΔLL−1)+(L−1)​γ​(𝒢)​ΔLL−1].\displaystyle\leq p_{L,2}\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)\Big[\sigma_{G^{L}}\big((\Delta_{L}+\sigma_{G^{L}}\delta_{L})^{L-1}-\Delta_{L}^{L-1}\big)+(L-1)\gamma(\mathcal{G})\Delta_{L}^{L-1}\Big]. (37c)
Proof.

By Lemma B.2 and the convolution theorem, each quantity ℙ~​(⋅)\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(\cdot) can be written as a sum of traces of products of Fourier operators. We isolate the trivial-representation contribution and bound the remaining terms using the decomposition μ^k​(λ)=ΔL​λ​(gk)+δL​Wk​(λ)\widehat{\mu}_{k}(\lambda)=\Delta_{L}\lambda(g_{k})+\delta_{L}W_{k}(\lambda). We spell out the details for ℙ~​(E)\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(E); the bounds for ℙ~​(Aℓ∩E)\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(A_{\ell}\cap E) and ℙ~​(Bℓ∩E)\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(B_{\ell}\cap E) follow analogously.

Estimation of ℙ~​(E)\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(E).

Let us start with ℙ~​(E)\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(E). By Lemma B.2, we have

ℙ~​(E)\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(E) =(μL∗⋯∗μ1)(G∗)\displaystyle=(\mu_{L}\ast\cdots\ast\mu_{1})(G_{\ast})
=1d​∑λ∈Λdλ​Tr​(μL∗⋯∗μ1^​(λ)​λ​(G∗)−1)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}d_{\lambda}\text{Tr}\left(\widehat{{\mu_{L}\ast\cdots\ast\mu_{1}}}(\lambda)\lambda(G_{\ast})^{-1}\right)
=1d∑λ∈ΛdλTr([∏k=L1μ^k​(λ)]⏟=:Π⁡(λ)λ(G∗)−1).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}d_{\lambda}\text{Tr}\Bigg(\underbrace{\left[\prod_{k=L}^{1}\widehat{\mu}_{k}(\lambda)\right]}_{=:\Pi(\lambda)}\lambda(G_{\ast})^{-1}\Bigg).
  • •

    For λ=𝟏\lambda=\mathbf{1}: μ^k​(𝟏)=1\widehat{\mu}_{k}(\mathbf{1})=1. Hence Π⁡(λ)=1\Pi(\lambda)=1, and we can obtain

    1d​dλ​Tr​(Π⁡(λ)​λ​(G∗)−1)=1d​d𝟏⋅d𝟏=1d.\displaystyle\frac{1}{d}d_{\lambda}\text{Tr}\left(\Pi(\lambda)\lambda(G_{\ast})^{-1}\right)=\frac{1}{d}d_{\mathbf{1}}\cdot d_{\mathbf{1}}=\frac{1}{d}.
  • •

    For λ≠𝟏\lambda\neq\mathbf{1}: by the decomposition μ^k​(λ)=ΔL​λ​(gk)+δL​Wk​(λ)\widehat{\mu}_{k}(\lambda)=\Delta_{L}\lambda(g_{k})+\delta_{L}W_{k}(\lambda) from Lemma B.3, we have

    Π⁡(λ)\displaystyle\Pi(\lambda) =∏k=L1(ΔL​λ​(gk)+δL​Wk​(λ))=ΔLL​∏k=L1λ⁡(gk)+Tres​(λ).\displaystyle=\prod_{k=L}^{1}\big(\Delta_{L}\lambda(g_{k})+\delta_{L}W_{k}(\lambda)\big)=\Delta_{L}^{L}\prod_{k=L}^{1}\lambda(g_{k})+T_{\mathrm{res}}(\lambda).

    Then the trace contribution by the first term is:

    Tr​(ΔLL​(∏k=L1λ⁡(gk))​λ​(G∗)−1)\displaystyle\text{Tr}\bigg(\Delta_{L}^{L}\big(\prod_{k=L}^{1}\lambda(g_{k})\big)\lambda(G_{\ast})^{-1}\bigg) =(ΔL)L​Tr​(λ⁡(∏k=L1gk)​λ​(G∗)−1)=dλ​(ΔL)L.\displaystyle=(\Delta_{L})^{L}\text{Tr}(\lambda(\prod_{k=L}^{1}g_{k})\lambda(G_{\ast})^{-1})=d_{\lambda}(\Delta_{L})^{L}.

    Summing this over all λ≠𝟏\lambda\neq\mathbf{1}, we obtain

    1d​∑λ≠𝟏dλ​Tr​(ΔLL​(∏k=L1λ⁡(gk))​λ​(G∗)−1)\displaystyle\frac{1}{d}\sum_{\lambda\neq\mathbf{1}}d_{\lambda}\text{Tr}\bigg(\Delta_{L}^{L}\big(\prod_{k=L}^{1}\lambda(g_{k})\big)\lambda(G_{\ast})^{-1}\bigg) =1d​∑λ≠𝟏dλ⋅dλ​(ΔL)L\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{\lambda\neq\mathbf{1}}d_{\lambda}\cdot d_{\lambda}(\Delta_{L})^{L}
    =(1−1d)​(ΔL)L,\displaystyle=\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)(\Delta_{L})^{L},

    where the last equality holds since ∑λ≠𝟏dλ2=d−1\sum_{\lambda\neq\mathbf{1}}d_{\lambda}^{2}=d-1 by Lemma B.2. Therefore, it suffices to control the operator norm of the residual term Tres​(λ)T_{\mathrm{res}}(\lambda). Notice that Tres​(λ)T_{\mathrm{res}}(\lambda) can be expanded into 2L−12^{L}-1 terms, each of the form ML⋯M1M_{L}\cdots M_{1}, where for each kk,

    Mk∈{ΔL​λ​(gk),δL​Wk​(λ)},M_{k}\in\left\{\Delta_{L}\lambda(g_{k}),\delta_{L}W_{k}(\lambda)\right\},

    and at least one factor MkM_{k} equals δL​Wk​(λ)\delta_{L}W_{k}(\lambda). We further decompose Tres​(λ)T_{\mathrm{res}}(\lambda) into two parts, Tres​(λ)=Tres,1​(λ)+Tres,2​(λ)T_{\mathrm{res}}(\lambda)=T_{\mathrm{res},1}(\lambda)+T_{\mathrm{res},2}(\lambda):

    • –

      Tres,1​(λ)T_{\mathrm{res},1}(\lambda) consists of the terms for which there exists a unique k∗∈[L]k^{\ast}\in[L] such that Mk∗=δL​Wk∗​(λ)M_{k^{\ast}}=\delta_{L}W_{k^{\ast}}(\lambda). In this case,

      |Tr​(δL​ΔLL−1​(∏k=Lk∗+1λ⁡(gk))​Wk∗​(λ)​(∏k=k∗−11λ⁡(gk))​λ​(G∗)−1)|\displaystyle\Big|\text{Tr}\bigg(\delta_{L}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}\Big(\prod_{k=L}^{k^{\ast}+1}\lambda(g_{k})\Big)W_{k^{\ast}}(\lambda)\Big(\prod_{k=k^{\ast}-1}^{1}\lambda(g_{k})\Big)\lambda(G_{\ast})^{-1}\bigg)\Big|
      =|δL​ΔLL−1​Tr​(Wk∗​(λ)​λ​(gk∗)−1)|\displaystyle=\Big|\delta_{L}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}\text{Tr}(W_{k^{\ast}}(\lambda)\lambda(g_{k^{\ast}})^{-1})\Big|
      =|δL​ΔLL−1​∑g∈GL∖{gk∗}Tr​(λ⁡(g​gk∗−1))|\displaystyle=\Big|\delta_{L}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}\sum_{g\in{G^{L}}\setminus\{g_{k^{\ast}}\}}\text{Tr}(\lambda(gg_{k^{\ast}}^{-1}))\Big|
      =δL​ΔLL−1​∑g∈GL∖{gk∗}|χλ​(g​gk∗−1)|\displaystyle=\delta_{L}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}\sum_{g\in{G^{L}}\setminus\{g_{k^{\ast}}\}}\Big|\chi_{\lambda}(gg_{k^{\ast}}^{-1})\Big|
      ≤δL​ΔLL−1​(L−1)⋅dλ​γ​(𝒢),\displaystyle\leq\delta_{L}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}(L-1)\cdot d_{\lambda}\gamma(\mathcal{G}), (38)

      where the last inequality uses g​gk∗−1≠egg_{k^{\ast}}^{-1}\neq e (here ee denotes the identity element of 𝒢\mathcal{G}) and the definition of γ⁡(𝒢)\gamma(\mathcal{G}). Since there are LL such terms in Tres,1​(λ)T_{\mathrm{res},1}(\lambda), we obtain

      |1d​∑λ≠𝟏dλ​Tr​(Tres,1​(λ)​λ​(G∗)−1)|≤(1−1d)​δL​ΔLL−1​(L−1)​L​γ​(𝒢).\displaystyle\Big|\frac{1}{d}\sum_{\lambda\neq\mathbf{1}}d_{\lambda}\text{Tr}\bigg(T_{\mathrm{res},1}(\lambda)\lambda(G_{\ast})^{-1}\bigg)\Big|\leq\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)\delta_{L}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}(L-1)L\gamma(\mathcal{G}).
    • –

      Tres,2​(λ)T_{\mathrm{res},2}(\lambda) collects the remaining 2L−1−L2^{L}-1-L terms, i.e., those for which at least two factors MkM_{k} equal δL​Wk​(λ)\delta_{L}W_{k}(\lambda). Then

      ‖Tres,2​(λ)‖op\displaystyle\|T_{\mathrm{res},2}(\lambda)\|_{\text{op}} =∥∑Mk∈{ΔL​λ​(gk),δL​Wk​(λ)},∑k=1L𝟙Mk=δL​Wk​(λ)≥2ML⋅,⋯,⋅M1∥op\displaystyle=\Bigg\|\sum_{M_{k}\in\{\Delta_{L}\lambda(g_{k}),\delta_{L}W_{k}(\lambda)\},\sum_{k=1}^{L}\mathds{1}_{M_{k}=\delta_{L}W_{k}(\lambda)}\geq 2}M_{L}\cdot,\cdots,\cdot M_{1}\Bigg\|_{\text{op}}
      ≤∑Mk∈{ΔL​λ​(gk),δL​Wk​(λ)},∑k=1L𝟙Mk=δL​Wk​(λ)≥2∏k=L1‖Mk‖op\displaystyle\leq\sum_{M_{k}\in\{\Delta_{L}\lambda(g_{k}),\delta_{L}W_{k}(\lambda)\},\sum_{k=1}^{L}\mathds{1}_{M_{k}=\delta_{L}W_{k}(\lambda)}\geq 2}\prod_{k=L}^{1}\|M_{k}\|_{\text{op}}
      ≤(a)​∑i=2L(Li)​ΔLL−i​(σGL​δL)i=(ΔL+σGL​δL)L−ΔLL−L​σGL​δL​ΔLL−1,\displaystyle\overset{(a)}{\leq}\sum_{i=2}^{L}\binom{L}{i}\Delta_{L}^{L-i}(\sigma_{{G^{L}}}\delta_{L})^{i}=(\Delta_{L}+\sigma_{{G^{L}}}\delta_{L})^{L}-\Delta_{L}^{L}-L\sigma_{{G^{L}}}\delta_{L}\Delta_{L}^{L-1},

      Here (a)(a) holds since ‖ΔL​λ​(gk)‖op≤ΔL\|\Delta_{L}\lambda(g_{k})\|_{\text{op}}\leq\Delta_{L}, ‖δL​Wk​(λ)‖op≤σGL​δL\|\delta_{L}W_{k}(\lambda)\|_{\text{op}}\leq\sigma_{G^{L}}\delta_{L}, and there are exactly (Li)\binom{L}{i} choices of indices for which ii different MkM_{k}’s equal δL​Wk​(λ)\delta_{L}W_{k}(\lambda). Consequently,

      |1d​∑λ≠𝟏dλ​Tr​(Tres,2​(λ)​λ​(G∗)−1)|≤1d​∑λ≠𝟏dλ⋅dλ​‖Tres,2​(λ)‖op​‖λ​(G∗)−1‖op\displaystyle\Big|\frac{1}{d}\sum_{\lambda\neq\mathbf{1}}d_{\lambda}\text{Tr}\bigg(T_{\mathrm{res},2}(\lambda)\lambda(G_{\ast})^{-1}\bigg)\Big|\leq\frac{1}{d}\sum_{\lambda\neq\mathbf{1}}d_{\lambda}\cdot d_{\lambda}\|T_{\mathrm{res},2}(\lambda)\|_{\text{op}}\|\lambda(G_{\ast})^{-1}\|_{\text{op}}
      =(1−1d)​((ΔL+σGL​δL)L−ΔLL−L​σGL​δL​ΔLL−1).\displaystyle=\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)\bigg((\Delta_{L}+\sigma_{{G^{L}}}\delta_{L})^{L}-\Delta_{L}^{L}-L\sigma_{{G^{L}}}\delta_{L}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}\bigg).

Putting everything together, we obtain

ℙ~​(E)=1d+(1−1d)​ΔLL+ℛE,\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(E)=\frac{1}{d}+\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)\Delta_{L}^{L}+\mathcal{R}_{E},

where the remainder term ℛE\mathcal{R}_{E} satisfies

|ℛE|≤(1−1d)​((ΔL+σGL​δL)L−ΔLL−L​σGL​δL​ΔLL−1+δL​ΔLL−1​(L−1)​L​γ​(𝒢)).|\mathcal{R}_{E}|\leq\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)\bigg((\Delta_{L}+\sigma_{G^{L}}\delta_{L})^{L}-\Delta_{L}^{L}-L\sigma_{G^{L}}\delta_{L}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}+\delta_{L}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}(L-1)L\gamma(\mathcal{G})\bigg).
Estimation of ℙ~​(Aℓ∩E)\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(A_{\ell}\cap E).

The analysis is similar to that of ℙ~​(E)\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(E). The key difference is that we replace the measure at step ℓ\ell by the Dirac measure pL,1​δgℓp_{L,1}\delta_{g_{\ell}}, since the ℓ\ell-th step takes the action gℓg_{\ell}. Correspondingly, its Fourier transform becomes pL,1​λ​(gℓ)p_{L,1}\lambda(g_{\ell}). Hence,

ℙ~​(Aℓ∩E)\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(A_{\ell}\cap E) =(μL∗⋯pL,1δgℓ⋯∗μ1)(G∗)\displaystyle=(\mu_{L}\ast\cdots p_{L,1}\delta_{g_{\ell}}\cdots\ast\mu_{1})(G_{\ast})
=1d∑λ∈ΛdλTr([μ^L(λ)⋯pL,1λ(gℓ)⋯μ^1(λ)]⏟=:ΠAℓ​(λ)λ(G∗)−1).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}d_{\lambda}\text{Tr}\Big(\underbrace{\left[\widehat{\mu}_{L}(\lambda)\cdots p_{L,1}\lambda(g_{\ell})\cdots\widehat{\mu}_{1}(\lambda)\right]}_{=:\Pi_{A_{\ell}}(\lambda)}\lambda(G_{\ast})^{-1}\Big).
  • •

    For λ=𝟏\lambda=\mathbf{1}: since μ^k​(𝟏)=1\widehat{\mu}_{k}(\mathbf{1})=1, we have ΠAℓ​(𝟏)=pL,1\Pi_{A_{\ell}}(\mathbf{1})=p_{L,1} and thus

    1d​dλ​Tr​(ΠAℓ​(λ)​λ​(G∗)−1)=pL,1d.\displaystyle\frac{1}{d}d_{\lambda}\text{Tr}\left(\Pi_{A_{\ell}}(\lambda)\lambda(G_{\ast})^{-1}\right)=\frac{p_{L,1}}{d}.
  • •

    For λ≠𝟏\lambda\neq\mathbf{1}: we can write

    ΠAℓ​(λ)\displaystyle\Pi_{A_{\ell}}(\lambda) =(∏k=Lℓ+1(ΔL​λ​(gk)+δL​Wk​(λ)))​(pL,1​λ​(gℓ))​(∏k=ℓ−11(ΔL​λ​(gk)+δL​Wk​(λ)))\displaystyle=\Big(\prod_{k=L}^{\ell+1}\big(\Delta_{L}\lambda(g_{k})+\delta_{L}W_{k}(\lambda)\big)\Big)\Big(p_{L,1}\lambda(g_{\ell})\Big)\Big(\prod_{k=\ell-1}^{1}\big(\Delta_{L}\lambda(g_{k})+\delta_{L}W_{k}(\lambda)\big)\Big)
    =pL,1​ΔLL−1​(∏k=L1λ⁡(gk))​λ​(gℓ)​(∏k=L1λ⁡(gk))+Tres,Aℓ​(λ)\displaystyle=p_{L,1}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}\Big(\prod_{k=L}^{1}\lambda(g_{k})\Big)\lambda(g_{\ell})\Big(\prod_{k=L}^{1}\lambda(g_{k})\Big)+T_{\mathrm{res},A_{\ell}}(\lambda)

    The trace contribution of the leading term is

    Tr​(pL,1​ΔLL−1​(∏k=L1λ⁡(gk))​λ​(G∗)−1)\displaystyle\text{Tr}\bigg(p_{L,1}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}\big(\prod_{k=L}^{1}\lambda(g_{k})\big)\lambda(G_{\ast})^{-1}\bigg) =pL,1​(ΔL)L−1​Tr​(λ⁡(∏k=L1gk)​λ​(G∗)−1)\displaystyle=p_{L,1}(\Delta_{L})^{L-1}\text{Tr}(\lambda(\prod_{k=L}^{1}g_{k})\lambda(G_{\ast})^{-1})
    =dλ​pL,1​(ΔL)L−1.\displaystyle=d_{\lambda}p_{L,1}(\Delta_{L})^{L-1}.

    Summing over all λ≠𝟏\lambda\neq\mathbf{1} yields

    1d​∑λ≠𝟏dλ​Tr​(pL,1​(ΔL)L−1​(∏k=L1λ⁡(gk))​λ​(G∗)−1)\displaystyle\frac{1}{d}\sum_{\lambda\neq\mathbf{1}}d_{\lambda}\text{Tr}\bigg(p_{L,1}(\Delta_{L})^{L-1}\big(\prod_{k=L}^{1}\lambda(g_{k})\big)\lambda(G_{\ast})^{-1}\bigg) =1d​∑λ≠𝟏dλ⋅dλ​pL,1​(ΔL)L−1\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{\lambda\neq\mathbf{1}}d_{\lambda}\cdot d_{\lambda}p_{L,1}(\Delta_{L})^{L-1}
    =(1−1d)​pL,1​(ΔL)L−1.\displaystyle=\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)p_{L,1}(\Delta_{L})^{L-1}.

    The residual term Tres,Aℓ​(λ)T_{\mathrm{res},A_{\ell}}(\lambda) can be controlled exactly as in the analysis of Tres​(λ)T_{\mathrm{res}}(\lambda), which gives

    |1d​∑λ≠𝟏dλ​Tr​(Tres,Aℓ​(λ)​λ​(G∗)−1)|\displaystyle\Big|\frac{1}{d}\sum_{\lambda\neq\mathbf{1}}d_{\lambda}\text{Tr}\bigg(T_{\mathrm{res},A_{\ell}}(\lambda)\lambda(G_{\ast})^{-1}\bigg)\Big|
    ≤pL,1​(1−1d)​((ΔL+σGL​δL)L−1−ΔLL−1−(L−1)​σGL​δL​ΔLL−2+δL​ΔLL−2​(L−1)2​γ​(𝒢)).\displaystyle\leq p_{L,1}\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)\bigg((\Delta_{L}+\sigma_{{G^{L}}}\delta_{L})^{L-1}-\Delta_{L}^{L-1}-(L-1)\sigma_{{G^{L}}}\delta_{L}\Delta_{L}^{L-2}+\delta_{L}\Delta_{L}^{L-2}(L-1)^{2}\gamma(\mathcal{G})\bigg).

Putting the above bounds together, we conclude that

ℙ~​(Aℓ∩E)=pL,1d+(1−1d)​pL,1​ΔLL−1+ℛA,\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(A_{\ell}\cap E)=\frac{p_{L,1}}{d}+\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)p_{L,1}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}+\mathcal{R}_{A},

where

|ℛA|≤pL,1​(1−1d)​((ΔL+σGL​δL)L−1−ΔLL−1−(L−1)​σGL​δL​ΔLL−2+δL​ΔLL−2​(L−1)2​γ​(𝒢)).|\mathcal{R}_{A}|\leq p_{L,1}\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)\bigg((\Delta_{L}+\sigma_{G^{L}}\delta_{L})^{L-1}-\Delta_{L}^{L-1}-(L-1)\sigma_{G^{L}}\delta_{L}\Delta_{L}^{L-2}+\delta_{L}\Delta_{L}^{L-2}(L-1)^{2}\gamma(\mathcal{G})\bigg).
Estimation of ℙ~​(Bℓ∩E)\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(B_{\ell}\cap E).

For Bℓ∩EB_{\ell}\cap E, at step ℓ\ell we use the measure pL,2​δGL∖{gℓ}p_{L,2}\delta_{G^{L}\setminus\{g_{\ell}\}}, whose Fourier operator is

μ^Bℓ​(λ)=pL,2​∑g∈GL∖{gℓ}λ⁡(g)=pL,2​Wℓ​(λ).\widehat{\mu}_{B_{\ell}}(\lambda)=p_{L,2}\sum_{g\in G^{L}\setminus\{g_{\ell}\}}\lambda(g)=p_{L,2}W_{\ell}(\lambda).

Hence,

ℙ~​(Bℓ∩E)\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(B_{\ell}\cap E) =(μL∗⋯pL,2δGL∖{gℓ}⋯∗μ1)(G∗)\displaystyle=(\mu_{L}\ast\cdots p_{L,2}\delta_{G^{L}\setminus\{g_{\ell}\}}\cdots\ast\mu_{1})(G_{\ast})
=1d∑λ∈ΛdλTr([μ^L(λ)⋯μ^Bℓ(λ)⋯μ^1(λ)]⏟=:ΠBℓ​(λ)λ(G∗)−1).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{\lambda\in\Lambda}d_{\lambda}\text{Tr}\Big(\underbrace{\left[\widehat{\mu}_{L}(\lambda)\cdots\widehat{\mu}_{B_{\ell}}(\lambda)\cdots\widehat{\mu}_{1}(\lambda)\right]}_{=:\Pi_{B_{\ell}}(\lambda)}\lambda(G_{\ast})^{-1}\Big).
  • •

    For λ=𝟏\lambda=\mathbf{1}: since μ^k​(𝟏)=1\widehat{\mu}_{k}(\mathbf{1})=1, we have ΠBℓ​(𝟏)=pL,2​(L−1)\Pi_{B_{\ell}}(\mathbf{1})=p_{L,2}(L-1), and thus

    1d​dλ​Tr​(ΠBℓ​(λ)​λ​(G∗)−1)=(L−1)⋅pL,2d.\displaystyle\frac{1}{d}d_{\lambda}\text{Tr}\left(\Pi_{B_{\ell}}(\lambda)\lambda(G_{\ast})^{-1}\right)=\frac{(L-1)\cdot p_{L,2}}{d}.
  • •

    For λ≠𝟏\lambda\neq\mathbf{1}: analogous to the decomposition of Tres​(λ)T_{\mathrm{res}}(\lambda), the operator ΠBℓ​(λ)\Pi_{B_{\ell}}(\lambda) can be expanded into 2L−12^{L-1} terms of the form ML⋯(pL,2Wℓ(λ))⋯M1M_{L}\cdots\big(p_{L,2}W_{\ell}(\lambda)\big)\cdots M_{1}, where, for each k≠ℓk\neq\ell,

    Mk∈{ΔL​λ​(gk),δL​Wk​(λ)}.M_{k}\in\{\Delta_{L}\lambda(g_{k}),\delta_{L}W_{k}(\lambda)\}.

    We further split ΠBℓ​(λ)\Pi_{B_{\ell}}(\lambda) into two parts,

    ΠBℓ​(λ)=TBℓ,1​(λ)+TBℓ,2​(λ).\Pi_{B_{\ell}}(\lambda)=T_{B_{\ell},1}(\lambda)+T_{B_{\ell},2}(\lambda).
    • –

      TBℓ,1T_{B_{\ell},1} consists of the unique term for which Mk=ΔL​λ​(gk)M_{k}=\Delta_{L}\lambda(g_{k}) for all k≠ℓk\neq\ell. In this case,

      |Tr​(ΔLL−1​(∏k=Lk∗+1λ⁡(gk))​pL,2​Wℓ​(λ)​(∏k=k∗−11λ⁡(gk))​λ​(G∗)−1)|\displaystyle\Big|\text{Tr}\bigg(\Delta_{L}^{L-1}\Big(\prod_{k=L}^{k^{\ast}+1}\lambda(g_{k})\Big)p_{L,2}W_{\ell}(\lambda)\Big(\prod_{k=k^{\ast}-1}^{1}\lambda(g_{k})\Big)\lambda(G_{\ast})^{-1}\bigg)\Big|
      ≤pL,2​ΔLL−1​(L−1)⋅dλ​γ​(𝒢),\displaystyle\leq p_{L,2}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}(L-1)\cdot d_{\lambda}\gamma(\mathcal{G}),

      where the inequality follows by an argument analogous to (38). Therefore, we have:

      |1d​∑λ≠𝟏dλ​Tr​(TBℓ,1​(λ)​λ​(G∗)−1)|≤(1−1d)​pL,2​ΔLL−1​(L−1)​γ​(𝒢).\displaystyle\Big|\frac{1}{d}\sum_{\lambda\neq\mathbf{1}}d_{\lambda}\text{Tr}\bigg(T_{B_{\ell},1}(\lambda)\lambda(G_{\ast})^{-1}\bigg)\Big|\leq\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)p_{L,2}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}(L-1)\gamma(\mathcal{G}).
    • –

      TBℓ,2T_{B_{\ell},2} collects the remaining terms, i.e., those for which at least one index k≠ℓk\neq\ell satisfies Mk=δL​Wk​(λ)M_{k}=\delta_{L}W_{k}(\lambda). Then

      ‖Tres,2​(λ)‖op\displaystyle\|T_{\mathrm{res},2}(\lambda)\|_{\text{op}} =∥∑Mk∈{ΔL​λ​(gk),δL​Wk​(λ)}​ for ​k≠ℓ,∑k≠ℓ𝟙Mk=δL​Wk​(λ)≥1ML⋯pL,2Wℓ(λ)⋯M1∥op\displaystyle=\Bigg\|\sum_{M_{k}\in\{\Delta_{L}\lambda(g_{k}),\delta_{L}W_{k}(\lambda)\}\text{ for }k\neq\ell,\sum_{k\neq\ell}\mathds{1}_{M_{k}=\delta_{L}W_{k}(\lambda)}\geq 1}M_{L}\cdots p_{L,2}W_{\ell}(\lambda)\cdots M_{1}\Bigg\|_{\text{op}}
      ≤pL,2​σGL​∑i=1L(Li)​ΔLL−i​(σGL​δL)i\displaystyle~~~~\leq p_{L,2}\sigma_{{G^{L}}}\sum_{i=1}^{L}\binom{L}{i}\Delta_{L}^{L-i}(\sigma_{{G^{L}}}\delta_{L})^{i}
      =pL,2​σGL​((ΔL+σGL​δL)L−1−ΔLL−1),\displaystyle~~~~=p_{L,2}\sigma_{{G^{L}}}\Big((\Delta_{L}+\sigma_{{G^{L}}}\delta_{L})^{L-1}-\Delta_{L}^{L-1}\Big),

      which can be shown by the same argument as in the bound for Tres,2T_{\mathrm{res},2}. Consequently,

      |1d​∑λ≠𝟏dλ​Tr​(TBℓ,2​(λ)​λ​(G∗)−1)|\displaystyle\Big|\frac{1}{d}\sum_{\lambda\neq\mathbf{1}}d_{\lambda}\text{Tr}\bigg(T_{B_{\ell},2}(\lambda)\lambda(G_{\ast})^{-1}\bigg)\Big| ≤1d​∑λ≠𝟏dλ⋅dλ​‖TBℓ,2‖op​‖λ​(G∗)−1‖op\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{d}\sum_{\lambda\neq\mathbf{1}}d_{\lambda}\cdot d_{\lambda}\|T_{B_{\ell},2}\|_{\text{op}}\|\lambda(G_{\ast})^{-1}\|_{\text{op}}
      =(1−1d)​pL,2​σGL​((ΔL+σGL​δL)L−1−ΔLL−1).\displaystyle=\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)p_{L,2}\sigma_{{G^{L}}}\Big((\Delta_{L}+\sigma_{{G^{L}}}\delta_{L})^{L-1}-\Delta_{L}^{L-1}\Big).

Putting everything together, we obtain

ℙ~​(Bℓ∩E)=(L−1)​pL,2d+ℛB,\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(B_{\ell}\cap E)=\frac{(L-1)p_{L,2}}{d}+\mathcal{R}_{B},

where the remainder term ℛB\mathcal{R}_{B} satisfies

|ℛB|≤(1−1d)​pL,2​(σGL​((ΔL+σGL​δL)L−1−ΔLL−1)+ΔLL−1​(L−1)​γ​(𝒢)).|\mathcal{R}_{B}|\leq\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)p_{L,2}\bigg(\sigma_{G^{L}}\Big((\Delta_{L}+\sigma_{G^{L}}\delta_{L})^{L-1}-\Delta_{L}^{L-1}\Big)+\Delta_{L}^{L-1}(L-1)\gamma(\mathcal{G})\bigg).

The expansions in Lemma B.4 immediately imply the following deviations of the posterior probabilities ρℓ,1\rho_{\ell,1} and ρℓ,2\rho_{\ell,2} from their corresponding priors.

Proposition B.1 (Posterior deviation and dominant term).

The posterior deviations admit the exact identities

ρℓ,1−pL,1\displaystyle\rho_{\ell,1}-p_{L,1} =pL,1​ΔLL−1​(1−ΔL)​(1−1d)+ℛA−pL,1​ℛEℙ~​(E),\displaystyle=\frac{p_{L,1}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}(1-\Delta_{L})\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)+\mathcal{R}_{A}-p_{L,1}\mathcal{R}_{E}}{\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(E)}, (39a)
pL,2−ρℓ,2L−1\displaystyle p_{L,2}-\frac{\rho_{\ell,2}}{L-1} =pL,2​ΔLL​(1−1d)+pL,2​ℛE−ℛBL−1ℙ~​(E).\displaystyle=\frac{p_{L,2}\Delta_{L}^{L}\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)+p_{L,2}\mathcal{R}_{E}-\frac{\mathcal{R}_{B}}{L-1}}{\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(E)}. (39b)

Moreover, if

σGL​δLΔL≪1L,\frac{\sigma_{G^{L}}\delta_{L}}{\Delta_{L}}\ll\frac{1}{L}, (40)

then the remainder terms satisfy

|ℛA|\displaystyle|\mathcal{R}_{A}| ≤pL,1​ΔLL−1​(1−1d)​(O⁡(σGL2​δL2ΔL2)+(L−1)2​γ​(𝒢)​δLΔL),\displaystyle\leq p_{L,1}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)\left(O\left(\frac{\sigma_{G^{L}}^{2}\delta_{L}^{2}}{\Delta_{L}^{2}}\right)+\frac{(L-1)^{2}\gamma(\mathcal{G})\delta_{L}}{\Delta_{L}}\right), (41a)
|ℛE|\displaystyle|\mathcal{R}_{E}| ≤ΔLL​(1−1d)​(O⁡(σGL2​δL2ΔL2)+(L−1)​L​γ​(𝒢)​δLΔL),\displaystyle\leq\Delta_{L}^{L}\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)\left(O\left(\frac{\sigma_{G^{L}}^{2}\delta_{L}^{2}}{\Delta_{L}^{2}}\right)+\frac{(L-1)L\gamma(\mathcal{G})\delta_{L}}{\Delta_{L}}\right), (41b)
|ℛB|L−1\displaystyle\frac{|\mathcal{R}_{B}|}{L-1} ≤pL,2​ΔLL−1​(1−1d)​(O⁡(σGL2​δL(L−1)​ΔL)+γ⁡(𝒢)).\displaystyle\leq p_{L,2}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)\left(O\left(\frac{\sigma_{G^{L}}^{2}\delta_{L}}{(L-1)\Delta_{L}}\right)+\gamma(\mathcal{G})\right). (41c)
Proof.

For ρℓ,1−pL,1\rho_{\ell,1}-p_{L,1}, by Lemma B.4 we have

ρℓ,1−pL,1\displaystyle\rho_{\ell,1}-p_{L,1} =ℙ~​(Aℓ∩E)−pL,1​ℙ~​(E)ℙ~​(E)\displaystyle=\frac{\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(A_{\ell}\cap E)-p_{L,1}\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(E)}{\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(E)}
=pL,1d+pL,1​ΔLL−1​(1−1d)+ℛA−pL,1​(1d+ΔLL​(1−1d)+ℛE)ℙ~​(E)\displaystyle=\frac{\frac{p_{L,1}}{d}+p_{L,1}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)+\mathcal{R}_{A}-p_{L,1}\Big(\frac{1}{d}+\Delta_{L}^{L}\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)+\mathcal{R}_{E}\Big)}{\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(E)}
=pL,1​ΔLL−1​(1−ΔL)​(1−1d)+ℛA−pL,1​ℛEℙ~​(E),\displaystyle=\frac{p_{L,1}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}(1-\Delta_{L})\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)+\mathcal{R}_{A}-p_{L,1}\mathcal{R}_{E}}{\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(E)},

which gives (39a). For pL,2−ρℓ,2L−1p_{L,2}-\frac{\rho_{\ell,2}}{L-1}, we similarly obtain

pL,2−ρℓ,2L−1\displaystyle p_{L,2}-\frac{\rho_{\ell,2}}{L-1} =pL,2​(L−1)​ℙ~​(E)−ℙ~​(Bℓ∩E)(L−1)​ℙ~​(E)\displaystyle=\frac{p_{L,2}(L-1)\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(E)-\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(B_{\ell}\cap E)}{(L-1)\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(E)}
=pL,2​(L−1)​(1d+ΔLL​(1−1d)+ℛE)−(L−1)​pL,2d−ℛB(L−1)​ℙ~​(E)\displaystyle=\frac{p_{L,2}(L-1)\Big(\frac{1}{d}+\Delta_{L}^{L}\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)+\mathcal{R}_{E}\Big)-\frac{(L-1)p_{L,2}}{d}-\mathcal{R}_{B}}{(L-1)\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(E)}
=pL,2​ΔLL​(1−1d)+pL,2​ℛE−ℛB/(L−1)ℙ~​(E),\displaystyle=\frac{p_{L,2}\Delta_{L}^{L}\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)+p_{L,2}\mathcal{R}_{E}-\mathcal{R}_{B}/(L-1)}{\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(E)},

which gives (39b).

It remains to bound ℛE\mathcal{R}_{E}, ℛA\mathcal{R}_{A}, and ℛB\mathcal{R}_{B} under (40). For notational simplicity, let x≜σGL​δL/ΔLx\triangleq\sigma_{G^{L}}\delta_{L}/\Delta_{L}. Then

(ΔL+σGL​δL)k=ΔLk​(1+x)k.(\Delta_{L}+\sigma_{G^{L}}\delta_{L})^{k}=\Delta_{L}^{k}(1+x)^{k}.

The expressions in the brackets for ℛE\mathcal{R}_{E} and ℛA\mathcal{R}_{A} contain

(1+x)k−1−k​x,k∈{L,L−1}.(1+x)^{k}-1-kx,\qquad k\in\{L,L-1\}.

Under x≪1/Lx\ll 1/L, the second-order Taylor remainder gives (1+x)k−1−k​x=O⁡(k2​x2)(1+x)^{k}-1-kx=O(k^{2}x^{2}), which implies

(ΔL+σGL​δL)k−ΔLk−k​σGL​δL​ΔLk−1=ΔLk⋅O⁡(k2​x2)=O⁡(k2​σGL2​δL2​ΔLk−2).(\Delta_{L}+\sigma_{G^{L}}\delta_{L})^{k}-\Delta_{L}^{k}-k\sigma_{G^{L}}\delta_{L}\Delta_{L}^{k-1}=\Delta_{L}^{k}\cdot O(k^{2}x^{2})=O\big(k^{2}\sigma_{G^{L}}^{2}\delta_{L}^{2}\Delta_{L}^{k-2}\big).

Bound for ℛB\mathcal{R}_{B}.

Here the bracket contains (ΔL+σGL​δL)L−1−ΔLL−1=ΔLL−1​((1+x)L−1−1)(\Delta_{L}+\sigma_{G^{L}}\delta_{L})^{L-1}-\Delta_{L}^{L-1}=\Delta_{L}^{L-1}\big((1+x)^{L-1}-1\big). Under x≪1/Lx\ll 1/L, the first-order estimate gives (1+x)L−1−1=O⁡((L−1)​x)(1+x)^{L-1}-1=O((L-1)x), hence

σGL​((ΔL+σGL​δL)L−1−ΔLL−1)=σGL​ΔLL−1⋅O⁡((L−1)​σGL​δL/ΔL)=O⁡((L−1)​σGL2​δL​ΔLL−2).\sigma_{G^{L}}\big((\Delta_{L}+\sigma_{G^{L}}\delta_{L})^{L-1}-\Delta_{L}^{L-1}\big)=\sigma_{G^{L}}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}\cdot O((L-1)\sigma_{G^{L}}\delta_{L}/\Delta_{L})=O\big((L-1)\sigma_{G^{L}}^{2}\delta_{L}\Delta_{L}^{L-2}\big).

Plugging this into the displayed bound for ℛB\mathcal{R}_{B} yields the stated control on |ℛB||\mathcal{R}_{B}|.

B.5 Gradient Characterization: Proof of Lemma 6.2

Combining the posterior deviations in Proposition B.1 with (35), we obtain the following characterization of the gradient, which is a formal version of Lemma 6.2.

Proposition B.2 (Gradient characterization).

Given problem length LL, suppose that

L2​δLΔL=o⁡(1)⋅(1−ΔL)andpL,2pL,1=o⁡(1)⋅(1−ΔL).\frac{L^{2}\delta_{L}}{\Delta_{L}}=o(1)\cdot(1-\Delta_{L})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\frac{p_{L,2}}{p_{L,1}}=o(1)\cdot(1-\Delta_{L}).

Then

∇q𝒥~L\displaystyle\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L} =Θ⁡(log⁡d/d𝗉)⋅pL,1​ΔLL−1​(1−1d)​(1−ΔL),\displaystyle=\Theta(\log d/d_{\mathsf{p}})\cdot p_{L,1}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)(1-\Delta_{L}),
|∇r𝒥~L|\displaystyle|\nabla_{r}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L}| =O⁡(1/d𝗉)⋅∇q𝒥~L.\displaystyle=O(1/d_{\mathsf{p}})\cdot\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L}.
Proof.

Recall that

∇q𝒥~L=12​L​d𝗉𝔼ZL[𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L⋅B⋅ℙ~​(E)​∑ℓ=1L((ρℓ,1−pL,1)​(2−𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L)+(pL,2−ρℓ,2L−1)​(1−𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L))⏟=:Jgap].\displaystyle\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L}=\frac{1}{2Ld_{\mathsf{p}}}\mathbb{E}_{Z^{L}}\Big[\mathbf{Attn}_{L}\cdot B\cdot\underbrace{\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(E)\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\Big((\rho_{\ell,1}-p_{L,1})(2-\mathbf{Attn}_{L})+\Big(p_{L,2}-\frac{\rho_{\ell,2}}{L-1}\Big)(1-\mathbf{Attn}_{L})\Big)}_{=:J_{\text{gap}}}\Big]. (42)

Note that 2−𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L≥12-\mathbf{Attn}_{L}\geq 1 and 1−𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L∈(0,1)1-\mathbf{Attn}_{L}\in(0,1). Under the stated assumptions, since σGL≤L−1\sigma_{G^{L}}\leq L-1, the condition σGL​δL/ΔL≪1/L\sigma_{G^{L}}\delta_{L}/\Delta_{L}\ll 1/L holds. Hence Proposition B.1 applies. We now verify that for JgapJ_{\text{gap}}, all remainder contributions are negligible compared to the leading term pL,1​ΔLL−1​(1−1d)​(1−ΔL)p_{L,1}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}\big(1-\frac{1}{d}\big)(1-\Delta_{L}).

  • •

    Bounding ℛA\mathcal{R}_{A}. By (41a) in Proposition B.1,

    |ℛA|\displaystyle|\mathcal{R}_{A}| ≤pL,1​ΔLL−1​(1−1d)​(O⁡(σGL2​δL2ΔL2)+(L−1)2​γ​(𝒢)​δLΔL).\displaystyle\leq p_{L,1}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)\left(O\left(\frac{\sigma_{G^{L}}^{2}\delta_{L}^{2}}{\Delta_{L}^{2}}\right)+\frac{(L-1)^{2}\gamma(\mathcal{G})\delta_{L}}{\Delta_{L}}\right).

    Using σGL≤L−1\sigma_{G^{L}}\leq L-1 and L2​δLΔL=o⁡(1)⋅(1−ΔL)\frac{L^{2}\delta_{L}}{\Delta_{L}}=o(1)\cdot(1-\Delta_{L}), we have

    σGL2​δL2ΔL2≤L2​δLΔL⋅δLΔL=o⁡(1)⋅(1−ΔL)⋅δLΔL=o⁡(1)⋅(1−ΔL),\frac{\sigma_{G^{L}}^{2}\delta_{L}^{2}}{\Delta_{L}^{2}}\leq\frac{L^{2}\delta_{L}}{\Delta_{L}}\cdot\frac{\delta_{L}}{\Delta_{L}}=o(1)\cdot(1-\Delta_{L})\cdot\frac{\delta_{L}}{\Delta_{L}}=o(1)\cdot(1-\Delta_{L}),

    and similarly

    (L−1)2​γ​(𝒢)​δLΔL≤γ⁡(𝒢)⋅o⁡(1)⋅(1−ΔL).\frac{(L-1)^{2}\gamma(\mathcal{G})\delta_{L}}{\Delta_{L}}\leq\gamma(\mathcal{G})\cdot o(1)\cdot(1-\Delta_{L}).

    Therefore,

    |ℛA|\displaystyle|\mathcal{R}_{A}| ≤pL,1​ΔLL−1​(1−1d)​(1−ΔL)​(o⁡(1)+o⁡(1)​γ​(𝒢))≪pL,1​ΔLL−1​(1−1d)​(1−ΔL).\displaystyle\leq p_{L,1}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)(1-\Delta_{L})\big(o(1)+o(1)\gamma(\mathcal{G})\big)\ll p_{L,1}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)(1-\Delta_{L}).
  • •

    Bounding ℛE\mathcal{R}_{E}. By (41b) in Proposition B.1,

    |ℛE|\displaystyle|\mathcal{R}_{E}| ≤ΔLL​(1−1d)​(O⁡(σGL2​δL2ΔL2)+(L−1)​L​γ​(𝒢)​δLΔL).\displaystyle\leq\Delta_{L}^{L}\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)\left(O\left(\frac{\sigma_{G^{L}}^{2}\delta_{L}^{2}}{\Delta_{L}^{2}}\right)+\frac{(L-1)L\gamma(\mathcal{G})\delta_{L}}{\Delta_{L}}\right).

    Using the same estimates as above and ΔL≤1\Delta_{L}\leq 1, we obtain

    |ℛE|≪ΔLL​(1−1d)​(1−ΔL).|\mathcal{R}_{E}|\ll\Delta_{L}^{L}\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)(1-\Delta_{L}).

    Consequently, pL,1​|ℛE|p_{L,1}|\mathcal{R}_{E}| is dominated by pL,1​ΔLL​(1−1d)​(1−ΔL)p_{L,1}\Delta_{L}^{L}\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)(1-\Delta_{L}).

  • •

    Bounding ℛB\mathcal{R}_{B}. By (41c) in Proposition B.1,

    |ℛB|L−1\displaystyle\frac{|\mathcal{R}_{B}|}{L-1} ≤pL,2​ΔLL−1​(1−1d)​(O⁡(σGL2​δL(L−1)​ΔL)+γ⁡(𝒢)).\displaystyle\leq p_{L,2}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)\left(O\left(\frac{\sigma_{G^{L}}^{2}\delta_{L}}{(L-1)\Delta_{L}}\right)+\gamma(\mathcal{G})\right).

    Using σGL≤L−1\sigma_{G^{L}}\leq L-1 and L2​δLΔL=o⁡(1)⋅(1−ΔL)\frac{L^{2}\delta_{L}}{\Delta_{L}}=o(1)\cdot(1-\Delta_{L}), we have

    σGL2​δL(L−1)​ΔL≤L2​δLΔL=o⁡(1)⋅(1−ΔL).\frac{\sigma_{G^{L}}^{2}\delta_{L}}{(L-1)\Delta_{L}}\leq\frac{L^{2}\delta_{L}}{\Delta_{L}}=o(1)\cdot(1-\Delta_{L}).

    Moreover, pL,2pL,1=o⁡(1)⋅(1−ΔL)\frac{p_{L,2}}{p_{L,1}}=o(1)\cdot(1-\Delta_{L}) implies

    pL,2​ΔLL−1≤pL,1​ΔLL−1⋅o⁡(1)⋅(1−ΔL).p_{L,2}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}\leq p_{L,1}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}\cdot o(1)\cdot(1-\Delta_{L}).

    Thus,

    |ℛB|L−1\displaystyle\frac{|\mathcal{R}_{B}|}{L-1} ≤pL,1​ΔLL−1​(1−1d)​(1−ΔL)​(o⁡(1)+γ⁡(𝒢)⋅o⁡(1))≪pL,1​ΔLL−1​(1−1d)​(1−ΔL).\displaystyle\leq p_{L,1}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)(1-\Delta_{L})\Big(o(1)+\gamma(\mathcal{G})\cdot o(1)\Big)\ll p_{L,1}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)(1-\Delta_{L}).

    Finally, the same assumption pL,2pL,1=o⁡(1)⋅(1−ΔL)\frac{p_{L,2}}{p_{L,1}}=o(1)\cdot(1-\Delta_{L}) also yields

    pL,2​ΔLL​(1−1d)≪pL,1​ΔLL−1​(1−1d)​(1−ΔL),p_{L,2}\Delta_{L}^{L}\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)\ll p_{L,1}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)(1-\Delta_{L}),

    so the contribution of the second posterior deviation term is dominated by the first term.

Plugging the above bounds into the expression for ∇q𝒥L\nabla_{q}\mathcal{J}_{L}, and using that 𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L=Θ⁡(1)\mathbf{Attn}_{L}=\Theta(1), which is implied by pL,2pL,1=o⁡(1)⋅(1−ΔL)\frac{p_{L,2}}{p_{L,1}}=o(1)\cdot(1-\Delta_{L}), we conclude that

∇q𝒥~L=Θ⁡(log⁡d/d𝗉)⋅pL,1​ΔLL−1​(1−1d)​(1−ΔL).\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L}=\Theta(\log d/d_{\mathsf{p}})\cdot p_{L,1}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}\Big(1-\frac{1}{d}\Big)(1-\Delta_{L}).

The analysis for |∇r𝒥~L||\nabla_{r}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L}| is similar. Alternatively, we may invoke the direct comparison bound in Lemma A.3 to obtain |∇r𝒥~L|=O⁡(1/d𝗉)⋅∇q𝒥~L|\nabla_{r}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L}|=O(1/d_{\mathsf{p}})\cdot\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L}. ∎

B.6 Exponentially Flat Region for Long-Horizon Tasks: Proof of Proposition 4.1

Following the same decomposition underlying Lemma B.4, we show that when the step-invariant probability tuple (pL,1,pL,2,pL,3)(p_{L,1},p_{L,2},p_{L,3}) has small effective margins ΔL:=pL,1−pL,3\Delta_{L}:=p_{L,1}-p_{L,3} and δL:=pL,2−pL,3\delta_{L}:=p_{L,2}-p_{L,3}, the resulting policy gradient is upper bounded by a quantity that decays exponentially in the horizon length LL. We then specialize this general exponential barrier to our concrete setting, which immediately yields Proposition 4.1.

Proposition B.3.

Under Assumptions 3.1–3.3, for any 2≤L≤Lmax2\leq L\leq L_{\max}, suppose the step-invariant probability tuple (pL,1,pL,2,pL,3)(p_{L,1},p_{L,2},p_{L,3}) satisfies, with ΔL:=pL,1−pL,3\Delta_{L}:=p_{L,1}-p_{L,3} and δL:=pL,2−pL,3\delta_{L}:=p_{L,2}-p_{L,3},

ΔL+L​δL≤O~​(d−Ω⁡(1)),pL,i≤d−Ω⁡(1)for ​i∈[3].\displaystyle\Delta_{L}+L\delta_{L}\leq\widetilde{O}\left(d^{-\Omega(1)}\right),\qquad p_{L,i}\leq d^{-\Omega(1)}\ \ \text{for }i\in[3]. (43)

Then,

|∇q𝒥~L|≤O~​(1d𝗉)⋅d−Ω⁡(L),|∇r𝒥~L|≤O~​(1d𝗉2)⋅d−Ω⁡(L).\left|\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L}\right|\leq\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{1}{d_{\mathsf{p}}}\right)\cdot d^{-\Omega(L)},\qquad\left|\nabla_{r}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L}\right|\leq\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{1}{d_{\mathsf{p}}^{2}}\right)\cdot d^{-\Omega(L)}. (44)
Proof.

A key takeaway from Lemma B.4 is that, when bounding the remainder contributions (e.g., ℛE\mathcal{R}_{E}), we decompose the remainder term Tres​(λ)T_{\mathrm{res}}(\lambda) into several parts. Independent of this finer decomposition, its operator norm admits the crude bound

‖Tres​(λ)‖op≤(ΔL+σGL​δL)L−ΔLL.\|T_{\mathrm{res}}(\lambda)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq(\Delta_{L}+\sigma_{G_{L}}\delta_{L})^{L}-\Delta_{L}^{L}.

Using this bound directly gives

ℛE≤(1−1d)​(ΔL+σGL​δL)L.\mathcal{R}_{E}\leq\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{d}\Bigr)(\Delta_{L}+\sigma_{G_{L}}\delta_{L})^{L}.

The same argument applies to ℛA\mathcal{R}_{A} and ℛB\mathcal{R}_{B}, yielding

ℛA≤(1−1d)​pL,1​(ΔL+σGL​δL)L−1,ℛB≤(1−1d)​pL,2​σGL​(ΔL+σGL​δL)L−1.\mathcal{R}_{A}\leq\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{d}\Bigr)p_{L,1}(\Delta_{L}+\sigma_{G_{L}}\delta_{L})^{L-1},\qquad\mathcal{R}_{B}\leq\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{d}\Bigr)p_{L,2}\sigma_{G_{L}}(\Delta_{L}+\sigma_{G_{L}}\delta_{L})^{L-1}.

Invoking (39) from Proposition B.1 and substituting the above bounds into (42), we obtain

|∇q𝒥~L|\displaystyle\left|\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L}\right| ≤O~​(Bd𝗉)​(pL,1​ΔLL−1+pL,1​(ΔL+σGL​δL)L−1+pL,2​σGLL−1​(ΔL+σGL​δL)L−1)\displaystyle\leq\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{B}{d_{\mathsf{p}}}\right)\Bigl(p_{L,1}\Delta_{L}^{L-1}+p_{L,1}(\Delta_{L}+\sigma_{G_{L}}\delta_{L})^{L-1}+p_{L,2}\frac{\sigma_{G_{L}}}{L-1}(\Delta_{L}+\sigma_{G_{L}}\delta_{L})^{L-1}\Bigr)
≤O~​(1d𝗉)⋅d−Ω⁡(L),\displaystyle\leq\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{1}{d_{\mathsf{p}}}\right)\cdot d^{-\Omega(L)},

where in the last step we use σGL≤L−1\sigma_{G_{L}}\leq L-1 together with the assumptions ΔL+L​δL≤O~​(d−Ω⁡(1))\Delta_{L}+L\delta_{L}\leq\widetilde{O}\left(d^{-\Omega(1)}\right) and pL,i≤d−Ω⁡(1)p_{L,i}\leq d^{-\Omega(1)} for i∈[3]i\in[3]. The bound for |∇r𝒥~L|\left|\nabla_{r}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L}\right| follows by the same reasoning and is omitted. ∎

Proposition B.4 (Proposition 4.1 restated).

Under Assumptions 3.1–3.3, suppose 𝖳𝖥θ(0)\mathsf{TF}_{\theta^{(0)}} is initialized according to Assumption 3.4. Then for any horizon L>2​CBL>2C_{B}, whenever the feature magnitudes satisfy max⁡{|r(t)|,|q(t)|}≤0.01\max\{|r^{(t)}|,|q^{(t)}|\}\leq 0.01, we have 𝒥L(t)=1d​(1±o⁡(1))\mathcal{J}_{L}^{(t)}=\frac{1}{d}(1\pm o(1)), and

|∇q𝒥~L(t)|≤O~​(1d𝗉)⋅d−Ω⁡(L),|∇r𝒥~L(t)|≤O~​(1d𝗉2)⋅d−Ω⁡(L).\big|\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L}^{(t)}\big|\leq\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{1}{d_{\mathsf{p}}}\right)\cdot d^{-\Omega(L)},\qquad\big|\nabla_{r}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L}^{(t)}\big|\leq\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{1}{d_{\mathsf{p}}^{2}}\right)\cdot d^{-\Omega(L)}.
Proof.

Since max⁡{|r(t)|,|q(t)|}≤0.01\max\{|r^{(t)}|,|q^{(t)}|\}\leq 0.01, the attention weights satisfy

𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L(t)​CB≤CB​e0.02e0.02+L−1<1,1−𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L(t)L−1​CB≤CBe−0.02+L−1<1.\mathbf{Attn}^{(t)}_{L}C_{B}\leq\frac{C_{B}e^{0.02}}{e^{0.02}+L-1}<1,\qquad\frac{1-\mathbf{Attn}^{(t)}_{L}}{L-1}C_{B}\leq\frac{C_{B}}{e^{-0.02}+L-1}<1.

Case 1: L<d0.01L<d^{0.01}.

pL,1(t)≤O⁡(1L+d1−CB​e0.02e0.02+L−1)=d−Ω⁡(1),pL,2(t)≤O⁡(1L+d1−CBe−0.02+L−1)≤d−0.5.p_{L,1}^{(t)}\leq O\left(\frac{1}{L+d^{1-\frac{C_{B}e^{0.02}}{e^{0.02}+L-1}}}\right)=d^{-\Omega(1)},\qquad p_{L,2}^{(t)}\leq O\left(\frac{1}{L+d^{1-\frac{C_{B}}{e^{-0.02}+L-1}}}\right)\leq d^{-0.5}.

and

B.7 Reward Characterization

Note that ℙ~​(E)\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(E) is exactly the expected reward for a fixed instance (y0,GL)(y_{0},G_{L}). Consequently,

𝒥L=𝔼ZL​[ℙ~​(E)].\mathcal{J}_{L}=\mathbb{E}_{Z^{L}}\big[\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(E)\big].

Therefore, the gradient characterization in Proposition B.2 immediately yields a corresponding characterization of the reward.

Lemma B.5.

Given a problem of length LL, suppose that

L2​δLΔL=o⁡(1)⋅(1−ΔL)andpL,2pL,1=o⁡(1)⋅(1−ΔL).\frac{L^{2}\delta_{L}}{\Delta_{L}}=o(1)\cdot(1-\Delta_{L})\qquad\text{and}\qquad\frac{p_{L,2}}{p_{L,1}}=o(1)\cdot(1-\Delta_{L}).

Then,

𝒥L=1d+(1−1d)​(1±o⁡(1))⋅ΔLL.\mathcal{J}_{L}=\frac{1}{d}+\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{d}\Bigr)(1\pm o(1))\cdot\Delta_{L}^{L}.

Moreover, by adapting the argument in Proposition B.3 to control the residual term ℛE\mathcal{R}_{E}, we obtain the following coarse upper bound.

Lemma B.6.

Given a problem of length LL, we have

|𝒥L−1d|≤(1−1d)​(ΔL+σGL​δL)L.\Big|\mathcal{J}_{L}-\frac{1}{d}\Big|\leq\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{d}\Bigr)\bigl(\Delta_{L}+\sigma_{G_{L}}\delta_{L}\bigr)^{L}.

Appendix C Learning Dynamics of Short-horizon RL

In this section, we focus on the regime L≤CBL\leq C_{B}. Our analysis tracks the training dynamics of the two scalar quantities qq and rr defined in (21a) and (21b). We proceed in three steps. First, we state an induction hypothesis that is maintained throughout training. Second, under this hypothesis, we derive one-step update bounds for qq and rr. Finally, we close the induction by showing that the hypothesis holds for all iterations.

We will focus on the RL training dynamics; the same proof structure and bookkeeping apply to SFT training. Accordingly, at the end of this section, we briefly list the key lemmas and the corresponding induction for SFT, and omit the details.

Induction C.1.

Given Ω⁡(1𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀​d)<ϵ<14\Omega(\frac{1}{\mathsf{polylog}d})<\epsilon<\frac{1}{4}, and let T1T_{1} be the first iteration such that 𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L(t)≥1−ϵ\mathbf{Attn}_{L}^{(t)}\geq 1-\epsilon. Then for every iteration t<T1t<T_{1}, the following statements hold:

  1. 1.

    O⁡(log⁡Lϵ)≥q(t)≥0O\big(\log\frac{L}{\epsilon}\big)\geq q^{(t)}\geq 0, and q(t)q^{(t)} is monotonically nondecreasing in tt (starting from 00);

  2. 2.

    |r(t)|≤O⁡(1/d𝗉)​q(t)|r^{(t)}|\leq O(1/d_{\mathsf{p}})q^{(t)}.

C.1 Attention and Logit Preliminaries

We first introduce several properties of the attention scores and logits if Induction C.1 holds.

If Induction C.1 holds for all iterations <t<t, then we have

    𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧a,ℓ−1→p,k(t)=1(L−1)+eq(t)−r(t)=1L−1​(1−𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L(t))\mathbf{Attn}^{(t)}_{a,\ell-1\to p,k}=\frac{1}{(L-1)+e^{q^{(t)}-r^{(t)}}}=\frac{1}{L-1}\big(1-\mathbf{Attn}_{L}^{(t)}\big) for k≠ℓk\neq\ell.

and the following bounds on the transition probabilities pL,2(t)p^{(t)}_{L,2} and pL,3(t)p^{(t)}_{L,3}.

      Here, the last inequality holds since ((k−1)​x+1−xL−1)​CB\big((k-1)x+\frac{1-x}{L-1}\big)C_{B} is monotonically increase for x≥1Lx\geq\frac{1}{L} and the minimum value is k​CBL=k+Ω⁡(1)\frac{kC_{B}}{L}=k+\Omega(1).

    Moreover, we have

    |∑j∈τ⁡(𝒴)ℰj(t)​∑r∈[m]σ′​(Λj,r(t))⋅(⟨Wj,r,Zp,ℓ⟩−Λj,r(t))|\displaystyle\Bigg|\sum_{j\in\tau(\mathcal{Y})}\mathcal{E}_{j}^{(t)}\sum_{r\in[m]}\sigma^{\prime}\big(\Lambda^{(t)}_{j,r}\big)\cdot\Big(\langle W_{j,r},Z_{p,\ell}\rangle-\Lambda^{(t)}_{j,r}\Big)\Bigg| ≤O⁡(B),\displaystyle\leq O(B), (54)

    which in turn leads to

    ≤∑k=1L(Lk)O(Nk)O(1dk+Ω⁡(1))𝔼ZL[(∏ℓ′=1Lπθ(t)(yℓ′∣yℓ′−1,GL))(∑ℓ=1L⋅𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧a,ℓ−1→p,ℓ𝔊ℓ(𝒗⋆))]\displaystyle\leq\sum_{k=1}^{L}\binom{L}{k}O(N^{k})O\Big(\frac{1}{d^{k+\Omega(1)}}\Big)\mathbb{E}_{Z^{L}}\Bigg[\Bigg(\prod_{\ell^{\prime}=1}^{L}\pi^{(t)}_{\theta}\big(y_{\ell^{\prime}}\mid y_{\ell^{\prime}-1},G^{L}\big)\Bigg)\Big(\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\cdot\mathbf{Attn}_{{a,\ell-1}\rightarrow p,\ell}\mathfrak{G}_{\ell}(\bm{v}^{\star})\Big)\Bigg]
    ≤O(1dΩ⁡(1))𝔼ZL[(∏ℓ′=1Lπθ(t)(yℓ′∣yℓ′−1,GL))(∑ℓ=1L⋅𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧a,ℓ−1→p,ℓ𝔊ℓ(𝒗⋆))].\displaystyle\leq O\Big(\frac{1}{d^{\Omega(1)}}\Big)\mathbb{E}_{Z^{L}}\Bigg[\Bigg(\prod_{\ell^{\prime}=1}^{L}\pi^{(t)}_{\theta}\big(y_{\ell^{\prime}}\mid y_{\ell^{\prime}-1},G^{L}\big)\Bigg)\Big(\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\cdot\mathbf{Attn}_{{a,\ell-1}\rightarrow p,\ell}\mathfrak{G}_{\ell}(\bm{v}^{\star})\Big)\Bigg]. (55)

Therefore, we put (47), (51), (55) together, and thus conclude that

∇q𝒥~L(t)\displaystyle\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L}^{(t)} =1L​d𝗉​𝔼ZL​[𝔍(t)​(y0,GL)]≥Ω⁡(log⁡dd𝗉​d𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L(t)​CB−1).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{Ld_{\mathsf{p}}}\mathbb{E}_{Z^{L}}\left[\mathfrak{J}^{(t)}(y_{0},G^{L})\right]\geq\Omega\Big(\frac{\log d}{d_{\mathsf{p}}d^{\mathbf{Attn}_{L}^{(t)}C_{B}-1}}\Big).

∎

Lemma C.4.

Assume that Induction C.1 holds for all iterations <t<t, when 𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L(t)≥1−L−1CB\mathbf{Attn}_{L}^{(t)}\geq 1-\frac{L-1}{C_{B}}, we have

∇q𝒥~L(t)\displaystyle\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L}^{(t)} =Θ⁡(log⁡dd𝗉​d𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L(t)​CB−1).\displaystyle=\Theta\Big(\frac{\log d}{d_{\mathsf{p}}d^{\mathbf{Attn}_{L}^{(t)}C_{B}-1}}\Big).
Proof.

By Lemma C.2, when 𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L(t)≥1−L−1CB\mathbf{Attn}_{L}^{(t)}\geq 1-\frac{L-1}{C_{B}}, we have ΔL(t),pL,1(t)=Ω⁡(1)\Delta_{L}^{(t)},p_{L,1}^{(t)}=\Omega(1), and δL(t)≤pL,2(t)≤O⁡(1/d)​(1−ΔL(t))\delta_{L}^{(t)}\leq p_{L,2}^{(t)}\leq O(1/d)(1-\Delta_{L}^{(t)}). Hence, the condition in Proposition B.2 holds, and we can directly apply it to complete the proof. ∎

Lemma C.5.

Assume that Induction C.1 holds for all iterations <t<t. Then,

|∇r𝒥~L(t)|≤O⁡(1d𝗉)​|∇q𝒥~L(t)|.\bigl|\nabla_{r}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}^{(t)}_{L}\bigr|\leq O\left(\frac{1}{d_{\mathsf{p}}}\right)\bigl|\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L}^{(t)}\bigr|.
Proof.

The claim follows from Lemma A.3, we thus omit the details. ∎

C.3 Proof of Theorem 4.1

By combining the gradient bounds in Lemmas C.3, C.4 and C.5, we show that the induction hypothesis Induction C.1 is maintained throughout this stage until q(t)q^{(t)} reaches the target scale Ω⁡(log⁡(L/ϵ))\Omega\bigl(\log(L/\epsilon)\bigr). At that point, we obtain 𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L(t)≥1−ϵ\mathbf{Attn}^{(t)}_{L}\geq 1-\epsilon, which leads to the following lemma.

Lemma C.6 (End of Constant-Length Training).

For any Ω⁡(1/𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀​d)<ϵ<L−1CB\Omega(1/\mathsf{polylog}d)<\epsilon<\frac{L-1}{C_{B}}, the induction hypothesis Induction C.1 holds for all iterations

t<T1=O⁡(d𝗉​d(1−ϵ)​CB−1⋅log⁡(L/ϵ)η​log⁡d).t<T_{1}=O\left(d_{\mathsf{p}}d^{(1-\epsilon)C_{B}-1}\cdot\frac{\log(L/\epsilon)}{\eta\log d}\right).

Moreover, at t=T1t=T_{1} we have: q(T1)≥Ω⁡(log⁡(L/ϵ))q^{(T_{1})}\geq\Omega(\log(L/\epsilon)); |r(T1)|≤O⁡(1d)​q(T1)\bigl|r^{(T_{1})}\bigr|\leq O\left(\frac{1}{d}\right)q^{(T_{1})}.

Proof.

Assume Induction C.1 holds up to iteration tt. Then Lemmas C.3 and C.4 imply that the policy gradient for qq is strictly positive and satisfies a lower bound of the form

∇q𝒥~L(t)≥Ω⁡(log⁡dd𝗉)⋅d−(1−ϵ)​CB+1,\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L}^{(t)}\geq\Omega\left(\frac{\log d}{d_{\mathsf{p}}}\right)\cdot d^{-(1-\epsilon)C_{B}+1},

where we used that along this stage 𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L(t)≤1−ϵ\mathbf{Attn}_{L}^{(t)}\leq 1-\epsilon. Under policy gradient update with step size η\eta, we therefore have the per-iteration increase

q(t+1)−q(t)=η​∇q𝒥~L(t)≥η⋅Ω⁡(log⁡dd𝗉)⋅d−(1−ϵ)​CB+1.q^{(t+1)}-q^{(t)}=\eta\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L}^{(t)}\geq\eta\cdot\Omega\left(\frac{\log d}{d_{\mathsf{p}}}\right)\cdot d^{-(1-\epsilon)C_{B}+1}.

Summing over iterations until q(t)q^{(t)} reaches Ω⁡(log⁡(L/ϵ))\Omega(\log(L/\epsilon)) yields

T1=O⁡(d𝗉η​log⁡d⋅log⁡(L/ϵ)⋅d(1−ϵ)​CB−1),T_{1}=O\left(\frac{d_{\mathsf{p}}}{\eta\log d}\cdot{\log(L/\epsilon)}\cdot d^{(1-\epsilon)C_{B}-1}\right),

as claimed.

Finally, Lemma C.5 gives |∇r𝒥~L(t)|≤O⁡(1d)​∇q𝒥~L(t)|\nabla_{r}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L}^{(t)}|\leq O(\frac{1}{d})\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L}^{(t)} throughout this stage, and hence r(t)r^{(t)} remains slaved to q(t)q^{(t)}, i.e., |r(t)|≤O⁡(1d)​q(t)|r^{(t)}|\leq O(\frac{1}{d})q^{(t)} for all t≤T1t\leq T_{1}. ∎

Theorem 4.1 follows immediately from Lemma C.6.

C.4 Proof of Theorem 4.2

The proof follows the same template as the RL case: we (i) set up an induction hypothesis controlling the key parameters, (ii) derive lower/upper bounds on the relevant gradients under this hypothesis, and (iii) combine these bounds to upper bound the time needed for q(t)q^{(t)} to reach the target scale, at which point the attention satisfies 𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L(t)≥1−ϵ\mathbf{Attn}^{(t)}_{L}\geq 1-\epsilon. In other words, Theorem 4.2 is obtained by assembling the lemmas below.

By comparing Lemma A.3 and Lemma A.4, we observe that while the gradient forms are structurally similar, the supervised analysis is more direct. This simplification arises because we only need to track the ground-truth trajectory defined by 𝒗=(y1,…,yL)\bm{v}=(y_{1},\dots,y_{L}). Consequently, we can establish an induction hypothesis analogous to Induction C.1.

Induction C.2.

For any length 2≤L≤𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀​d2\leq L\leq\mathsf{polylog}d, fix any Ω⁡(1𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀​d)<ϵ<min⁡{12​(1−1CB),L−12​L}\Omega(\frac{1}{\mathsf{polylog}d})<\epsilon<\min\{\frac{1}{2}(1-\frac{1}{C_{B}}),\frac{L-1}{2L}\}, and let T1T_{1} be the first iteration such that 𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L(t)≥1−ϵ\mathbf{Attn}_{L}^{(t)}\geq 1-\epsilon. Then for every iteration t<T1t<T_{1}, the following statements hold:

    O⁡(log⁡Lϵ)≥q(t)≥0O(\log\frac{L}{\epsilon})\geq q^{(t)}\geq 0, and q(t)q^{(t)} is monotonically nondecreasing in tt (starting from 00);

  2. 2.

    |r(t)|≤O⁡(1/d𝗉)​q(t)|r^{(t)}|\leq O(1/d_{\mathsf{p}})q^{(t)}.

Building on this induction, we characterize the gradient dynamics through the following lemmas.

Lemma C.7.

Assume that Induction C.2 holds for all iterations <t<t, then we have

  • •

    if 𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L(t)≤1CB\mathbf{Attn}_{L}^{(t)}\leq\frac{1}{C_{B}}, then

    −∇q𝖫𝗈𝗌𝗌L(t)≥Ω⁡(log⁡dd𝗉​L).\displaystyle-\nabla_{q}\mathsf{Loss}^{(t)}_{L}\geq\Omega\Big(\frac{\log d}{d_{\mathsf{p}}L}\Big).

    else, we have

Assume that Induction C.2 holds for all iterations <t<t. Then,

|∇r𝖫𝗈𝗌𝗌L(t)|≤O⁡(1d𝗉)​|∇q𝖫𝗈𝗌𝗌L(t)|.\bigl|\nabla_{r}\mathsf{Loss}^{(t)}_{L}\bigr|\leq O\left(\frac{1}{d_{\mathsf{p}}}\right)\bigl|\nabla_{q}\mathsf{Loss}^{(t)}_{L}\bigr|.

By combining the results above, we obtain the total training time required to reach the target attention level:

Lemma C.9 (End of Training).

For any constant length 2≤L≤𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀​d2\leq L\leq\mathsf{polylog}d, fix any Ω⁡(1𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒𝗅𝗈𝗀​d)<ϵ<min⁡{12​(1−1CB),L−12​L}\Omega(\frac{1}{\mathsf{polylog}d})<\epsilon<\min\{\frac{1}{2}(1-\frac{1}{C_{B}}),\frac{L-1}{2L}\}, the induction hypothesis Induction C.2 holds for all iterations

t<T1=O⁡(d𝗉​d(1−ϵ)​CB−1⋅log⁡(L/ϵ)η​ϵ​log⁡d+L​d𝗉η​log⁡d).t<T_{1}=O\left(d_{\mathsf{p}}d^{(1-\epsilon)C_{B}-1}\cdot\frac{\log(L/\epsilon)}{\eta\epsilon\log d}+\frac{Ld_{\mathsf{p}}}{\eta\log d}\right).
