Appendix D Learning Dynamics of Mixed-difficulty RL

In this section, we study the mixed-difficulty setting, where tasks of different lengths are interleaved. By combining the constant-length analysis in Appendix C with the gradient characterizations from Appendix B, we analyze two regimes of the difficulty ratio RR: (i) the large difficulty ratio regime R=ω⁡(1)R=\omega(1), which gives rise to grokking-style dynamics, and (ii) the moderate difficulty ratio regime R=O⁡(1)R=O(1), which leads to smoother relay dynamics.

We begin by reviewing the mixed-difficulty setup and introducing some timestamps that will be useful for characterizing the overall learning dynamics.

Mixed-difficulty setup.

Let R>1R>1 denote the difficulty ratio, and set the starting (effectively short) horizon to be L1:=CBL_{1}:=C_{B}. Define the horizon set ℒR={L1,L2,…,LK}\mathcal{L}_{R}=\{L_{1},L_{2},\ldots,L_{K}\} recursively by

Lk=min⁡{⌈R​Lk−1⌉,Lmax},2≤k≤K,L_{k}=\min\{\lceil RL_{k-1}\rceil,L_{\max}\},\qquad 2\leq k\leq K,

where K=⌈logR⁡(Lmax/L1)⌉K=\left\lceil\log_{R}(L_{\max}/L_{1})\right\rceil, so that LK=LmaxL_{K}=L_{\max}. For simplicity, we focus on the case R≥2R\geq 2 throughout.

Mastery and visible return states.

For any Li∈ℒRL_{i}\in\mathcal{L}_{R}, we say the horizon LiL_{i} has visible return at time tt if

𝒥Li(t)≥0.01.\mathcal{J}_{L_{i}}^{(t)}\geq 0.01. (56)

Denote the first iteration such that LiL_{i} has visible return as T𝗏𝗂𝗌,iT_{\mathsf{vis},i}. We say the horizon LiL_{i} is mastered at time tt if

𝒥Li(t)≥0.99.\mathcal{J}_{L_{i}}^{(t)}\geq 0.99. (57)

Denote the first iteration such that LiL_{i} is mastered as T𝗆𝖺𝗌,iT_{\mathsf{mas},i}.

Plateau between consecutive horizons.

For k∈{1,…,K−1}k\in\{1,\ldots,K-1\}, define

𝒯k≜T𝗏𝗂𝗌,k+1−T𝗆𝖺𝗌,k=|{t|𝒥Lk(t)≥0.99,𝒥Lk+1(t)<0.01}|.{\mathcal{T}}_{k}\triangleq T_{\mathsf{vis},k+1}-T_{\mathsf{mas},k}=\left|\left\{t\middle|\mathcal{J}_{L_{k}}^{(t)}\geq 0.99,\ \mathcal{J}_{L_{k+1}}^{(t)}<0.01\right\}\right|. (58)

In words, 𝒯k{\mathcal{T}}_{k} counts the number of iterations during which LkL_{k} is already mastered while Lk+1L_{k+1} has not yet achieved a visible return.

D.1 Analysis of Large Difficulty Gap Regime

In this subsection, we analyze the large difficulty ratio regime, where R=ω⁡(1)R=\omega(1). Following the similar proof strategy as in Appendix C, we start with the induction hypothesis that is expected to hold through the training process.

Induction D.1.

Given Ω⁡(1𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒​log⁡d)<ϵ<14\Omega\big(\frac{1}{\mathsf{poly}\log d}\big)<\epsilon<\frac{1}{4}, and let T⋆T^{\star} be the first iteration such that 𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧Lmax(t)≥1−ϵ\mathbf{Attn}_{L_{\max}}^{(t)}\geq 1-\epsilon. Then, for all iterations t<T⋆t<T^{\star}, we have the following holds:

  1. 1.

    0≤q(t)≤O⁡(log⁡Lmaxϵ)0\leq q^{(t)}\leq O\Big(\log\frac{L_{\max}}{\epsilon}\Big), and q(t)q^{(t)} monotonically increases.

  2. 2.

    |r(t)|≤O⁡(1/d𝗉)​q(t)|r^{(t)}|\leq O(1/d_{\mathsf{p}})q^{(t)}.

D.1.1 Properties of the Attention Scores and Critical Thresholds

We record some properties of the attention scores and critical thresholds.

Lemma D.1.

If Induction D.1 holds for all iterations <t<t, then we have

  1. 1.

    𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L(t)=eq(t)−r(t)eq(t)−r(t)+(L−1)≥1L\mathbf{Attn}_{L}^{(t)}=\frac{e^{q^{(t)}-r^{(t)}}}{e^{q^{(t)}-r^{(t)}}+(L-1)}\geq\frac{1}{L};

  2. 2.

    𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧a,ℓ−1→p,k(t)=1(L−1)+eq(t)−r(t)=1L−1​(1−𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L(t))\mathbf{Attn}^{(t)}_{a,\ell-1\to p,k}=\frac{1}{(L-1)+e^{q^{(t)}-r^{(t)}}}=\frac{1}{L-1}\big(1-\mathbf{Attn}_{L}^{(t)}\big) for k≠ℓk\neq\ell.

Lemma D.2 (Critical threshold of qq).

If Induction D.1 holds, then given L∈ℒRL\in\mathcal{L}_{R}, the critical threshold of qq required to satisfy 𝒥L≥1−ξ\mathcal{J}_{L}\geq 1-\xi for some constant 0<ξ≤10<\xi\leq 1 is given by:

q\displaystyle q ≥log⁡L−1CB−1+f⁡(log⁡L−log⁡log⁡11−ξlog⁡d)\displaystyle\geq\log\frac{L-1}{C_{B}-1}+f\Big(\frac{\log L-\log\log\frac{1}{1-\xi}}{\log d}\Big)
≥log⁡L−1CB−1+CBCB−1⋅log⁡L−log⁡log⁡11−ξlog⁡d+𝒪⁡(log2​Llog2​d).\displaystyle\geq\log\frac{L-1}{C_{B}-1}+\frac{C_{B}}{C_{B}-1}\cdot\frac{\log L-\log\log\frac{1}{1-\xi}}{\log d}+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{\log^{2}L}{\log^{2}d}\right).

where f⁡(x)=log⁡(1+x1−x/(CB−1))f(x)=\log\Big(\frac{1+x}{1-x/(C_B-1)}\Big). Similarly, the critical threshold of qq required to satisfy 𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L≥1−ξ\mathbf{Attn}_{L}\geq 1-\xi for any 0<ξ≤10<\xi\leq 1 is given by:

q≥log⁡(1−ξ)​(L−1)ξ.\displaystyle q\geq\log\frac{(1-\xi)(L-1)}{\xi}.
Proof.

Given 𝒥L≥1−ξ\mathcal{J}_{L}\geq 1-\xi, by Lemma B.5, we have

ΔL≥(1−ξ)1/L=1−−log⁡(1−ξ)L.\displaystyle\Delta_{L}\geq(1-\xi)^{1/L}=1-\frac{-\log(1-\xi)}{L}.

Then, by Lemma A.7, we can derive that

𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L≥1CB+log⁡L−log⁡(−log⁡(1−ξ))CB​log⁡d.\mathbf{Attn}_{L}\geq\frac{1}{C_{B}}+\frac{\log L-\log(-\log(1-\xi))}{C_{B}\log d}.

Hence, applying Lemma D.1, we have

q≥log⁡(L−1)+log⁡(𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L1−𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L)≥log⁡L−1CB−1+f⁡(log⁡L−log⁡log⁡11−ξlog⁡d).\displaystyle q\geq\log(L-1)+\log\Big(\frac{\attn_L}{1-\attn_L}\Big)\geq\log\frac{L-1}{C_{B}-1}+f\left(\frac{\log L-\log\log\frac{1}{1-\xi}}{\log d}\right).

Here, we then use the first-order Taylor expansion for f⁡(x)f(x) to get the second inequality. ∎

Notice that in the large difficulty ratio regime, the changes in log⁡L\log L between two consecutive horizons are Ω⁡(log⁡R)≫1\Omega(\log R)\gg 1, which is much larger than the log⁡Llog⁡d≤O⁡(1)\frac{\log L}{\log d}\leq O(1) term. Therefore, the above lemma implies that the change in qq between two consecutive horizons is dominated by Ω⁡(log⁡R)\Omega(\log R).

D.1.2 Warm-up Stage for L1L_{1}

We define the warm-up stage as the period during which the starting horizon L1L_{1} reaches the mastery state, namely 0≤t<T𝗆𝖺𝗌,10\leq t<T_{\mathsf{mas},1}. At initialization, the attention scores are essentially uniform across horizons. We will show that, during this stage, the only non-negligible gradient contribution comes from the effectively short horizon L1L_{1}.

We first record several basic properties of qq, rr, and the attention scores throughout the warm-up stage.

Lemma D.3.

If Induction D.1 holds, then for all iterations 0≤t<T𝗆𝖺𝗌,10\leq t<T_{\mathsf{mas},1}:

  1. 1.

    0≤q(t)≤O⁡(L1log⁡d)0\leq q^{(t)}\leq O\left(\frac{L_{1}}{\log d}\right), and q(t)q^{(t)} is monotonically increasing in tt.

  2. 2.

    |r(t)|≤O⁡(1d𝗉)​q(t)|r^{(t)}|\leq O\left(\frac{1}{d_{\mathsf{p}}}\right)q^{(t)}.

Proof.

The range of q(t)q^{(t)} is a direct consequence of Lemma D.2. The monotonicity of q(t)q^{(t)} and the bound on r(t)r^{(t)} follow directly from Induction D.1. ∎

Lemma D.4.

If Induction D.1 holds, then for all iterations 0≤t<T𝗆𝖺𝗌,10\leq t<T_{\mathsf{mas},1} and for any horizon LiL_{i} with i≥2i\geq 2, we have

𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧𝖺𝗇𝗌,ℓ−1→k(t)≤O⁡(1Li)=o⁡(1),∀ℓ∈[Li],k∈[ℓ].\mathbf{Attn}^{(t)}_{\mathsf{ans},\ell-1\to k}\leq O\left(\frac{1}{L_{i}}\right)=o(1),\qquad\forall\ell\in[L_{i}],k\in[\ell].
Proof.

This follows directly from Lemma D.1. Moreover, since R=ω⁡(1)R=\omega(1) in this regime, we have Li≥ω⁡(1)L_{i}\geq\omega(1) for all i≥2i\geq 2, so the bound is indeed o⁡(1)o(1) as dd grows. ∎

Combining the above with the same reasoning as in Proposition B.4, we can verify that the condition (43) in Proposition B.3 holds for all longer horizons during warm-up, which yields the following.

Lemma D.5.

If Induction D.1 holds, then for all iterations 0≤t<T𝗆𝖺𝗌,10\leq t<T_{\mathsf{mas},1} and for any horizon LiL_{i} with i≥2i\geq 2, we have

|∇q𝒥~Li(t)|≤O~​(1d𝗉)⋅d−Ω⁡(Li),|∇r𝒥~Li(t)|≤O~​(1d𝗉2)⋅d−Ω⁡(Li).\big|\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{i}}^{(t)}\big|\leq\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{1}{d_{\mathsf{p}}}\right)\cdot d^{-\Omega(L_{i})},\qquad\big|\nabla_{r}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{i}}^{(t)}\big|\leq\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{1}{d_{\mathsf{p}}^{2}}\right)\cdot d^{-\Omega(L_{i})}.

Compared with Lemmas C.3 and C.4 in Appendix C, Lemma D.5 shows that during warm-up, the gradients contributed by longer horizons LiL_{i} (for i≥2i\geq 2) are negligible relative to the shortest horizon L1=CBL_{1}=C_{B}. Therefore, we can apply the constant-length analysis from Appendix C to the warm-up stage for L1L_{1}, which yields the following characterization at the end of warm-up.

Lemma D.6.

Induction D.1 holds through 0≤t<T𝗆𝖺𝗌,10\leq t<T_{\mathsf{mas},1} with

T𝗆𝖺𝗌,1=O⁡(K​Lmax​L1η​log2​d),T_{\mathsf{mas},1}=O\left(\frac{KL_{\max}L_{1}}{\eta\log^{2}d}\right),

and at time T𝗆𝖺𝗌,1T_{\mathsf{mas},1} we have q(T𝗆𝖺𝗌,1)≥Ω⁡(log⁡L1log⁡d)q^{(T_{\mathsf{mas},1})}\geq\Omega\left(\frac{\log L_{1}}{\log d}\right).

D.1.3 Transition Between Mastery States

Since we have established that the initial horizon can reach the mastery state, we next analyze how mastery propagates across consecutive horizons. Specifically, we study the transition from horizon ii to horizon i+1i+1 over the time interval [T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i,T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i+1)[T_{\mathsf{mas},i},\,T_{\mathsf{mas},i+1}).

Recall the definition K=⌈logR⁡(Lmax/L1)⌉K=\left\lceil\log_{R}\big(L_{\max}/L_{1}\big)\right\rceil. By construction, the horizons grow by a factor RR up to index K−1K-1, while the last step may be truncated so that LK=LmaxL_{K}=L_{\max}; consequently, LK/LK−1L_{K}/L_{K-1} is not necessarily equal to RR. For notational convenience, we therefore restrict attention to i∈{1,…,K−2}i\in\{1,\ldots,K-2\}, and fix an arbitrary i⋆∈{1,…,K−2}i^{\star}\in\{1,\ldots,K-2\} for the remainder of the analysis. Moreover, we absorb the gradient term ∇q𝒥LK\nabla_{q}\mathcal{J}_{L_{K}} into ∇q𝒥LK−1\nabla_{q}\mathcal{J}_{L_{K-1}}, since for all times prior to T𝗆𝖺𝗌,K−1T_{\mathsf{mas},K-1}, ∇q𝒥LK\nabla_{q}\mathcal{J}_{L_{K}} can be upper bounded by ∇q𝒥LK−1\nabla_{q}\mathcal{J}_{L_{K-1}}.

By the critical threshold of qq in Lemma D.2, we have the following characterization of the attention scores:

Lemma D.7.

If Induction D.1 holds, then for all iterations T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i⋆≤t<T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i⋆+1T_{\mathsf{mas},i^{\star}}\leq t<T_{\mathsf{mas},i^{\star}+1}:

  1. 1.

    if i⋆>1i^{\star}>1, then for any i<i⋆i<i^{\star}, we have

    𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧Li(t)≥1−O⁡(1Ri⋆−i)⋅(1−𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧Li⋆(t))=1−o⁡(1).\displaystyle\mathbf{Attn}_{L_{i}}^{(t)}\geq 1-O\Big(\frac{1}{R^{i^{\star}-i}}\Big)\cdot(1-\mathbf{Attn}_{L_{i^{\star}}}^{(t)})=1-o(1).
  2. 2.

    for i=i⋆i=i^{\star}, we have

    1CB+Ω⁡(log⁡Lilog⁡d)<𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧Li(t)≤1−Ω⁡(1R).\displaystyle\frac{1}{C_{B}}+\Omega\Big(\frac{\log L_{i}}{\log d}\Big)<\mathbf{Attn}_{L_{i}}^{(t)}\leq 1-\Omega\Big(\frac{1}{R}\Big).
  3. 3.

    if i⋆<K−2i^{\star}<K-2, then for any i>i⋆+1i>i^{\star}+1, we have

    𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧Li(t)≤O⁡(1Li).\displaystyle\mathbf{Attn}_{L_{i}}^{(t)}\leq O\left(\frac{1}{L_{i}}\right).

This immediately implies the following characterization of the logits:

Lemma D.8.

If Induction D.1 holds, then for all iterations T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i⋆≤t<T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i⋆+1T_{\mathsf{mas},i^{\star}}\leq t<T_{\mathsf{mas},i^{\star}+1}:

  1. 1.

    if i⋆>1i^{\star}>1, then for any i<i⋆i<i^{\star}, we have (pLi,1(t))Li≥Ω⁡(𝒥Li⋆(t))=Ω⁡(1)(p_{L_{i},1}^{(t)})^{L_{i}}\geq\Omega(\mathcal{J}^{(t)}_{L_{i^{\star}}})=\Omega(1), and also

    Ω⁡(1dCB−1)≤1−pLi,1(t)≤O⁡(1d(1−e−q(t)​R−(i⋆−i)​Li⋆)​CB−1).\displaystyle\Omega\Big(\frac{1}{d^{C_{B}-1}}\Big)\leq 1-p_{L_{i},1}^{(t)}\leq O\Big(\frac{1}{d^{(1-{e^{-q^{(t)}}R^{-(i^{\star}-i)}L_{i^{\star}}})C_{B}-1}}\Big).
  2. 2.

    for i=i⋆i=i^{\star}, we have

    1−pLi,1(t)≥Ω⁡(1d(1−Θ⁡(e−q(t)​Li))​CB−1).\displaystyle 1-p_{L_{i},1}^{(t)}\geq\Omega\Big(\frac{1}{d^{(1-\Theta({e^{-q^{(t)}}L_{i}}))C_{B}-1}}\Big).
  3. 3.

    if i⋆<K−2i^{\star}<K-2, then for any i>i⋆+1i>i^{\star}+1, we have

    pLi,1(t)≤O⁡(1d).\displaystyle p_{L_{i},1}^{(t)}\leq O\left(\frac{1}{d}\right).

The logit conditions imply that for any i<i⋆i<i^{\star}, we can invoke the gradient characterization in Proposition B.2, and for any i>i⋆+1i>i^{\star}+1, we can invoke the gradient characterization in Proposition B.3. Therefore, we have the following characterization of the gradient:

Lemma D.9.

If Induction D.1 holds, then for all iterations T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i⋆≤t<T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i⋆+1T_{\mathsf{mas},i^{\star}}\leq t<T_{\mathsf{mas},i^{\star}+1},

  1. 1.

    if i⋆>1i^{\star}>1, then for any i<i⋆i<i^{\star}, we have

    Ω⁡(1dCB−1)⋅log⁡dd𝗉≤∇q𝒥~Li(t)≤O⁡(1d(1−Li⋆eq(t)​Ri⋆−i)​CB−1)⋅log⁡dd𝗉\displaystyle\Omega\Big(\frac{1}{d^{C_{B}-1}}\Big)\cdot\frac{\log d}{d_{\mathsf{p}}}\leq\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{i}}^{(t)}\leq O\Big(\frac{1}{d^{(1-\frac{L_{i^{\star}}}{e^{q^{(t)}}R^{i^{\star}-i}})C_{B}-1}}\Big)\cdot\frac{\log d}{d_{\mathsf{p}}}
  2. 2.

    for i=i⋆i=i^{\star}, we have

    ∇q𝒥~Li(t)=Ω⁡(1d(1−Θ⁡(e−q(t)​Li))​CB−1)⋅log⁡dd𝗉\displaystyle\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{i}}^{(t)}=\Omega\Big(\frac{1}{d^{(1-\Theta({e^{-q^{(t)}}L_{i}}))C_{B}-1}}\Big)\cdot\frac{\log d}{d_{\mathsf{p}}}
  3. 3.

    if i⋆<K−2i^{\star}<K-2, then for any i>i⋆+1i>i^{\star}+1, we have

    |∇q𝒥~Li(t)|≤O~​(1d𝗉)⋅d−Ω⁡(Li).\displaystyle|\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{i}}^{(t)}|\leq\widetilde{O}\Big(\frac{1}{d_{\mathsf{p}}}\Big)\cdot d^{-\Omega(L_{i})}.

Lemma D.9 immediately implies a gradient lower bound for 𝒥mix,R\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{mix},R} during [T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i⋆,T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i⋆+1)[T_{\mathsf{mas},i^{\star}},T_{\mathsf{mas},i^{\star}+1}):

Lemma D.10.

If Induction D.1 holds, then for all iterations T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i⋆≤t<T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i⋆+1T_{\mathsf{mas},i^{\star}}\leq t<T_{\mathsf{mas},i^{\star}+1}, we have

∇q𝒥~mix,R(t)≥log⁡dK​d𝗉​Ω​(i⋆dCB−1).\displaystyle\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathrm{mix},R}^{(t)}\geq\frac{\log d}{Kd_{\mathsf{p}}}\Omega\Big(\frac{i^{\star}}{d^{C_{B}-1}}\Big).
Proof.

By Lemma D.9, when R≤o⁡(log⁡d)R\leq o(\log d), we have

∇q𝒥~Li⋆(t)/∇q𝒥~Li(t)≤O⁡(d1/R)=O⁡(elog⁡d/R)≫1.\displaystyle\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{i^{\star}}}^{(t)}/\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{i}}^{(t)}\leq O\big(d^{1/R}\big)=O(e^{\log d/R})\gg 1.

Thus ∇q𝒥~Li⋆(t)\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{i^{\star}}}^{(t)} dominates the gradient of short horizons, which leads to the following lower bound:

∇q𝒥~mix,R(t)≥log⁡dK​d𝗉​Ω​(1d(1−1R)​CB−1).\displaystyle\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathrm{mix},R}^{(t)}\geq\frac{\log d}{Kd_{\mathsf{p}}}\Omega\Big(\frac{1}{d^{(1-\frac{1}{R})C_{B}-1}}\Big).

On the other hand, we have

∇q𝒥~mix,R(t)≥1K​∑i=1i⋆∇q𝒥~Li(t)≥Ω⁡(i⋆​log⁡dK​d𝗉​dCB−1).\displaystyle\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathrm{mix},R}^{(t)}\geq\frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=1}^{i^{\star}}\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{i}}^{(t)}\geq\Omega\Big(\frac{i^{\star}\log d}{Kd_{\mathsf{p}}d^{C_{B}-1}}\Big).

Further noting that i⋆≤K−2≤O⁡(log⁡d)i^{\star}\leq K-2\leq O(\log d), thus when R≤o⁡(log⁡d)R\leq o(\log d), we have dCBR≥i⋆d^{\frac{C_{B}}{R}}\geq i^{\star}, which implies that in both cases, we have

∇q𝒥~mix,R(t)≥log⁡dK​d𝗉​Ω​(i⋆dCB−1).\displaystyle\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathrm{mix},R}^{(t)}\geq\frac{\log d}{Kd_{\mathsf{p}}}\Omega\Big(\frac{i^{\star}}{d^{C_{B}-1}}\Big).

∎

So far, we have already controlled the gradient for the horizons before or after the current consecutive mastery state. In the following, we are going to exam ∇q𝒥~Li⋆(t)+∇r𝒥~Li⋆+1(t)\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{i^{\star}}}^{(t)}+\nabla_{r}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{i^{\star}+1}}^{(t)}.

Lemma D.11.

If Induction D.1 holds, then for all iterations T𝗏𝗂𝗌,i⋆+1≤t<T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i⋆+1T_{\mathsf{vis},i^{\star}+1}\leq t<T_{\mathsf{mas},i^{\star}+1}, we have

∇q𝒥~Li⋆(t)+∇q𝒥~Li⋆+1(t)≥Ω⁡(log⁡dLi⋆+1​d𝗉)\displaystyle\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{i^{\star}}}^{(t)}+\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{i^{\star}+1}}^{(t)}\geq\Omega\Big(\frac{\log d}{L_{i^{\star}+1}d_{\mathsf{p}}}\Big)
Proof.

By the critical threshold of qq in Lemma D.2, when t≥T𝗏𝗂𝗌,i⋆+1t\geq T_{\mathsf{vis},i^{\star}+1}, we have pLi⋆+1,1(t)≥1−O⁡(1Li⋆+1)p_{L_{i^{\star}}+1,1}^{(t)}\geq 1-O(\frac{1}{L_{i^{\star}+1}}). Hence, the conditions of Proposition B.2 are satisfied, and invoking it, we then obtain

∇q𝒥~Li⋆+1(t)≥Ω⁡(log⁡dd𝗉)​(1−pLi⋆+1,1(t)).\displaystyle\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{i^{\star}}+1}^{(t)}\geq\Omega\Big(\frac{\log d}{d_{\mathsf{p}}}\Big)(1-p_{L_{i^{\star}}+1,1}^{(t)}).

On the other hand, since t≤T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i⋆+1t\leq T_{\mathsf{mas},i^{\star}+1}, again by Lemma D.2, we have pLi⋆,1(t)≤1−Ω⁡(1Li⋆)p_{L_{i^{\star}},1}^{(t)}\leq 1-\Omega(\frac{1}{L_{i^{\star}}}). Thus, we have

∇q𝒥~Li⋆+1(t)≥Ω⁡(log⁡dLi⋆+1​d𝗉),\displaystyle\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{i^{\star}}+1}^{(t)}\geq\Omega\Big(\frac{\log d}{L_{i^{\star}+1}d_{\mathsf{p}}}\Big),

which completes the proof. ∎

In the following, we are going to show that during the time period [T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i⋆,T𝗏𝗂𝗌,i⋆+1)[T_{\mathsf{mas},i^{\star}},T_{\mathsf{vis},i^{\star}+1}), there exists a major period during which the gradient is dominated by the current mastery state Li⋆L_{i^{\star}}.

Lemma D.12.

If Induction D.1 holds, then during [T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i⋆,T𝗏𝗂𝗌,i⋆+1)[T_{\mathsf{mas},i^{\star}},T_{\mathsf{vis},i^{\star}+1}), when

q(t)∈[Ω⁡(log⁡R0.01​Li⋆),O⁡(log⁡R0.99​Li⋆)]\displaystyle q^{(t)}\in[\Omega(\log R^{0.01}L_{i^{\star}}),\,O(\log R^{0.99}L_{i^{\star}})] (59)

we have

∇q𝒥~Li⋆(t)+∇q𝒥~Li⋆+1(t)=(1+o⁡(1))​∇q𝒥~Li⋆(t).\displaystyle\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{i^{\star}}}^{(t)}+\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{i^{\star}+1}}^{(t)}=(1+o(1))\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{i^{\star}}}^{(t)}.

Moreover,

∇q𝒥~Li⋆(t)=Θ⁡(1d(1−e−q(t)​Li⋆)​CB−1)⋅log⁡dd𝗉.\displaystyle\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{i^{\star}}}^{(t)}=\Theta\Big(\frac{1}{d^{(1-e^{-q^{(t)}}L_{i^{\star}})C_{B}-1}}\Big)\cdot\frac{\log d}{d_{\mathsf{p}}}.
Proof.

By the critical threshold of qq in Lemma D.2,

Ω⁡(log⁡Li⋆)≤q(t)≤O⁡(log⁡R​Li⋆)=O⁡(log⁡Li⋆+1).\Omega(\log L_{i^{\star}})\leq q^{(t)}\leq O(\log RL_{i^{\star}})=O(\log L_{i^{\star}+1}).

So the condition (59) is well-defined. Furthermore, by Lemma D.2, when (59) holds, we have pLi⋆+1,1(t)≤O⁡(1d)p_{L_{i^{\star}}+1,1}^{(t)}\leq O(\frac{1}{d}). Hence applying Proposition B.3, and we have

|∇q𝒥~Li⋆+1(t)|≤O~​(1d𝗉)⋅d−Ω⁡(Li⋆+1).\displaystyle\big|\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{i^{\star}}+1}^{(t)}\big|\leq\widetilde{O}\Big(\frac{1}{d_{\mathsf{p}}}\Big)\cdot d^{-\Omega(L_{i^{\star}+1})}.

Furthermore, (59) combined with Lemma D.2 implies that

1−𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧Li⋆(t)=Θ⁡(e−q(t)​Li⋆).\displaystyle 1-\mathbf{Attn}_{L_{i^{\star}}}^{(t)}=\Theta(e^{-q^{(t)}}L_{i^{\star}}).

Hence,

1−pLi⋆,1(t)=Θ⁡(1d(1−e−q(t)​Li⋆)​CB−1).\displaystyle 1-p_{L_{i^{\star}},1}^{(t)}=\Theta\Big(\frac{1}{d^{(1-e^{-q^{(t)}}L_{i^{\star}})C_{B}-1}}\Big).

Therefore, invoking Proposition B.2, we complete the proof. ∎

Putting everything together, we can then characterize the grokking-style behaviour happening during the transition period [T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i⋆,T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i⋆+1)[T_{\mathsf{mas},i^{\star}},T_{\mathsf{mas},i^{\star}+1}).

Lemma D.13.

Induction D.1 holds through [T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i⋆,T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i⋆+1)[T_{\mathsf{mas},i^{\star}},T_{\mathsf{mas},i^{\star}+1}), where T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i⋆+1=T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i⋆+O⁡(dCB−1​K​d𝗉​log⁡Rη​i⋆​log⁡d)T_{\mathsf{mas},i^{\star}+1}=T_{\mathsf{mas},i^{\star}}+{O}\Big(\frac{d^{C_{B}-1}Kd_{\mathsf{p}}\log R}{\eta i^{\star}\log d}\Big)

  1. 1.

    the reward of JLi⋆+1J_{L_{i^{\star}+1}} saturates below 0.010.01 for a time period of

    𝒯k≥Ω⁡(dCB−1​K​d𝗉i⋆​η​log⁡d)⋅log⁡R1+CB​R−0.01​log⁡d.\displaystyle{\mathcal{T}}_{k}\geq\Omega\Big(\frac{d^{C_{B}-1}Kd_{\mathsf{p}}}{i^{\star}\eta\log d}\Big)\cdot\frac{\log R}{1+C_{B}R^{-0.01}\log d}.
  2. 2.

    T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i⋆+1−T𝗏𝗂𝗌,i⋆+1≤O⁡(Li⋆+1​d𝗉​Kη​log⁡d)T_{\mathsf{mas},i^{\star}+1}-T_{\mathsf{vis},i^{\star}+1}\leq O(\frac{L_{i^{\star}+1}d_{\mathsf{p}}K}{\eta\log d}).

Proof.

The existence of T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i⋆+1=T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i⋆+O⁡(dCB−1​K​d𝗉​log⁡Rη​i⋆​log⁡d)T_{\mathsf{mas},i^{\star}+1}=T_{\mathsf{mas},i^{\star}}+{O}\Big(\frac{d^{C_{B}-1}Kd_{\mathsf{p}}\log R}{\eta i^{\star}\log d}\Big) is guaranteed by the gradient lower bound in Lemma D.10. Moreover, the second item is guaranteed by the gradient lower bound in Lemma D.11. Then we focus on the first statement. We approximate the total number of iterations 𝒯i⋆{\mathcal{T}}_{i^{\star}} by the integral

𝒯i⋆≳∫Ω⁡(log⁡R0.01​Li⋆)O⁡(log⁡R0.99​Li⋆)d​qη​∇q​𝒥~mix,R.\displaystyle{\mathcal{T}}_{i^{\star}}\gtrsim\int_{\Omega(\log R^{0.01}L_{i^{\star}})}^{O(\log R^{0.99}L_{i^{\star}})}\frac{dq}{\eta\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathrm{mix},R}}.

By Lemma D.12, we can have a naive upper bound on the gradient:

∇q𝒥~mix,R≤i⋆K⋅∇q𝒥~Li⋆(t)≤O⁡(i⋆​log⁡dK​d𝗉)⋅1d(1−e−q(t)​Li⋆)​CB−1.\displaystyle\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{\mathrm{mix},R}\leq\frac{i^{\star}}{K}\cdot\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{i^{\star}}}^{(t)}\leq O\Big(\frac{i^{\star}\log d}{Kd_{\mathsf{p}}}\Big)\cdot\frac{1}{d^{(1-e^{-q^{(t)}}L_{i^{\star}})C_{B}-1}}.

Plugging this into the integral, we have

𝒯i⋆\displaystyle{\mathcal{T}}_{i^{\star}} ≥Ω⁡(dCB−1​K​d𝗉i⋆​η​log⁡d)​∫log⁡R0.01log⁡R0.99d−CB​e−q​𝑑q=Ω⁡(dCB−1​K​d𝗉i⋆​η​log⁡d)​∫R−0.99R−0.01e−(CB​log⁡d)​uu​𝑑u\displaystyle\geq\Omega\Big(\frac{d^{C_{B}-1}Kd_{\mathsf{p}}}{i^{\star}\eta\log d}\Big)\int_{\log R^{0.01}}^{\log R^{0.99}}d^{-C_{B}e^{-q}}dq=\Omega\Big(\frac{d^{C_{B}-1}Kd_{\mathsf{p}}}{i^{\star}\eta\log d}\Big)\int_{R^{-0.99}}^{R^{-0.01}}\frac{e^{-(C_{B}\log d)u}}{u}du
≥Ω(dCB−1​K​d𝗉i⋆​η​log⁡d)⋅e−(CB​R−0.01​log⁡d)∫R−0.99R−0.011udu\displaystyle\geq\Omega\Big(\frac{d^{C_{B}-1}Kd_{\mathsf{p}}}{i^{\star}\eta\log d}\Big)\cdot e^{-(C_{B}R^{-0.01}\log d)}\int_{R^{-0.99}}^{R^{-0.01}}\frac{1}{u}du
≥Ω⁡(dCB−1​K​d𝗉i⋆​η​log⁡d)⋅e−(CB​R−0.01​log⁡d)⋅log⁡R\displaystyle\geq\Omega\Big(\frac{d^{C_{B}-1}Kd_{\mathsf{p}}}{i^{\star}\eta\log d}\Big)\cdot e^{-(C_{B}R^{-0.01}\log d)}\cdot\log R
≥Ω⁡(dCB−1​K​d𝗉i⋆​η​log⁡d)⋅log⁡R1+CB​R−0.01​log⁡d,\displaystyle\geq\Omega\Big(\frac{d^{C_{B}-1}Kd_{\mathsf{p}}}{i^{\star}\eta\log d}\Big)\cdot\frac{\log R}{1+C_{B}R^{-0.01}\log d},

where we use the Taylor expansion for the last inequality. ∎

D.1.4 Proof of Theorem 5.1 and Corollary 5.1

Proof.

For any k∈{1,…,K−2}k\in\{1,\ldots,K-2\}, Lemma D.13 implies

𝒯k\displaystyle{\mathcal{T}}_{k} ≥Ω⁡(dCB−1​K​d𝗉k​η​log⁡d)⋅log⁡R1+CB​R−0.01​log⁡d\displaystyle\geq\Omega\Big(\frac{d^{C_{B}-1}\,K\,d_{\mathsf{p}}}{k\,\eta\log d}\Big)\cdot\frac{\log R}{1+C_{B}R^{-0.01}\log d}
≥Ω~​(dCB−1​d𝗉η​log⁡d),\displaystyle\geq\widetilde{\Omega}\Big(\frac{d^{C_{B}-1}\,d_{\mathsf{p}}}{\eta\log d}\Big),

where the last inequality uses log⁡R1+CB​R−0.01​log⁡d=Ω⁡(1/log⁡d)\frac{\log R}{1+C_{B}R^{-0.01}\log d}=\Omega(1/\log d) and K/k=Ω~​(1)K/k=\widetilde{\Omega}(1).

Moreover,

T𝗆𝖺𝗌,k+1−T𝗏𝗂𝗌,k+1≤O⁡(Lk+1​d𝗉​Kη​log⁡d)≤O⁡(d𝗉2​Kη​log⁡d)≪𝒯k,T_{\mathsf{mas},k+1}-T_{\mathsf{vis},k+1}\leq O\Big(\frac{L_{k+1}\,d_{\mathsf{p}}\,K}{\eta\log d}\Big)\leq O\Big(\frac{d_{\mathsf{p}}^{2}\,K}{\eta\log d}\Big)\ll{\mathcal{T}}_{k},

since d𝗉=dcxd_{\mathsf{p}}=d^{c_{x}} and cx<CB−1c_{x}<C_{B}-1. Therefore,

T𝗆𝖺𝗌,k+1−T𝗆𝖺𝗌,k≥Ω~​(dCB−1​d𝗉η​log⁡d).\displaystyle T_{\mathsf{mas},k+1}-T_{\mathsf{mas},k}\geq\widetilde{\Omega}\Big(\frac{d^{C_{B}-1}\,d_{\mathsf{p}}}{\eta\log d}\Big).

On the other hand, Lemma D.13 also gives the matching upper bound

T𝗆𝖺𝗌,k+1−T𝗆𝖺𝗌,k≤O~​(dCB−1​d𝗉η​log⁡d).\displaystyle T_{\mathsf{mas},k+1}-T_{\mathsf{mas},k}\leq\widetilde{O}\Big(\frac{d^{C_{B}-1}\,d_{\mathsf{p}}}{\eta\log d}\Big).

Summing over k∈{1,…,K−2}k\in\{1,\ldots,K-2\}, we obtain

T𝗆𝖺𝗌,K−1−T𝗆𝖺𝗌,1=Θ~​(dCB−1​d𝗉η​log⁡d).\displaystyle T_{\mathsf{mas},K-1}-T_{\mathsf{mas},1}=\widetilde{\Theta}\Big(\frac{d^{C_{B}-1}\,d_{\mathsf{p}}}{\eta\log d}\Big).

Finally, by Lemma D.6, the time spent in the warm-up stage is negligible compared to T𝗆𝖺𝗌,K−1−T𝗆𝖺𝗌,1T_{\mathsf{mas},K-1}-T_{\mathsf{mas},1}. Moreover, the final step can be bounded as

T𝗆𝖺𝗌,K−T𝗆𝖺𝗌,K−1≤O⁡(T𝗆𝖺𝗌,K−1−T𝗆𝖺𝗌,K−2).T_{\mathsf{mas},K}-T_{\mathsf{mas},K-1}\leq O\big(T_{\mathsf{mas},K-1}-T_{\mathsf{mas},K-2}\big).

This completes the proof. ∎

D.2 Analysis of Moderate Difficulty Ratio Regime

In this subsection, we analyze the moderate difficulty ratio regime, where 2≤R=O⁡(1)2\leq R=O(1). Our overall proof strategy follows that of the large difficulty ratio regime, with several adjustments to account for the smaller gap between two consecutive scales.

We begin by stating the induction hypothesis, which we expect to remain valid throughout training.

Induction D.2.

Given Ω⁡(1𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗒​log⁡d)<ϵ<14\Omega\big(\frac{1}{\mathsf{poly}\log d}\big)<\epsilon<\frac{1}{4}, and let T⋆T^{\star} be the first iteration such that 𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧Lmax(t)≥1−ϵ\mathbf{Attn}_{L_{\max}}^{(t)}\geq 1-\epsilon. Then, for all iterations t<T⋆t<T^{\star}, we have the following holds:

  1. 1.

    0≤q(t)≤O⁡(log⁡Lmaxϵ)0\leq q^{(t)}\leq O\Big(\log\frac{L_{\max}}{\epsilon}\Big), and q(t)q^{(t)} monotonically increases.

  2. 2.

    |r(t)|≤O⁡(1/d𝗉)​q(t)|r^{(t)}|\leq O(1/d_{\mathsf{p}})q^{(t)}.

D.2.1 Properties of the Attention Scores and Critical Thresholds

We record several basic properties of the attention scores and the critical thresholds.

Lemma D.14.

If Induction D.2 holds for all iterations <t<t, then:

  1. 1.
    𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L(t)=eq(t)−r(t)eq(t)−r(t)+(L−1)≥1L;\mathbf{Attn}_{L}^{(t)}=\frac{e^{q^{(t)}-r^{(t)}}}{e^{q^{(t)}-r^{(t)}}+(L-1)}\ \geq\ \frac{1}{L};
  2. 2.

    for any k≠ℓk\neq\ell,

    𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧a,ℓ−1→p,k(t)=1(L−1)+eq(t)−r(t)=1L−1​(1−𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L(t)).\mathbf{Attn}^{(t)}_{a,\ell-1\to p,k}=\frac{1}{(L-1)+e^{q^{(t)}-r^{(t)}}}=\frac{1}{L-1}\big(1-\mathbf{Attn}_{L}^{(t)}\big).
Lemma D.15 (Critical threshold of qq).

If Induction D.1 holds, then for any L∈ℒRL\in\mathcal{L}_{R}, a sufficient threshold on qq for 𝒥L≥1−ξ\mathcal{J}_{L}\geq 1-\xi, where 0<ξ≤10<\xi\leq 1 is a constant, is

q≥log⁡L−1CB−1+f⁡(log⁡L−log⁡log⁡11−ξlog⁡d),\displaystyle q\ \geq\ \log\frac{L-1}{C_{B}-1}+f\Big(\frac{\log L-\log\log\frac{1}{1-\xi}}{\log d}\Big),

where f⁡(x)=log⁡(1+x1−x/(CB−1))f(x)=\log\Big(\frac{1+x}{1-x/(C_B-1)}\Big). Similarly, a sufficient threshold on qq for 𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧L≥1−ξ\mathbf{Attn}_{L}\geq 1-\xi is

q≥log⁡(1−ξ)​(L−1)ξ.q\ \geq\ \log\frac{(1-\xi)(L-1)}{\xi}.

The above lemmas mirror their counterparts in the large-difficulty regime. However, to track the variation of the critical threshold when LL increases only by a constant factor RR, we need a more careful comparison than the coarse Taylor-expansion argument used for widely separated scales.

Lemma D.16.

If Induction D.2 holds and 0<ξ≤10<\xi\leq 1 is a constant, let qξ​(L)q_{\xi}(L) denote the critical threshold of qq required to ensure 𝒥L,1≥1−ξ\mathcal{J}_{L,1}\geq 1-\xi. Then for any Lk,Lk+1∈ℒRL_{k},L_{k+1}\in\mathcal{L}_{R},

qξ​(Lk+1)−qξ​(Lk)=log⁡R⋅(1+O⁡(1/log⁡d)).q_{\xi}(L_{k+1})-q_{\xi}(L_{k})=\log R\cdot\Big(1+O(1/\log d)\Big).
Proof.

By Lemma D.15, we have

d​qξ​(L)d​L=1L​[1+1log⁡d⋅CB(1+X⁡(L))​(CB−1−X⁡(L))],\frac{dq_{\xi}(L)}{dL}=\frac{1}{L}\left[1+\frac{1}{\log d}\cdot\frac{C_{B}}{(1+X(L))(C_{B}-1-X(L))}\right],

where X⁡(L)=log⁡L−log⁡log⁡11−ξlog⁡dX(L)=\frac{\log L-\log\log\frac{1}{1-\xi}}{\log d}. Since 0≤X⁡(L)≤1+O⁡(1/log⁡d)0\leq X(L)\leq 1+O(1/\log d), it follows that d​qξ​(L)d​L=1L​(1+O⁡(1/log⁡d))\frac{dq_{\xi}(L)}{dL}=\frac{1}{L}\big(1+O(1/\log d)\big). Therefore,

qξ​(Lk+1)−qξ​(Lk)\displaystyle q_{\xi}(L_{k+1})-q_{\xi}(L_{k}) =∫LkLk+11L​(1+O⁡(1/log⁡d))​𝑑L\displaystyle=\int_{L_{k}}^{L_{k+1}}\frac{1}{L}\big(1+O(1/\log d)\big)\,dL
=log⁡R⋅(1+O⁡(1/log⁡d)).\displaystyle=\log R\cdot\Big(1+O(1/\log d)\Big).

∎

D.2.2 Warm-up Stage for L1L_{1}

We define the warm-up stage as the period during which the starting horizon L1L_{1} reaches the mastery state, namely 0≤t<T𝗆𝖺𝗌,10\leq t<T_{\mathsf{mas},1}. The analysis is similar to the large difficulty ratio regime, but with some modifications since LiL_{i} with i≥2i\geq 2 could be relatively small and still at the constant-length regime.

Lemma D.17.

If Induction D.2 holds, then for all iterations 0≤t<T𝗆𝖺𝗌,10\leq t<T_{\mathsf{mas},1}:

  1. 1.

    0≤q(t)≤O⁡(L1log⁡d)0\leq q^{(t)}\leq O\left(\frac{L_{1}}{\log d}\right), and q(t)q^{(t)} is monotonically increasing in tt.

  2. 2.

    |r(t)|≤O⁡(1d𝗉)​q(t)|r^{(t)}|\leq O\left(\frac{1}{d_{\mathsf{p}}}\right)q^{(t)}.

Lemma D.18.

If Induction D.2 holds, then for all iterations 0≤t<T𝗆𝖺𝗌,10\leq t<T_{\mathsf{mas},1}, and for any Li∈ℒRL_{i}\in\mathcal{L}_{R} with i≥2i\geq 2, we have

  1. 1.

    if Li=O⁡(1)L_{i}=O(1), then 1−CB​𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧Li(t)≥1−10.99​Ri−1+11-C_{B}\mathbf{Attn}^{(t)}_{L_{i}}\geq 1-\frac{1}{0.99R^{i-1}+1};

  2. 2.

    else, 𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧Li(t)≤O⁡(1Li)=o⁡(1)\mathbf{Attn}^{(t)}_{L_{i}}\leq O\left(\frac{1}{L_{i}}\right)=o(1).

Proof.

The second item is similar to the large difficulty ratio regime. For the first item, by Lemma D.17, we have

𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧Li(t)≤1(Li−1)⋅e−O⁡(L1/log⁡d)+1=1Ri−1​CB⋅e−O⁡(L1/log⁡d)+1.\displaystyle\mathbf{Attn}^{(t)}_{L_{i}}\leq\frac{1}{(L_{i}-1)\cdot e^{-O(L_{1}/\log d)}+1}=\frac{1}{R^{i-1}C_{B}\cdot e^{-O(L_{1}/\log d)}+1}.

Hence,

1−CB​𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧Li(t)≥1−10.99​Ri−1+1.\displaystyle 1-C_{B}\mathbf{Attn}^{(t)}_{L_{i}}\geq 1-\frac{1}{0.99R^{i-1}+1}.

∎

Similarly as Lemma D.5, the condition (43) in Proposition B.3 holds for Li=ω⁡(1)L_{i}=\omega(1), which yields the following.

Lemma D.19.

If Induction D.2 holds, then for all iterations 0≤t<T𝗆𝖺𝗌,10\leq t<T_{\mathsf{mas},1} and for any horizon Li=ω⁡(1)L_{i}=\omega(1), we have

|∇q𝒥~Li(t)|≤O~​(1d𝗉)⋅d−Ω⁡(Li),|∇r𝒥~Li(t)|≤O~​(1d𝗉2)⋅d−Ω⁡(Li).\big|\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{i}}^{(t)}\big|\leq\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{1}{d_{\mathsf{p}}}\right)\cdot d^{-\Omega(L_{i})},\qquad\big|\nabla_{r}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{i}}^{(t)}\big|\leq\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{1}{d_{\mathsf{p}}^{2}}\right)\cdot d^{-\Omega(L_{i})}.

Lemma D.18 shows that even some longer horizons LiL_{i} are still at the constant-length regime, its target attention scores are still below 1CB\frac{1}{C_{B}}, which means pLi,1(t)≤d−Ω⁡(1)p^{(t)}_{L_{i},1}\leq d^{-\Omega(1)} is still close to 00. However, directly applying Proposition B.3 to Li=O⁡(1)L_{i}=O(1) only gives a bound of d−Ω⁡(Li)d^{-\Omega(L_{i})}, which may be too loose in the constant-length regime. Thus we use a variant of Proposition B.3 and precise characterization of 1−CB​𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧Li(t)1-C_{B}\mathbf{Attn}^{(t)}_{L_{i}} to get a more precise bound.

Lemma D.20.

If Induction D.2 holds, then for all iterations 0≤t<T𝗆𝖺𝗌,10\leq t<T_{\mathsf{mas},1} and for any horizon Li=O⁡(1)L_{i}=O(1) with i≥2i\geq 2, we have

|∇q𝒥~Li(t)|≤O~​(1d𝗉)⋅d−Li​(1−10.99​Ri−1+1),|∇r𝒥~Li(t)|≤O~​(1d𝗉2)⋅d−Li​(1−10.99​Ri−1+1).\big|\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{i}}^{(t)}\big|\leq\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{1}{d_{\mathsf{p}}}\right)\cdot d^{-L_{i}(1-\frac{1}{0.99R^{i-1}+1})},\qquad\big|\nabla_{r}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{i}}^{(t)}\big|\leq\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{1}{d_{\mathsf{p}}^{2}}\right)\cdot d^{-L_{i}(1-\frac{1}{0.99R^{i-1}+1})}.

Since Li≥Ri−1​CBL_{i}\geq R^{i-1}C_{B}, we have Li​(1−10.99​Ri−1+1)≥CB+Ω⁡(1)L_{i}(1-\frac{1}{0.99R^{i-1}+1})\geq C_{B}+\Omega(1). Compared with Lemma C.3 in Appendix C, Lemma D.19 and Lemma D.20 show that during warm-up the gradients contributed by longer horizons LiL_{i} (for i≥2i\geq 2) are negligible relative to the shortest horizon L1=CBL_{1}=C_{B}. Therefore, we can apply the constant-length analysis from Appendix C to the warm-up stage for L1L_{1}, which yields the following characterization at the end of warm-up.

Lemma D.21.

Induction D.2 holds through 0≤t<T𝗆𝖺𝗌,10\leq t<T_{\mathsf{mas},1} with

T𝗆𝖺𝗌,1=O⁡(K​Lmax​L1η​log2​d),T_{\mathsf{mas},1}=O\left(\frac{KL_{\max}L_{1}}{\eta\log^{2}d}\right),

and at time T𝗆𝖺𝗌,1T_{\mathsf{mas},1} we have q(T𝗆𝖺𝗌,1)≥Ω⁡(log⁡L1log⁡d)q^{(T_{\mathsf{mas},1})}\geq\Omega\left(\frac{\log L_{1}}{\log d}\right).

D.2.3 Transition between mastery states

In this part, we analyze the transition of the mastery state across consecutive horizons. Concretely, we focus on the time interval [T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i,T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i+1)[T_{\mathsf{mas},i},\,T_{\mathsf{mas},i+1}) for i∈{1,…,K−2}i\in\{1,\dots,K-2\}. As before, we fix an arbitrary i⋆∈{1,…,K−2}i^{\star}\in\{1,\dots,K-2\} for the remainder of the analysis (The restriction i≤K−2i\leq K-2 excludes the final truncated step where LK/LK−1L_{K}/L_{K-1} is not necessarily RR.)

By the critical threshold of qq in Lemma D.15, we have the following characterization of the attention scores:

Lemma D.22.

If Induction D.2 holds, then for all iterations T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i⋆≤t<T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i⋆+1T_{\mathsf{mas},i^{\star}}\leq t<T_{\mathsf{mas},i^{\star}+1}:

    if i⋆>1i^{\star}>1, then for any i<i⋆i<i^{\star}, we have

    𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧Li(t)−𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧Li⋆(t)≥Ω⁡(1).\displaystyle\mathbf{Attn}_{L_{i}}^{(t)}-\mathbf{Attn}_{L_{i^{\star}}}^{(t)}\geq\Omega(1).
  2. 2.

    for i=i⋆i=i^{\star}, we have

    1CB+Ω⁡(log⁡Lilog⁡d)<𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧Li(t)≤1−Ω⁡(1).\displaystyle\frac{1}{C_{B}}+\Omega\Big(\frac{\log L_{i}}{\log d}\Big)<\mathbf{Attn}_{L_{i}}^{(t)}\leq 1-\Omega(1).
  3. 3.

    if i=i⋆+1i=i^{\star}+1, we have

    1R​CB≤𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧Li(t)≤1CB+O⁡(log⁡Lilog⁡d).\displaystyle\frac{1}{RC_{B}}\leq\mathbf{Attn}_{L_{i}}^{(t)}\leq\frac{1}{C_{B}}+O\Big(\frac{\log L_{i}}{\log d}\Big).
  4. 4.

    if i⋆<K−2i^{\star}<K-2, then for any i>i⋆+1i>i^{\star}+1, we have

    • •

      if Li=O⁡(1)L_{i}=O(1), then 1−CB​𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧Li(t)≥1−10.99​Ri−i⋆−1+11-C_{B}\mathbf{Attn}^{(t)}_{L_{i}}\geq 1-\frac{1}{0.99R^{i-i^{\star}-1}+1};

    • •

      else, 𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧Li(t)≤O⁡(1Li)=o⁡(1)\mathbf{Attn}^{(t)}_{L_{i}}\leq O\left(\frac{1}{L_{i}}\right)=o(1).

This immediately implies the following characterization of the logits:

Lemma D.23.

If Induction D.2 holds, then for all iterations T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i⋆≤t<T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i⋆+1T_{\mathsf{mas},i^{\star}}\leq t<T_{\mathsf{mas},i^{\star}+1}:

  1. 1.

    if i⋆>1i^{\star}>1, then for any i<i⋆i<i^{\star}, we have (pLi,1(t))Li≥Ω⁡(𝒥Li⋆(t))=Ω⁡(1)(p_{L_{i},1}^{(t)})^{L_{i}}\geq\Omega(\mathcal{J}^{(t)}_{L_{i^{\star}}})=\Omega(1), and also

    1−pLi,1(t)≤d−Ω⁡(1)​(1−pLi⋆,1(t)).\displaystyle 1-p_{L_{i},1}^{(t)}\leq d^{-\Omega(1)}\Big(1-p_{L_{i^{\star}},1}^{(t)}\Big).
  2. 2.

    for i=i⋆i=i^{\star}, we have

    1−pLi,1(t)=Θ⁡(d−(1−1eq(t)/(Li−1)+1)​CB+1)≥Ω⁡(d−(1−Ω⁡(1))​CB+1).\displaystyle 1-p_{L_{i},1}^{(t)}=\Theta\Big({d^{-\big(1-\frac{1}{e^{q^{(t)}}/(L_{i}-1)+1}\big)C_{B}+1}}\Big)\geq\Omega(d^{-(1-\Omega(1))C_{B}+1}).

    if i=i⋆+1i=i^{\star}+1, we have

The logit conditions also guarantee that for any i≤i⋆+1i\leq i^{\star}+1, we can invoke the gradient characterization in Proposition B.2, and for any i>i⋆+1i>i^{\star}+1, we can invoke the gradient characterization in Proposition B.3 and the variant in Lemma D.20. Therefore, we have the following characterization of the gradient:

Lemma D.24.

If Induction D.1 holds, then for all iterations T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i⋆≤t<T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i⋆+1T_{\mathsf{mas},i^{\star}}\leq t<T_{\mathsf{mas},i^{\star}+1},

    if i⋆<K−2i^{\star}<K-2, then for any i>i⋆+1i>i^{\star}+1, we have

Thus, to control the gradient of 𝒥mix,R\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{mix},R} during [T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i⋆,T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i⋆+1)[T_{\mathsf{mas},i^{\star}},T_{\mathsf{mas},i^{\star}+1}), we only need to focus on the gradient of Li⋆L_{i^{\star}} and Li⋆+1L_{i^{\star}+1}. Similar to Lemma D.11, we have the following lower bound for the period that the reward of Li⋆+1L_{i^{\star}+1} becomes visible.

Lemma D.25.

If Induction D.2 holds, then for all iterations T𝗏𝗂𝗌,i⋆+1≤t<T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i⋆+1T_{\mathsf{vis},i^{\star}+1}\leq t<T_{\mathsf{mas},i^{\star}+1}, we have

∇q𝒥~Li⋆(t)+∇q𝒥~Li⋆+1(t)≥Ω⁡(log⁡dLi⋆+1​d𝗉).\displaystyle\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{i^{\star}}}^{(t)}+\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{i^{\star}+1}}^{(t)}\geq\Omega\Big(\frac{\log d}{L_{i^{\star}+1}d_{\mathsf{p}}}\Big).

Now we turn to the period [T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i⋆,T𝗏𝗂𝗌,i⋆+1)[T_{\mathsf{mas},i^{\star}},T_{\mathsf{vis},i^{\star}+1}). The main difference from the large difficulty ratio regime is that in this stage, Li⋆L_{i^{\star}} and Li⋆+1L_{i^{\star}+1} will jointly decide a gradient lower bound for 𝒥mix,R\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{mix},R}, which is significantly larger than the one in the long-plateau stage in the large difficulty ratio regime.

Lemma D.26.

If Induction D.2 holds, then during [T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i⋆,T𝗏𝗂𝗌,i⋆+1)[T_{\mathsf{mas},i^{\star}},T_{\mathsf{vis},i^{\star}+1}), we have

∇q𝒥~Li⋆(t)+∇q𝒥~Li⋆+1(t)≥Ω⁡(d−R​CBR+CB+1)⋅log⁡dd𝗉.\displaystyle\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{i^{\star}}}^{(t)}+\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{i^{\star}+1}}^{(t)}\geq\Omega\Big({d^{-\frac{RC_{B}}{R+C_{B}}+1}}\Big)\cdot\frac{\log d}{d_{\mathsf{p}}}.
Proof.

Notice that during [T𝗆𝖺𝗌,i⋆,T𝗏𝗂𝗌,i⋆+1)[T_{\mathsf{mas},i^{\star}},T_{\mathsf{vis},i^{\star}+1}), by Lemma D.24, ∇q𝒥~Li⋆(t)\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{i^{\star}}}^{(t)} is dominated by the term 1−pLi⋆,1(t)1-p_{L_{i^{\star}},1}^{(t)}. On the other hand, for Li⋆+1L_{i^{\star}+1}, by Lemma D.22 and Lemma D.24, we have ∇q𝒥~Li⋆+1(t)\nabla_{q}\widetilde{\mathcal{J}}_{L_{i^{\star}}+1}^{(t)} firstly dominated by the term (pLi⋆+1,1(t))Li⋆+1(p_{L_{i^{\star}+1},1}^{(t)})^{L_{i^{\star}+1}}, which will increase as qq increases, and then by the term (1−pLi⋆+1,1(t))(1-p_{L_{i^{\star}+1},1}^{(t)}) when (pLi⋆+1,1(t))Li⋆+1(p_{L_{i^{\star}+1},1}^{(t)})^{L_{i^{\star}+1}} reaches the constant level, and (1−pLi⋆+1,1(t))(1-p_{L_{i^{\star}+1},1}^{(t)}) is lower bounded by Ω⁡(1/Li⋆+1)\Omega(1/L_{i^{\star}+1}). Therefore, to lower bound the gradient summation, we only need to find the time tt when (pLi⋆+1,1(t))Li⋆+1(p_{L_{i^{\star}+1},1}^{(t)})^{L_{i^{\star}+1}} reaches the same level as 1−pLi⋆,1(t)1-p_{L_{i^{\star}},1}^{(t)}. Thus, consider

CB⋅𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧Li⋆−1=Li⋆+1​(1−CB⋅𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐧Li⋆+1),C_{B}\cdot\mathbf{Attn}_{L_{i^{\star}}}-1=L_{i^{\star}+1}(1-C_{B}\cdot\mathbf{Attn}_{L_{i^{\star}+1}}),

which can be rewritten as

CB​eqeq+Li⋆−1−1=Li⋆+1​(1−CB​eqeq+Li⋆+1−1)\displaystyle C_{B}\frac{e^{q}}{e^{q}+L_{i^{\star}}-1}-1=L_{i^{\star}+1}\left(1-C_{B}\frac{e^{q}}{e^{q}+L_{i^{\star}+1}-1}\right) (60)

which is a quadratic equation in eqe^{q}. D.2.4 Proof of Theorem 5.2 and Corollary 5.2

Proof.

Theorem 5.2 follows immediately from Lemmas D.25 and D.27 together with the bound K=O⁡(log⁡d)K=O(\log d).

For Corollary 5.2, we apply Lemma D.27 iteratively for K−2K-2 transitions (from horizon 11 up to horizon K−1K-1):

T𝗆𝖺𝗌,K−1−T𝗆𝖺𝗌,1\displaystyle T_{\mathsf{mas},K-1}-T_{\mathsf{mas},1} ≤O⁡(dR​CBR+CB−1​K​d𝗉η​log⁡d)⋅(K−2)​log⁡R+O⁡(d𝗉​Kη​log⁡d)⋅L1​(RK−1−1R−1)\displaystyle\leq O\Big(\frac{d^{\frac{RC_{B}}{R+C_{B}}-1}\,K\,d_{\mathsf{p}}}{\eta\log d}\Big)\cdot(K-2)\log R\;+\;O\Big(\frac{d_{\mathsf{p}}K}{\eta\log d}\Big)\cdot L_{1}\Big(\frac{R^{K-1}-1}{R-1}\Big)
≤O~​(d𝗉η)⋅dR​CBR+CB−1+O~​(d𝗉η)⋅Lmax,\displaystyle\leq\widetilde{O}\Big(\frac{d_{\mathsf{p}}}{\eta}\Big)\cdot d^{\frac{RC_{B}}{R+C_{B}}-1}\;+\;\widetilde{O}\Big(\frac{d_{\mathsf{p}}}{\eta}\Big)\cdot L_{\max},

where the last inequality uses K=O⁡(log⁡d)K=O(\log d) and RK−1=O⁡(Lmax)R^{K-1}=O(L_{\max}). Combining this with the condition Lmax=O⁡(dcx)L_{\max}=O(d^{c_{x}}) and cx<2​CB2+CB≤R​CBR+CBc_{x}<\frac{2C_{B}}{2+C_{B}}\leq\frac{RC_{B}}{R+C_{B}}, we obtain

T𝗆𝖺𝗌,K−1−T𝗆𝖺𝗌,1≤O~​(d𝗉η)⋅dR​CBR+CB−1.\displaystyle T_{\mathsf{mas},K-1}-T_{\mathsf{mas},1}\leq\widetilde{O}\Big(\frac{d_{\mathsf{p}}}{\eta}\Big)\cdot d^{\frac{RC_{B}}{R+C_{B}}-1}.

Finally, by Lemma D.21, the time spent in the warm-up stage is negligible compared to T𝗆𝖺𝗌,K−1−T𝗆𝖺𝗌,1T_{\mathsf{mas},K-1}-T_{\mathsf{mas},1}. Moreover, we can bound the final step by T𝗆𝖺𝗌,K−T𝗆𝖺𝗌,K−1≤O⁡(T𝗆𝖺𝗌,K−1−T𝗆𝖺𝗌,K−2)T_{\mathsf{mas},K}-T_{\mathsf{mas},K-1}\leq O\big(T_{\mathsf{mas},K-1}-T_{\mathsf{mas},K-2}\big). This completes the proof. ∎
